talks.speaker: Dr Caroline Turnage-Butterbaugh
talks.title: Zeros of the Riemann zeta-function on the critical line
talks.abstract:
The Riemann Hypothesis (RH) asserts that the complex zeros of the Riemann zeta-function lie on a vertical line known as the critical line. Riemann proposed RH in his groundbreaking 1859 paper, which laid the foundation towards the eventual proof of the Prime Number Theorem. Evidence in favor of RH comes in many forms, including zero-free regions (areas of the complex plane devoid of zeros) and zero-density estimates, which bound the number of zeros which lie more than a fixed distance from the critical line. Recently, significant progress has been made in proving another type of evidence in favor of RH: lower bounds on the proportion of zeros lying on the critical line. 

These new advances use a method constructed by Montgomery in 1973 to study the vertical distribution of the zeros under the assumption of RH. In particular, Montgomery proved that, under RH, at least 2/3 of the zeros of the Riemann zeta-function are simple. In recent joint work with Baluyot, Goldston, and Suriajaya, we showed how to remove RH from Montgomery’s theorem, and, upon assuming a much weaker hypothesis than RH, proved that at least 67.25% of the zeros are simple and on the critical line. In August 2026, an unreleased research model of Claude rendered the argument unconditional, and September 2026 Lamzouri provided a new, simplified proof of the unconditional result.

This broadly accessible talk explores the rich landscape of these recent, exciting developments.

talks.speaker: Dr Chad Topaz
talks.title: Data Science, Social Justice, and the Criminal Legal System
talks.abstract: I spent the first part of my career modelling pattern formation in fluids, chemical systems, and biological swarms. Then I changed course: similar mathematical habits of mind, new questions about justice. In this talk I examine parts of the criminal legal system of the United States and show what quantitative approaches can reveal about them. We will see how data document, at the scale of entire systems, racial inequities that individuals and communities experience one case at a time We will also confront the special care demanded when data are produced by the very institutions under scrutiny. Dr Yunupingu envisioned education holding Indigenous and Western knowledges together, with mathematics as a meeting point. In that spirit, I will argue that communities’ lived knowledge of injustice and the mathematical sciences complement one another in the pursuit of justice. This talk is broadly accessible, with no specific technical background assumed.

talks.speaker: Dr Neena Gupta
talks.title: Some Problems and Challenges in Affine Algebraic Geometry
talks.abstract: In this talk we shall discuss a few fundamental problems in the area of Affine Algebraic Geometry including the Epimorphism Problem of Abhyankar–Sathaye, Affine Fibration problem, Affine form problem, the Zariski Cancellation Problem and the Linearisation Problem. We shall also discuss a few recent developments on them and how they are interconnected.

talks.speaker: Mr Christopher de Haer
talks.title: Learning and Working With Others How Can We Make 1 + 1 = 3

talks.speaker: Dr Scott Boivin Lindstrom
talks.title: What I wish every student knew about tertiary maths
talks.abstract: Is there a mathematician in me? What does studying higher maths look like? Where do mathematicians work? These are the questions nearly every young person has about tertiary maths. And they don’t even realize they have them. I certainly didn’t. And while I’m quite lucky to have stumbled blindly into such a wonderful and mysterious career, I’d be ever-so-delighted if more young folks actually knew their options. So let’s talk about them.

talks.speaker: Dr Anthony Morphett
talks.title: Modelling diseases with mathematics, and how to prepare for the zombie apocalypse
talks.abstract: Mathematics can be a powerful tool to help us understand real-world phenomena and to guide decision making. A good example of this is infectious disease modelling, where mathematics can predict how a disease is likely to spread and help choose ways to control it. In this presentation we’ll explore some of the mathematics of modelling disease epidemics using nothing more sophisticated than Microsoft Excel and about year 9 maths, and we’ll apply it to a (hopefully hypothetical!) zombie outbreak and see what lessons it may teach us about surviving a zombie apocalypse.

talks.speaker: Dr Geoffrey Pearce
talks.title: Modular Origami for Mathematical Inspiration
talks.abstract: Modular origami is a popular artform that involves creating elaborate 3-dimensional structures by fitting together a number of folded paper ‘modules’. It has some fascinating connections with various mathematical fields (including graph theory, group theory and geometry) which allow for interesting exploration of ideas beyond the boundaries of the maths curriculum. I aim to explain some of these connections, and will describe some ideas for using modular origami in extension or co-curricular activities for secondary or upper primary students. (Please note that this talk will focus on mathematical ideas, and – mainly for timing reasons – will not include a tutorial for making modular origami models. However I will give some suggestions for good online resources for learning how to fold modules and assemble them.)

talks.speaker: Dr Brendan Florio
talks.title: Vertical collaborative learning in the mathematics classroom
talks.abstract:
“I hate mathematics”.

“I’m not a maths person”.

As a research mathematician thrust into high school teaching in a low socioeconomic area in 2021, these are the obstacles I had to overcome in my maths classroom. A large majority of students were self-excluding from learning as they believed they were innately incapable. How could I foster an environment of learning which is inclusive of not just the keen, participating students, but also those students who had already opted out of their own mathematical learning? How did my experience here translate into the tertiary system, where these obstacles also exist for our service teaching cohort? In this talk, I will describe my method to create a collaborative learning environment which is safe, inclusive, and accessible for all students.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Roslyn Hickson
talks.title: Roslyn Hickson
talks.abstract:
Sometimes we can’t answer a question by trying things and seeing what happens. We can’t tell some people to wear masks and others not, just to find out how many need to wear one to prevent an outbreak. Releasing modified mosquitoes could permanently change an ecosystem, and we can’t un-release them. But decisions still need to be made, and usually under a deadline.

This talk is about what mathematics does in that gap, and how we can use models to run experiments we can’t run in real life. A model is where you get to explore and be wrong with fewer real consequences, if any.

I will share three stories from nearly twenty years of modelling to inform decisions like these, both about how I got involved in the work and about how the mathematics helped. I’ll start with Mathematics-in-Industry Study Groups, where partners arrive knowing they need help, though not always knowing what to ask. The second story is the modelling of mask wearing on Sydney’s train network in 2020. The third is current work in progress with communities in the Torres Strait on mosquito control. Along the way I will talk about what we knew, what we didn’t, and how often the useful thing turned out to be the questions rather than the answers.

talks.speaker: Dr Christopher Lustri
talks.title: The Devil's Invention: Unpacking Stokes' Phenomenon using Divergent Series
talks.abstract:
Divergent series have historically been seen as a barrier to understanding. In asymptotic analysis, however, divergence is a source of information. I will show how divergent asymptotic series can be used to study an important phenomenon in differential equations: the sudden appearance or disappearance of exponentially small (or non-perturbative) effects known as Stokes' phenomenon. I will first introduce this phenomenon and explain how it can be understood through exponential asymptotics and divergent resummation, including ideas from resurgence.

I will then turn to discrete systems, focusing on the discrete nonlinear Schr"{o}dinger equation. Standard asymptotic methods break down for this system, revealing a new layer of structure in the problem. I will explain how Borel transforms and conformal mapping can be used to overcome this breakdown and recover exponentially small information that would otherwise be lost. Here, Stokes phenomenon provides a way to understand a critical feature of the solutions: the only standing waves that can exist are centred either on a lattice site or halfway between two sites. I will show how careful asymptotic analysis can determine the exponentially small eigenvalues associated with these solutions, and use them to explain their stability.

talks.speaker: Dr Johanna Knapp
talks.title: The physical mathematics of stringy extra dimensions
talks.abstract: String theory is a theoretical framework that unifies all known fundamental forces of nature. It also predicts the existence of extra space-time dimensions. The mathematical structure of the extra dimensions determines the physics we observe in our universe. It is possible to use theoretical physics methodology, such as quantum field theory, to study the mathematical properties of stringy extra dimensions. The physics results then translate into provable mathematical conjectures. After providing an overview of the general concepts, the talk will focus on Calabi-Yau spaces as candidates for extra dimensions. These provide a particularly rich, interdisciplinary area of research for mathematicians and string theorists. We will discuss how Calabi-Yaus and their moduli spaces can be studied via certain supersymmetric field theories.

talks.speaker: Dr Joshua Zahl
talks.title: The Besicovitch compression phenomenon \& the Kakeya set conjecture
talks.abstract:
In 1919, Besicovitch constructed a compact set in the plane with Lebesgue measure 0 that contains a unit line segment pointing in every direction. Such objects are now called measure 0 Besicovitch sets (aka Kakeya sets). By replacing a measure zero Besicovitch set by its $\delta$-thickening, one obtains a collection of $1 \times \delta$ rectangles pointing in different directions, the sum of whose areas is 1, but whose union has very small volume. The existence of such collections of rectangles is called the Besicovitch compression phenomenon.

The Kakeya set conjecture is a quantitative statement controlling the strength of the Besicovitch compression phenomenon. In this talk, I will discuss connections between the Besicovitch compression phenomenon, the Kakeya set conjecture, and questions in harmonic analysis and PDE.
talks.affiliation: Chern Institute of Mathematics, Nankai University

talks.speaker: Prof Gary Froyland
talks.title: Spectral Approaches to Complex Dynamics
talks.abstract:
The weather and the climate, along with social processes, biological processes, and engineering processes, are all dynamical systems because they are governed by a set of micro-rules at the level of individual states that describe how processes evolve over time. Complex dynamical systems incorporate elements of unpredictability (nearby initial states quickly diverge from one another) and emergence (macroscopic system behaviour is not apparent from the set of micro-rules due to many interacting components).

Emergent behaviour in complex dynamical systems is typically connected with the appearance of macro-structures that persist for a certain amount of time. Examples of such macro-structures include eddies in the ocean, cyclonic storms or heatwaves in the atmosphere, and the coalescing of societal opinion around a particular issue. It is these macro-phenomena that impact our daily world, but it remains challenging to identify key organising emergent phenomena from micro-rules or spatiotemporal observations. Part of the difficulty arises from the usually complicated nonlinear dynamics of the micro-rules. To access these macro-phenomena, we use a linear operator induced by the micro-dynamics. This linear operator – the transfer operator – acts on ensembles of individual states, and its linearity enables one to access a huge toolbox from linear analysis.

In this talk, we gently introduce the transfer operator and its associated spectral theory. We also make connections to a dynamic spectral geometry of evolving manifolds, centred on the dynamic Laplace operator. Several example analyses are presented, ranging across problems in climate, physical oceanography, and atmospheric science.

talks.speaker: Dr Reymond Akpanya
talks.title: On 3-Connected Cubic Planar Graphs and their Strong Embeddings on Orientable Surfaces
talks.abstract:
Although the strong embedding of a 3-connected planar graph on the sphere is unique, the graph may admit inequivalent strong embeddings on surfaces of positive genus. For cubic planar graphs, strong embeddings on the projective plane, torus, and Klein bottle can be characterised in terms of certain subgraphs of the dual graph. We exploit this characterisation to investigate strong embeddings of cubic planar graphs on surfaces of positive genus. In particular, we establish that a 3-connected cubic planar graph has no strong embedding on any orientable surface of positive genus if and only if it is the dual of an Apollonian network.

This is joint work with Alice C. Niemeyer and Meike Weiß.

talks.speaker: Dr Yulia Alexandr
talks.authors: Yulia Alexandr, Hao Duan, Guido Montúfar
talks.title: Algebraic invariants of self-attention
talks.abstract:
Self-attention is a central component of transformers in machine learning. Replacing the softmax function with the identity gives lightning self-attention, a family of cubic polynomial maps. Which cubic polynomial maps are realizable by lightning self-attention, and what polynomial equations characterize them?

We relate the geometry of the associated varieties to Chow varieties and tuples of quadratic forms with common factors and rank constraints. We derive explicit polynomial invariants involving determinantal and Veronese-type equations and Sylvester resultants, and obtain a set-theoretic characterization in the rank-one case.

talks.speaker: Mr Vishnuram Arumugam
talks.title: Multicirculants and Generalised Quadrangles
talks.abstract:
We consider multicirculant structures on the incidence and point graphs of finite generalized quadrangles of order $(q,q)$, where $q>1$. We showed that if there exists a semiregular automorphism of the incidence graph that interchange points and lines with $m$ vertex-orbits and $2q$ is not a square, then
$m=a(q^2+1)$ for some divisor $a$ of $q+1$. \\

For the point graph, we proved that it is neither a circulant nor a bicirculant, while it is a tricirculant if and only if $q=2$. For the incidence graph, we showed that it is neither a circulant nor a bicirculant,  it is a tricirculant if and only if $q=2$, it is never a tetracirculant, can be a pentacirculant only if $2q$ is a square, and it is a hexacirculant if and only if $q=2$. \\

This is joint work with Bo\v{s}tjan Frelih and Klavdija Kutnar.

talks.speaker: Dr Michael Assis
talks.title: Characterizing sonobe unit origami
talks.abstract: Sonobe units are rhombi folded from a square of paper featuring two pockets and two flaps each. Units are assembled such that each flap is inserted into a corresponding pocket of another unit. Origami designers have used sonobe units in modular origami designs since the 1960s, mainly folding polyhedra, although higher genus surfaces can also be assembled. No systematic attempt has been made to characterize the design constraints and valid surfaces that can be assembled. Generically, sonobe surfaces can be represented as directed 4-regular ribbon multigraphs. We show that valid ribbon graphs must avoid a particular minor that would require self-intersection and offer conjectures regarding a full characterization.

talks.speaker: Mr Luka Carroll
talks.title: The complexity of the epimorphism problem onto the bicyclic monoid
talks.abstract: The \textit{bicyclic monoid} (or \textit{bicyclic semigroup}) $\mathcal{B}$ is the infinite monoid on two generators $a,b$ subject only to the relation $ab=1$. The monoid $\mathcal{B}$ is a fundamental algebraic structure that has found numerous applications in algebra, combinatorics, and theoretical computer science. The monoid $\mathcal{B}$ is an \textit{inverse monoid}; that is, $\mathcal{B}$ is a monoid in which every $x\in\mathcal{B}$ has a unique \textit{generalised inverse} $x^{-1}\in\mathcal{B}$, meaning $x^{-1}$ satisfies only the identities $xx^{-1}x=x$ and $x^{-1}xx^{-1}=x^{-1}$ rather than the stronger identity $xx^{-1}=x^{-1}x=1$ satisfied by group inverses. In this talk we consider the computational complexity of the \textit{epimorphism problem} for the bicyclic monoid. This is the problem of deciding if there exists a surjective homomorphism from an arbitrary, finitely presented inverse monoid $\mathcal{M}$ onto the bicyclic monoid (or, equivalently, if $\mathcal{M}$ has a quotient that is isomorphic to $\mathcal{B}$). We analyse this problem via a reduction to \textit{Presburger arithmetic}, the first-order theory of linear arithmetic over the integers. Through this analysis we gain new insights into the complexity of an extension of Presburger arithmetic. This is joint work with Murray Elder.

talks.speaker: Mr Marcus Chijoff
talks.authors: Marcus Chijoff, Michal Ferov, Stephan Tornier
talks.title: The Scale of (P)-closed Groups Acting On Trees
talks.abstract: The scale function is central to the study of totally disconnected locally compact groups, of which groups acting on trees are an important example. Recent work by Reid-Smith used graph-based combinatorial structures to parametrise closed groups acting on trees satisfying Tits' independence property (P). Properties of the group associated to a local action diagram can be determined entirely from the local action diagram itself. We show how the scale function can be computed from a groups associated local action diagram. Furthermore, we use this to show how a group being uniscalar and unimodular can also be determined from the associated local action diagram.

talks.speaker: Mr Daniel Collison
talks.title: Graph Coloring with TQFTs
talks.abstract: The Four Color Theorem, which states that any planar graph can be colored using only four colors such that adjacent faces receive different colors, was proved by Appel and Haken in 1976. In this talk, I will discuss a recent approach to graph coloring using a TQFT-valued cube of resolutions built from two-dimensional cobordisms, which may be nonorientable. The resulting construction categorifies the celebrated Penrose polynomial; in particular, the four color case comes with a refinement of the classical Penrose criterion.

talks.speaker: Mr John Mel Dacaymat
talks.title: A simpler criterion for block-transitive, poset-imprimitive 2-designs
talks.abstract: A set of points and a collection of its subsets (blocks) form a 2-design if every block has the same size and any two points lie in a constant number of blocks. In a 2025 study, Amarra, Devillers and Praeger proved conditions to obtain 2-designs that admit a block-transitive group of automorphisms leaving invariant multiple point partitions. The invariant partitions form a partially-ordered set (poset) and thus, such designs are described as poset-imprimitive. We establish a simpler set of equivalent conditions to the 2025 result. We apply it on known infinite families to demonstrate its computational advantage. We then utilize it to arrive at new constructions for posets with no previously known examples. These new infinite families are obtained by extending the underlying poset of some existing constructions.

talks.speaker: Prof Murray Elder
talks.authors: Alex Bishop, Murray Elder, Alex Evetts, Paul Gallot, Alex Levine
talks.title: The word problem of $\mathbb Z$ is not EDT0L
talks.abstract:
We prove that the word problem for the infinite cyclic group is not EDT0L, and that the only way a group can have EDT0L word problem is if it is torsion (conjecture: finite).

EDT0L languages are in general more descriptive than regular languages, but this work suggests perhaps not when it comes to word problems.

talks.speaker: Mr Fawwaz Fakhrurrozi
talks.authors: Fawwaz Fakhrurrozi, Binzhou Xia, Sanming Zhou
talks.title: Cores of Cayley graphs on cyclic groups and elementary Abelian p-groups
talks.abstract: A graph is called a core if every endomorphism of the graph is also an automorphism. Up to isomorphism, every graph contains a unique induced subgraph that is a core, which is called the core of the graph. In this paper, we study the cores of Cayley graphs on cyclic groups, also known as circulant graphs, and Cayley graphs on elementary Abelian $p$-groups. For circulant graphs, we obtain some conditions under which we can determine the cores of circulant graphs of prime power order and integral circulant graphs. Moreover, we prove that the cores of Cayley graphs on elementary Abelian $p$-groups of order at most $p^3$ must also be Cayley graphs on elementary Abelian p-groups. Further, we present several conditions under which we can determine the core of integral Cayley graphs on elementary Abelian $p$-groups. Along the way, we also obtained some properties of Cayley graphs with complete cores.

talks.speaker: Mr Matthias Fresacher
talks.title: Toward post-quantum cryptography using diagram monoids and their representations
talks.abstract:
Public-key cryptography began in 1976 with Diffie-Hellman key exchange, but many number-theoretic schemes are vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm. Hence scalable quantum computers would force a shift to different foundations. While post-quantum candidates exist, many proposed platforms monoids still admit linear algebra attacks. This motivates looking for platform monoids with large non-trivial representations, usually measured by their Representation Gap (RepGap).

This talk presents recent work in exploring diagram monoids as platform monoids. Specifically whether the semigroup theoretical notion of twisted products in the sense of East, Gray, Muhammed and Ruškuc can modify diagram monoids in ways that increase their RepGap and what structural features control this. Along the way, semigroup theoretic byproducts are established including that 'tightness' is a natural canonical property of a twisting.

This is ongoing joint work with Willow Stewart and Daniel Tubbenhauer.

talks.speaker: Dr Alexandr Garbali
talks.title: Positivity of the basic hypergeometric series
talks.abstract: The basic (q-deformed) hypergeometric series ${}_{n+1}\phi_{n}$ whose upper and lower parameters are non-negative integer powers of $q$ satisfying a certain constraint can be, after a normalisation, computed as a positive polynomial. I will discuss several formulas for this polynomial including two generating functions for statistics on multiset permutations and a finite sum of products of $q$-binomial coefficients.

talks.speaker: Dr Stephen Glasby
talks.title: The maximizing input for $\omega^{-r}\sum_{i=0}^r\binom{m}{i}$ where $\omega>1$ and $r\in\{0,1,\dots,m\}$
talks.abstract:
The function 
$g_{\omega}(r)=\omega^{-r}\sum_{i=0}^r\binom{m}{i}$,
$0\le r\le m$, is unimodal. In some cases there is a precise formula for the maximizing input $r_0(\omega,m)$. For example, $r_0(\omega,m)=\lfloor (m+2)/(\omega+1)\rfloor$ for
$m\in\{3,4,5,\dots\}$. This talk gives sharp bounds $r_0(\omega,m)$ if
$\omega\geq 3$ or if $1<\omega\leq 3$ and $m$ is `large enough'. 
The `large enough' hypothesis can be dropped if a certain conjectured
upper bound for $\binom{m}{r}/(\sum_{i=0}^r\binom{m}{i})$ holds.

talks.speaker: Mr Ethan Kealley
talks.title: On the Hermitian Veronesean

talks.speaker: Mr Christopher Leak
talks.title: Partitioned Set Homomorphisms and Products of Partitions
talks.abstract:
The partitions of a non-empty set form a complete lattice under the refinement order, where we say a partition is finer than (or a refinement of) another if every part of the first partition is contained in some part of the latter partition.
More generally, we can discuss a pair consisting of a set and a partition of that set, and we can consider a kind of structure preserving function between such pairs, such that the refinement order is a special case.
In this talk, I explore a construction of a product of these objects, how they interact with the refinement order and a interesting application to the study of Cartesian Decompositions of sets.

talks.speaker: Dr Melissa Lee
talks.title: Elusive groups and the Polycirculant Conjecture
talks.abstract:
A derangement is a permutation with no fixed points. A classical theorem of Jordan asserts that every primitive group contains a derangement. However, there exist transitive groups with no derangements of prime order -- such groups are called elusive. Elusive groups have been widely studied over the past several decades, partly due to their connection to Polycirculant Conjecture and Semiregularity Problem. 
In this talk I will discuss very recent joint work with Saul Freedman, settling both of these problems, which had been open for 40 years.

talks.speaker: Dr Florian Lehner
talks.title: From invariant tree decompositions to decompositions of permutation groups
talks.abstract:
Group-invariant tree decompositions of graphs have found many uses not only in graph theory, but also in geometric and topological group theory. Examples include elegant proofs of Stallings’ theorem on ends of groups by Dunwoody and Krön, as well as similar results on decompositions of permutation groups acting on vertex sets such as Smith’s box product decomposition of primitive permutation groups and a Stallings'-type theorem for quasi-transitive graphs due to Hamann, Lehner, Miraftab, and Rühmann.

Möller asked whether this latter Stallings'-type theorem gives a decomposition of the automorphism group of these graphs as well. We give an affirmative answer to this question, showing that the full automorphism group can indeed be built up from smaller, local pieces. Our approach uses the recently introduced theory of graphs of group actions which can be seen as a permutation group theoretic version of Bass-Serre theory.

talks.speaker: Dr Peter McNamara
talks.title: On A Schur Positive Function
talks.abstract: I will tell a story about a Schur-positive symmetric function that appeared in my work, and the way in which the proof of Schur-positivity was obtained, including a realisation that I already knew a key piece of information a decade prior.

talks.speaker: Mr Euan Mendoza
talks.authors: Murray Elder, Chang (Aaron) He, Luke Mathieson, Euan Mendoza, Youming Qiao
talks.title: From Graph Connectivity to Tensor Indecomposability: A Strong Krull--Remak--Schmidt type theorem for Mixed Tensors
talks.abstract: Mixed tensors generalise several combinatorial and algebraic structures. Interestingly, decompositions of graphs into their connected components are equivalent to direct sum decompositions of the corresponding graphical tensors. In this talk we present a efficient reduction from the mixed tensor isomorphism problem to the computational mixed tensor automorphism problem. Such a result is inspired by the reduction from the graph isomorphism problem to the computational graph isomorphism problem, which relies on decompositions of graphs into their connected components. A key ingredient of this reduction is a Krull--Remak--Schmidt type theorem for mixed tensors with a stronger condition requiring that each decomposition is unique into embedded subtensors. The centroid algebra corresponding to mixed tensors plays an important role in this reduction. This result unifies several Krull--Remak--Schmidt type results for \(p\)-groups of class \(2\) and exponent \(p\), homogenous polynomials of fixed degree, (Lie) algebras and three tensors investigated by Wilson (2010), Harrison (1977) and Strassen (1987). This is joint work with Murray Elder, Chang (Aaron) He, Luke Mathieson and Youming Qiao.

talks.speaker: Mr Max Mikkelsen
talks.title: New examples of Coxeter systems realising arbitrary hypergraph index
talks.abstract:
\emph{Hypergraph index} is a numerical invariant of Coxeter systems governed entirely by the combinatorics of the underlying Dynkin diagram.
Levcovitz introduced hypergraph index in the class of right-angled Coxeter systems, and showed that it completely determines the large-scale geometric property of \emph{divergence} within this setting.
Dani, Naqvi, Soroko and Thomas then generalised hypergraph index to arbitrary Coxeter systems and conjectured that it continues to determine divergence in this case.
While it is algorithmically feasible to compute this invariant for any given Coxeter system, it is considerably harder to construct sequences of Coxeter systems realising arbitrary values of hypergraph index.
We outline a new method for constructing families of examples, and explain how it generalises an earlier right-angled sequence found by Dani and Thomas.

talks.speaker: Prof Péter Pál Pach
talks.title: The Alon-Jaeger-Tarsi conjecture via group ring identities
talks.abstract: The Alon-Jaeger-Tarsi conjecture states that for any finite field $\mathbb{F}$ of size at least 4  and any nonsingular matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}$ there exists a vector $x$ such that neither $x$ nor $Ax$ has a 0 component. In this talk we discuss the proof of this result for $|\mathbb{F}|>79$  and further applications of our method about coset covers and additive bases. Joint work with János Nagy and István Tomon.
talks.affiliation: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Adam Piggott
talks.authors: Murray Elder, Adam Piggott and Kane Townsend
talks.title: Isomorphism for 1-counter groups is in \(\mathsf{NP}\)
talks.abstract:
We prove that the following problem is in \(\mathsf{NP}\): on input two 1-counter automata which accept the word problems of groups \(G\) and \(H\), decide whether \(G\) and \(H\) are isomorphic. This contrasts with work of S\'enizergues and Wei\ss\ (ICALP 2018) who give a doubly exponential space
bound where the input is two pushdown automata (or equivalently two context-free grammars) accepting the word problem for groups.

talks.speaker: Mx Anthony Pisani
talks.title: Maximal subgroups of the 18- and 19-dimensional finite classical groups
talks.abstract: The finite classical groups account for six of the eighteen families of finite simple groups in the much-f\^{e}ted Classification of Finite Simple Groups. Together with the alternating groups, they are the only such groups for which a comprehensive classification of maximal subgroups still seems entirely out of reach. Nevertheless, building on substantial work of Aschbacher, Kleidman, and Liebeck (among others), Bray, Holt, and Roney--Dougal give a classification for classical groups in dimensions up to 12, which Schr\"oder and Rogers extend to dimensions 13--17. In this talk, I will discuss the process of determining the classification for dimensions 18 and 19, along with some considerations of what the path to higher dimensions may hold.

talks.speaker: Mr Ganesha Lapenangga Putra
talks.authors: Ganesha Lapenangga Putra, Christopher Duffy, Sanming Zhou
talks.title: Perfect Codes in Circulants of Degree $2p^\ell-1$
talks.abstract:
We fully classify the set of circulant graphs with degree $2p^\ell-1$ that admit a perfect code, for odd prime $p$ where $p$ is relatively prime to $\frac{n}{p^\ell}$ as the restriction.
For the case $\ell = 1$ we further refine the result by lifting the condition that $p$ is relatively prime $\frac{n}{p^\ell}$.
In both cases we provide a construction for an infinite family of such perfect codes.
For the $\ell = 1$ case we provide further constructions for the case where $S_0$ is periodic and where $C$ is periodic.

talks.speaker: Dr Colin David Reid
talks.authors: Adrien Le Boudec and Colin D. Reid
talks.title: Lattices determined by their commensurator
talks.abstract: Two subgroups $A$ and $B$ of a group $G$ are commensurable if their intersection has finite index in both, and the commensurator of a subgroup is the stabiliser of its commensurability class under conjugation.  We find conditions on pairs $(G,\Gamma)$, where $G$ is a locally compact group and $\Gamma$ is a uniform lattice (i.e. a discrete cocompact subgroup) of $G$, such that the commensurator $C = \mathrm{Comm}_G(\Gamma)$ is dense in $G$, but every finitely generated commensurated subgroup of $C$ is virtually contained in $\Gamma$.  In particular, these conditions hold for $G$ the automorphism group of a regular tree, answering a question raised by Bass--Kulkarni in 1990, and also for lattices in right-angled buildings arising from graph products of finite groups.  We also obtain a general property of finitely generated commensurated subgroups of a group that may be of independent interest.

talks.speaker: Dr Gabor Somlai
talks.title: Conjugacy classes of the symmetric group do not tile
talks.abstract:
A pair $(X,Y)$ of subsets of a finite group $G$ is called a \emph{tiling} of $G$ if every element of $G$ can be written uniquely in the form $xy$, where $x\in X$ and $y\in Y$. In this case, each of $X$ and $Y$ is a tile of $G$. Rothaus and Thompson, and later Fang and Xia studied whether the set of transpositions is a tile of $S_n$. 

We show that any conjugacy class of the symmetric group other than the trivial class of the identity element and the class of transpositions does not tile the group. In the case of the alternating group, we also show that no normal set not containing the identity element tiles the group.  We exclude some of the conjugacy classes using elementary combinatorial methods. However, for certain conjugacy classes containing elements of order two, this method does not work, so we rule those out using classical representation theory methods.

Joint work with Binzhou Xia and Sanming Zhou.

talks.speaker: Mr Rafael Borges de Souza
talks.authors: Rafael Borges de Souza, Roozbeh Hazrat
talks.title: The Talents of the Talented Monoid: Detecting Graph Structure
talks.abstract: The talented monoid $T_E$ is a graded invariant associated with a directed graph $E$, arising naturally from the graded structure of the Leavitt path algebra $L_K(E)$. It can be realized as the monoid of graded finitely generated projective $L_K(E)$-modules and viewed as a graded analogue of the graph monoid $M_E$. In this work, we investigate how order-theoretic properties of $T_E$ reflect structural and dynamical features of the underlying graph. We establish connections between properties of the talented monoid and graph-theoretic features, including cycles, exits, periodicity, and strongly connected components. We then explore the extent to which $T_E$ can detect finer features of the graph that are not captured by the ordinary graph monoid $M_E$. In particular, we investigate whether and how properties of $T_E$ can be used to detect infinite emitters.

talks.speaker: Mr Attawut Wongpradit
talks.title: Tiling Deficient Boards with Trominoes and Alien Tiles
talks.abstract: This talk investigates tiling problems on deficient boards. Traditionally, a deficient board tiling involves taking a grid which is missing a single unit square, and covering it with $L$-trominoes. Building upon the foundational work introduced by Golomb, we extend these problems by introducing non-standard ``alien'' tiles, where  an alien tile is a polyomino of a different size or shape from the standard tile. The talk will focus on the combinatorial effects of incorporating alien tiles into standard grids, exploring which grid sizes are tileable for different types of alien tile. We will present key results and discuss open questions regarding the tileability of deficient boards under these modified conditions.

talks.speaker: Prof AISHA ALQAHTANI
talks.authors: Muhammad Yasir, N. Ameer Ahammad, Aisha M. Alqahtani, Yahia Said
talks.title: Heat Transport Efficiency in Rheology of Radiated Casson Material Due to Porous Shrinking Cylinder
talks.abstract: In several industrial and thermal management systems, maintaining continuous thermal propagation is essential because it makes thermal engineering mechanisms and machinery more efficient. It is therefore a promising development for the augmentation of thermal power energy to use thermal radiation, heat source/sink, and nanoparticles in a heat-carrying dynamics of non- Newtonian fluids. This article presents a unique contribution by thoroughly examining the mass transfer and thermal properties of Casson fluid in motile microorganism suspensions over a shrinking cylinder. The physical characteristics of the problem are governed by partial differential equations, which are converted to ordinary differential equations using appropriate similarity variables. To find the duality of solutions, the Bvp4c solver from MATLAB is used in the solution approach. The various flow characteristics of Casson fluid have been illustrated with graphs. The engineering quantities, such as friction factor, Sherwood number, Nusselt number, and density number have also been computed and graphically depicted. The study’s main finding reveals that higher suction strength enhanced the skin friction coefficient and transportation rate in the shrinking zone. It is noteworthy that a higher Eckert number and thermal radiation decreased the thermal transport rate, whereas reaction rate increased the solutal transfer rate. The results also demonstrated that in the second branch solution, with increasing magnetic and Casson factors, the fluid flow velocity distribution decreases, while in the first branch solution, it increases. These findings add important insights into optimizing heat transport in modern systems of engineering.

talks.speaker: Prof Luke Bennetts
talks.title: On the differences between wave propagation through broken and unbroken ice covers
talks.abstract: I will present results from a mathematical model that aids interpretation of field observations and physical models regarding wave propagation through the sea ice covered ocean, as it transitions from an unbroken to a broken state. I will show that the limiting cases of broken and unbroken ice covers can be captured analytically. I will then use the model predictions to adapt the wave propagation scheme in a wave–ice interaction model (WIM), including the introduction of a term to reflect incident waves at an unbroken ice edge, and show how the changes influence WIM predictions.

talks.speaker: Mr Aaron Gibson-John
talks.authors: Aaron Gibson-John, Prof Spiridon Penev, A/Prof Pierre Lafaye De Micheaux, A/Prof Samuel Mallinson, Prof Scott Sisson
talks.title: Quality Prediction in Multistage Manufacturing
talks.abstract: Modern manufacturing processes generate large volumes of data across successive stages of production. Motivated by thermal inkjet printhead manufacturing, this talk explores statistical approaches to understanding process variation and predicting product quality. I will discuss statistical process control (SPC), stream-of-variation (SoV) modelling and changepoint detection, alongside opportunities to combine these approaches with machine learning for earlier fault detection.

talks.speaker: Dr Grant Keady
talks.title: On torsional rigidity of (tangential) n-gons
talks.abstract:
Polya and Szego asked, in their 1951 `Isoperimetric Inequalities' book,:
Amongst (convex) polygons , $n$-gons, with a given area, does the regular $n$-gon have the greatest torsional rigidity.
Symmetrisation techniques give the result for triangles and quadrilaterals but not for $n\ge{5}$.

The same functional is also the square of the Bergmann analytic content, and is related to exit times of Brownian motion.

They also asked the question `does regular optimise' for other domain functionals.
In recent decades it has been settled for conformal inner radius and for logarithmic capacity (outer radius/transfinite diameter).

Papers this year have settled, affirmatively, that, for all $n$, regular maximises the torsional rigidity for tangential n-gons. (arXiv:2607.28768v1)
Further questions abound: e.g. `stability', how asymmetry, departures from regular, affect the torsional rigidity.

Good bounds, including mine (IMA Jnl of Applied Maths, 2021 -and arXiv) and developments from this, will be useful.
The latter half of the talk will be on these developments since my talk at the 2022 ANZIAM Conference.

See also links from:
https://sites.google.com/site/keadyperthunis/home/papers

talks.speaker: Dr Paul Charles Leopardi
talks.title: Is the translation of applied mathematics facing an AI-generated crisis?
talks.abstract:
Automated tools can now produce candidate models, algorithms, code,
and even formal proofs at very low cost. In pure mathematics this has
raised a question about understanding: a proof can be certified
without being \emph{digested}. This talk asks what the matching
question is for applied mathematics \cite{ICIAM2026,SIAM2026}.

I suggest that the question is about \emph{translation}: \emph{assessment} of
how well a model or method works in theory and how much it helps in practice,
\emph{adaptation} of the mathematical method to the problem and
the software to the computing environment, and \emph{adoption} into
sustained community use. Because every model simplifies reality, it
carries \emph{applicability debt} that should be managed by a \emph{web
of skills} including applied mathematics, domain specialization, and
research software engineering. While generative AI makes it cheap to
generate candidate models and implement candidate methods, and speeds up
routine software porting, other aspects of translation remain tied to
human judgment. When generation runs ahead
of translation, applicability debt goes unmanaged and adoption is
pushed toward unverified shortcuts, risking a \emph{crisis of
application}.

To illustrate how translation works and where it can stall or
short-circuit, I draw on examples including some from numerical analysis,
climate modelling \cite{Dunne2025,Henn2026}, and twenty years of citations to
my algorithms for partitioning the sphere into regions of equal area
\cite{Leopardi2024,Leopardi2026}.

I end with questions for discussion. Who is responsible for
translation? How can we sustain the web of skills? And how might
societies such as AustMS and ANZIAM respond?

talks.speaker: Dr Simon Marshall
talks.title: On third-vertex problems in spherical trigonometry
talks.abstract: Calculating the coordinates of the third vertex of a spherical triangle, given two sides and the coordinates of the other vertices, is a non-linear problem that generally requires an iterative numerical solution. Significant gains in computational efficiency can be achieved by using linear methods that do not require iteration. A scalar triple product, derived from the Gramian determinant, can be combined with scalar products involving the other vertices to form a system of linear equations for the unknown coordinates of the third vertex. The solution to these equations coincides—to within the limits of machine error—with the iterative solution and with solutions to problems that can be solved exactly via formulae. Various calculations in spherical geometry are discussed, and applications to geodesy and celestial navigation are demonstrated.

talks.speaker: Dr Peter Heiss Synak
talks.authors: Alice Wei, Christian Hafner, Aleksei Kalinov, Peter Heiss Synak, Chris Wojtan
talks.title: Circles of Confidence for Multi-Label Geometry Completion
talks.abstract: Inside–outside classification is widely used for geometry processing tasks such as surface reconstruction, geometry completion, and calculating signed distance fields. In my talk I will introduce a new integral formulation of this problem, which assigns confidence scores that points are inside or outside, given incomplete boundary geometry. Even though this geometric construction does not appear in previous work, I will show that it is unexpectedly linked to both the well-established generalized winding number (GWN) and pseudonormal methods for geometry completion, and it provably reduces to either one of them for specific values of a control parameter. The results obtained with this method frequently outperform screened Poisson surface reconstruction (PSR), GWN, and the pseudonormal method in terms of quality, and are at least on par with them on all of our examples.

talks.speaker: Dr Simon Watt
talks.title: Rescaling the chaotic mixing problem with blinking vortices
talks.abstract:
We study the effects of two-dimensional chaotic advection 
on a chemical system characterised by competitive 
exothermic and endothermic reactions. In previous studies, in which advective flow and reaction processes were assumed to dominate weak diffusive effects, two distinct behaviours
were observed in the system. The first, when the stirring 
is fast and the reaction is slow. In this case, flame
quenching occurs. In contrast, when the stirring is slow and
the reaction is fast, local temperature perturbations lead
to a stationary flame with a complex filament structure.
When the diffusion process is more influential, a third type
of behaviour is possible, in which an expanding swirling 
travelling wave develops. This work will recast the problem
as a reaction-diffusion-advection problem to a combustion
problem with added advection.

talks.speaker: Dr Doungporn Wiwatanapataphee
talks.title: Towards Non-Intrusive Assessment of Fluids Beneath Intact Offshore Well Plugs: Initial Flow and Acoustic–Elastic Modelling Results
talks.abstract: Non-intrusive assessment of fluids beneath intact offshore well plugs could support intervention planning by providing information about concealed gas and pressure before barrier removal. Interpreting remotely measured signals, however, requires a physical model that distinguishes fluid-state effects from variations in the plug, casing, formation and measurement system. This work presents a staged computational framework linking subplug fluid dynamics to acoustic and structural responses. The formulated model combines axisymmetric compressible flow, governed by phase-mass, momentum and total-energy conservation, with a three-dimensional acoustic–elastic finite-element representation of the fluid, intact cement plug, steel casing and surrounding formation. Static pressure loading introduces an approximate initial-stress correction, while transient casing excitation generates pressure and acceleration histories at virtual receivers. The formulation incorporates interface traction and normal-motion coupling, material damping and approximate radiation boundaries. Separate reduced inverse and synthetic detection examples examine pressure–gas ambiguity and the statistical requirements for evaluating detection performance. Initial calculations assess conservation, energy consistency and numerical sensitivity, establishing a basis for subsequent model refinement. The significance of the framework lies in connecting predicted fluid conditions to observable signals while explicitly testing whether those signals contain sufficient independent information for inference. Conservative two-way CFD–structure coupling and independent laboratory validation are proposed as the next stages towards an uncertainty-aware assessment method.

talks.speaker: Prof Dominic Verity
talks.title: A Complicial Odyssey. Journeying back to my mathematical home.

talks.speaker: Dr Bryce Clarke
talks.title: Restriction limits as weighted limits
talks.abstract: It is often beneficial to view mathematical structures as enriched categories, as it allows us to use the many fruitful results and perspectives of enriched category theory, such as weighted limits. Restriction categories are a mathematical structure which capture the notion of partial map, axiomatising the example of sets and partial functions. Many concepts in category theory, such as limits, admit analogous formulations in restriction category theory, however it is natural to seek some kind of structural justification as to why these formulations are ``correct''. Cockett and Garner (2014) showed that restriction categories are certain kinds of enriched categories, whose base of enrichment is a (virtual) double category. In this talk, I will extend this result to show that restriction distributors (or profunctors) are enriched distributors for the same base of enrichment, and demonstrate how restriction limits are examples of weighted limits in the resulting (virtual) double category of restriction categories, functors, and distributors. This talk is based on joint work with Nathanael Arkor, Vít Jelínek, Theofilos Tsantilas, Hayato Nasu, and Yorgo Chamoun.

talks.speaker: Dr Rob Cornish
talks.title: A categorical account of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
talks.abstract: Metropolis-Hastings (MH) is a foundational Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. In this paper, we ask whether it is possible to formulate and analyse MH in terms of categorical probability, using a recent involutive framework for MH-type procedures as a concrete case study. We show how basic MCMC concepts such as invariance and reversibility can be formulated in Markov categories, and how one part of the MH kernel can be analysed using standard CD categories. To go further, we then study enrichments of CD categories over commutative monoids. This gives an expressive setting for reasoning abstractly about a range of important probabilistic concepts, including substochastic kernels, finite and sigma-finite measures, absolute continuity, singular measures, and Lebesgue decompositions. Using these tools, we give synthetic necessary and sufficient conditions for a general MH-type sampler to be reversible with respect to a given target distribution.

talks.speaker: Prof Michael Johnson
talks.title: Category theoretic vote counting
talks.abstract:
This talk follows the authors' analysis of Australian voting systems using category theoretic techniques.

The primary innovation is the use of multisets in a way that quite dramatically changes the description and analysis of different voting systems including preferential voting (called "the Alternative Vote" internationally), as used in electing the Australian House of Representatives, and variations on Hare-Clark and other "Single Transferable Vote" systems, as used in electing the Senate, the upper houses in four states, and the lower houses in Tasmania and the ACT.

We note that forming multisets over a base set is a functorial operation which we denote MSet. Furthermore MSet is the base functor of a monad.  Meanwhile, multisets over a base set themselves form a commutative monoid.  And the process of turning a list of elements into a multiset of the same elements forms a natural transformation between the functor List and the functor MSet.  These properties are used in the analysis of voting systems, and have in fact led to some remarkable simplifications.

As well as demonstrating an unexpected application of relatively elementary category theory to a novel area, this talk will likely teach even well-informed Australians some surprising things that they didn't know about their own electoral systems.

The analysis is based on the ideas developed in [1].

Reference
[1] Jacobs, Johnson and Buckland:  Counting Votes with Multisets.
arXiv [2606.05218]

talks.speaker: Dr Marcello Lanfranchi
talks.title: The Lie Group-Lie algebra correspondence in tangent categories
talks.abstract:
Classic Lie theory establishes a correspondence between Lie groups and Lie algebras. An analogous correspondence also exists for group objects in affine schemes. Both smooth manifolds and affine schemes form tangent categories, which provide a categorical context for differential geometry.

In this talk, we show how to construct the Lie correspondence entirely from the tangent structure. We define Lie groups in a tangent category as group objects that admit the tangent space at the unit and construct the internal Lie algebra as the representing object of a certain functor. Lastly, we show that our construction generalizes the usual Lie correspondence in both differential and algebraic geometry.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03449

talks.speaker: Dr Jean-Simon Lemay
talks.title: A Comonad from Algebraically-Free Commutative Monoids
talks.abstract:
It is well-known that using the universal property of free commutative monoids gives rise to a monad on a symmetric monoidal category, where the monad structure corresponds to multiplying monomials. In this talk, I will explain how the universal property of algebraically-free commutative monoids also gives rise to a comonad on an additive symmetric monoidal category, where the comonad structure corresponds to finite partitions of monomials. Moreover, this coKleisli category of this comonad is also a Cartesian diffferential categories. Examples include the category of modules, given by the usual symmetric algebras, and the category of sets and relations, given by finite multisets.

This is joint work with Jerry Zhang (UNSW)

talks.speaker: Mrs Sepideh Mohammadi
talks.title: Dold–Kan equivalences and moment categories
talks.abstract:
The Dold--Kan correspondence gives an equivalence between simplicial abelian groups and chain complexes. In this talk, we introduce Lack and Street’s categorical approach to this correspondence and explore generalisations using different factorisation systems.

We focus on moment categories, taking the category of finite intervals as a concrete example. Here we can describe normalisation and its inverse explicitly, and see how the factorisation of maps enters the construction. We then discuss sufficient conditions for a Dold--Kan type equivalence for centric moment categories.

talks.speaker: Mr Areeb Shah Mohammed
talks.title: A restriction category approach to partial stochastic maps
talks.abstract:
Markov categories, and more generally CD categories, are a categorical structure for probability that has seen much development in recent years. Many operations in probability theory involve constructions (limits, integrals, etc.) that may fail to be defined (or finite). Categorically, this suggests thinking of them as ``partially defined stochastic maps'': not only having non-deterministic output, but also possibly only being defined on some subset of its domain. Partiality in a probabilistic context is often studied in terms of sub-stochastic maps. However, the notion of partiality there is much closer to there being a \emph{non-zero probability} of the map not being defined, rather than there being a sub-object where it is undefined.

Restriction categories are a categorical framework for partial maps that has shown considerable utility. In this talk I will discuss a construction of a CD category that is additionally a restriction category from a suitable kind of Markov category. This construction turns out to preserve many properties of importance in categorical probability, and furthermore semantically captures the notion of there being a \emph{sub-space} of definition (rather than a probability). Time permitting, I will also discuss an approach to formalizing the relation between the two aforementioned CD categories (namely, the sub-stochastic map category and the restriction category) associated to a suitable Markov category.

talks.speaker: Mr Joel Richardson
talks.title: Categories of Homomorphic Expansions
talks.abstract: Homomorphic expansions, a kind of invariant from low-dimensional topology, sometimes encode solutions to interesting problems from quantum algebra. Homomorphic expansions of braids are closely related to Drinfel'd associators, and those of the Goldman--Turaev Lie bialgebra of loops in the punctured disk are closely related to solutions of the Kashiwara--Vergne equations. In this talk, we show that homomorphic expansions form a category, and through this category retell the story of how Drinfel'd associators inject into Kashiwara--Vergne solutions.

talks.speaker: Mr Jinwen XU
talks.title: TBA
talks.abstract: TBA

talks.speaker: Mr Declan Zammit
talks.title: Normal Isofibrations of $\infty$-Categories
talks.abstract:
Recently Riehl and Verity introduced the notion of an $\infty$-cosmos: a kind of category in which one can develop a formal theory of $\infty$-categories. This formal theory generalises, for example, the analytic theory of quasicategories. In this talk we will introduce a particularly nice subclass of $\infty$-cosmoi which we call normal $\infty$-cosmoi, whose axioms are generally more amenable than those of $\infty$-cosmoi. The key  is to generalise a class of maps called normal isofibrations from $2$-category theory into the $\infty$-categorical setting.

Joint work with Steve Lack.

talks.speaker: Mr Leyao Zha
talks.title: Tychonoff condition on schemes
talks.abstract:
In algebraic geometry, we have the well known comparison between schemes and topological spaces: the Hausdorff condition on topological spaces should be equivalent to the separated condition on schemes. In topology, Hausdorff is just one of the separation axioms, while other separation axioms are sometimes useful as well. 

We will look at another separation axiom, \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tychonoff_space}{Tychonoff} (sometimes called completely regular). It is a much stronger separation axiom than Hausdorff, and it is related to the study of commutative $C^*$-algebra. In this talk we will attempt to generalize the Tychonoff axiom to schemes, and argue why it is a reasonable definition to give.

talks.speaker: Dr Nicolas Barnafi
talks.authors: Nicolás Barnafi, Benjamín Cisternas, Felipe Galarce, Ernesto Castillo
talks.title: The pseudostress formulation of Navier-Stokes: practical formulation and pressure estimation
talks.abstract:
The pseudostress formulation of Navier-Stokes consists in converting the pressure-velocity formulation into an equivalent one in terms of stress and velocity, with pressure computed as a post-process. The main motivations for this formulation are (1) a fundamental change in the
structure of the nonlinearity of the equation, and (2) a better approximation for stress, which is a quantity of physical interest that can be challenging to approximate numerically.

One structural advantage of this equation that we levarage in this talk is the lack of differential operators in the saddle structure of the problem, which allows for richer sub-problems that do not "lose information". Throughout this talk, that concept will be applied to compute a pressure recovery formulation that is competitive and in cases better than state of the art algorithms, and we will conclude with
discussions on how to adapt this formulation to obtain stable time discretizations that are amenable to realistic large scale simulations.

talks.speaker: Prof Victor Calo
talks.authors: Carlos Uriarte and Victor M. Calo
talks.title: Stabilised on-the-fly adaptivity from a minimum-residual multiscale Galerkin realisation
talks.abstract: Adaptive finite element methods rely on a stable discretisation. For singularly perturbed and indefinite problems, the Galerkin residual no longer tracks the error, and marking may refine the wrong elements. Residual minimisation restores stability, but usually at the expense of broken test spaces, stabilisation parameters, or an ill-conditioned ambient solve. We present a minimum-residual realisation on three nested scales (coarse, fine, ambient) of a single continuous Galerkin space. Only the coarse and fine problems are solved, and no broken space or tuning parameter is needed. The coarse-to-fine correction is computable, and its energy equals the drop in the residual. We define markers as monotone set functions, with D\"orfler marking as the additive case, and show that the objective (the energy) decides which candidates are selected. A chain of computable constants measures how much of that decision the discrete solve realises. A three-branch algorithm, monitored by saturation and reliability indicators, contracts the error. We illustrate the theory on one- and two-dimensional finite element studies.

talks.speaker: Dr Quanling Deng
talks.title: HyPadé: High-Order Time Integration with Tunable Dissipation for Hyperbolic and Stiff Problems
talks.abstract: Hochbruck and Ostermann’s influential work on exponential integrators established a framework for accurately treating stiff and highly oscillatory problems through matrix exponentials and related $\phi$-functions. Building on this broader direction in time integration, we present HyPadé, a closed-form family of high-order rational Padé integrators for hyperbolic and stiff linear problems. For odd orders, a parameter  $p_\infty$ controls high-frequency dissipation while preserving high-order accuracy. A stability identity establishes A-stability, quantifies the dissipation on the imaginary axis, and recovers the energy-preserving diagonal Padé limit as $p_\infty\to 1$ . I will describe the arbitrary-order construction, its coupling with exponential-Rosenbrock methods for semilinear problems, and a matrix-free Krylov implementation. Numerical experiments include stiff non-autonomous tests and large linear wave problems, where HyPadé combines accurate resolution of relevant modes with damping of unresolved ones. The talk will also discuss where the approach is effective and its limitations for rapidly varying Jacobians and unresolved forcing features. This is joint work with Victor Calo.

talks.speaker: Dr Jing Gao
talks.title: When Squaring Changes the Boundary Conditions
talks.abstract: Spectral methods often construct higher-order operators by composing discrete differentiation matrices. Does this preserve the boundary conditions of the original problem? We study this question for a Jacobi W-system whose basis functions vanish at both endpoints. Although its first-derivative matrix is skew-Hermitian, its finite square has different limits for odd and even truncation dimensions: the corresponding operators are the periodic and antiperiodic Laplacians, rather than the Dirichlet Laplacian. We identify the source of this unexpected behaviour and show that a correction restores convergence to the Dirichlet Laplacian. The result demonstrates that desirable structure in a first-order discretisation does not, by itself, guarantee a correct higher-order operator.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Quoc Thong Le Gia
talks.authors: Quoc T. Le Gia, Ian H. Sloan, Holger Wendland
talks.title: Solving parametric Darcy's equations using divergence-free kernels
talks.abstract:
We study the approximation of expected velocity fields for Darcy flow with random permeability. The log-permeability is represented by a truncated Karhunen--Lo\`eve expansion, and each resulting parametric Darcy problem is discretized by radial basis function collocation using analytically
divergence-free kernels. This construction enforces the incompressibility constraint pointwise and allows collocation at scattered points, including points on curved boundaries. We derive mixed parametric derivative estimates for the exact solution and a corresponding estimate for the discrete solution under stated uniform stability assumptions on the collocation system. These bounds support a quasi-Monte Carlo error analysis for bounded linear functionals of the expected velocity. Combining spatial discretization, Karhunen--Lo\`eve truncation, and randomly shifted lattice-rule errors yields
a total error bound of the form $C(h^\rho+s^{-\chi}+M^{-r})$, with rates determined by the stated regularity, summability, and stability assumptions. Numerical examples on square and curved-boundary domains illustrate the spatial method; a
stochastic example compares Monte Carlo and Sobol' point estimates of the expected velocity.

talks.speaker: Dr Alexander Gilbert
talks.title: A higher order lattice-based method for high-dimensional numerical integration using periodisation
talks.abstract: This talk will introduce a weighted quadrature rule using transformed lattice points for numerical integration of non-periodic functions over the unit cube. The key idea is to first apply a periodising transformation to map the original non-periodic integrand to the product of a smooth periodic function and a non-smooth density, then to choose the ``optimal'' quadrature weights corresponding to lattice quadrature points applied to this transformed periodic integrand and density. Alternatively, our method can be viewed as approximating the transformed periodic integrand by a kernel interpolant using lattice points and then integrating this interpolant exactly. Leveraging this connection to lattice kernel interpolation we are able to show higher order convergence rates for non-periodic functions with mixed derivatives up to order $\alpha \geq 1$ that are square-integrable with respect to the Chebyshev density. Additionally, by considering subsampled lattice rules, we are able to show convergence rates close to order $\alpha - 1/2$, independent of dimension, or order $\alpha$, with a moderate dimension dependent factor. The periodising transformation can be viewed as a smooth extension of the tent transform and is also similar to Sidi transforms. Finally, I will present numerical results for both the full lattice rule and the subsampled alternative.

talks.speaker: Ms Longxin Liu
talks.title: Numerical Quadrature and Discrete Riesz Structure in RVPINNs
talks.abstract:
Robust variational physics-informed neural networks (RVPINNs) formulate training through discrete dual norms of variational residuals. In practice, we assemble the residual vector and the Gram matrix defining the discrete Riesz map numerically, so quadrature may affect not only the scalar loss but also the residual representation and the information extracted from it.

We study how quadrature perturbations propagate through the discrete Riesz representative and residual norm in finite-dimensional test spaces. In particular, we distinguish perturbations of the residual vector from perturbations of the Gram matrix and examine how numerical quadrature interacts with nested test spaces, where differences between discrete Riesz representatives provide hierarchical information. This viewpoint separates quadrature error from trial approximation and test-space resolution, and provides a framework for assessing when quadrature-computed RVPINN quantities can be trusted.

The main ideas will be illustrated with representative numerical examples.

talks.speaker: Ms Maxine Petschack
talks.authors: Max Petschack, Jan de Gier, Liam Hodgkinson, Sasha Garbali
talks.title: Neural Knot Invariants
talks.abstract:
The use of machine learning techniques in Mathematics is an exciting developing field that has made significant inroads in the past 5 years. One domain of particular interest has been the study of knot theory using machine learning methods, such as the 2020 work by Gukov et al. Inspired by this, we developed a contrastive learning framework for
training a neural network to act as a knot invariant, ie. learning to convert knot diagrams into high dimensional representations in a manner that is invariant under Reidemeister moves. Our main goals are to expand
on and test this framework, and to build a bespoke neural network from first principles that acts as a fast and complete knot invariant, with potential for interpretability/theorem extraction work afterwards.

talks.speaker: Prof Weifeng Qiu
talks.title: An Interface Green's Function Framework for Complete Discrete $W^{1,\infty}$ Analysis of Discontinuous Galerkin Methods
talks.abstract:
Pointwise error analysis of discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods for the Poisson equation has received considerable attention over the past two decades. However, on convex polyhedral domains, existing analyses can only establish
\emph{nearly} (with a logarithmic factor) optimal error estimates in the $L^{\infty}$ norm and optimal error estimates in the broken $W^{1,\infty}$ seminorm for several DG methods. Since numerical solutions obtained by DG methods may have jumps
across mesh interfaces, and the broken $W^{1,\infty}$ seminorm does not control these jumps, a complete discrete
$W^{1,\infty}$ theory for DG methods for the Poisson equation on convex polyhedral domains has remained unavailable.
Here, by a complete discrete $W^{1,\infty}$ theory, we mean that the maximum-norm of the broken gradient and
the maximum norm of the interface jumps are estimated simultaneously.

In this paper, we develop an interface Green's function framework for the complete discrete $W^{1,\infty}$ analysis of DG methods on convex polyhedral domains. The proposed framework introduces new interface Green's functions that represent the jumps of numerical solutions of DG methods across mesh interfaces. Its central analytical ingredient is a new local energy estimate for these Green's functions, obtained by exploiting a cancellation between neighboring discrete delta functions. This local energy estimate differs fundamentally from existing Green's function estimates and enables us to derive maximum-norm estimates for the jumps of numerical solutions across mesh interfaces without
introducing additional logarithmic factors.

Via the proposed framework, we establish optimal error estimates in the complete discrete $W^{1,\infty}$ norm for the symmetric interior penalty DG method, the hybrid mixed DG method, and two representative hybridizable DG methods
for the Poisson equation in convex polyhedral domains.
In particular, we derive optimal maximum-norm estimates for interface jumps, numerical fluxes, and broken gradients.
We further extend the framework to the $C^0$ interior penalty method for the biharmonic equation on convex polygonal
domains and obtain maximum-norm estimates for the jumps of the normal derivative. The interface Green's function
framework is sufficiently general to be applicable to a broad class of nonconforming methods and is valid on general
polyhedral meshes.

talks.speaker: Dr Sergio Rojas
talks.title: Stable Time-Stepping via Residual Minimisation: From Finite Elements to Neural Networks
talks.abstract:
Residual minimisation provides a systematic framework for constructing stable numerical approximations of partial differential equations. While its foundations are well established for stationary problems, extending this approach to time-dependent equations introduces additional challenges, particularly in choosing residual norms and relating them to the natural stability properties of the underlying evolution problem.

In this talk, we present a time-stepping minimum-residual framework for transient coercive variational problems, applicable to both finite-element and neural-network approximations. Starting from the Backward Euler method, we propose measuring the residual at each time level using the dual norm induced by the steady spatial test-space norm, appropriately scaled by the time step. This choice leads to stability estimates controlling a discrete parabolic energy quantity, up to the time-discretisation error, without requiring time-step-dependent spatial test norms.

We develop conforming and broken-test formulations and establish error estimates independent of the trial approximation's representation. When we use finite-dimensional test spaces, we augment the computable discrete residual with an additional term that accounts for unresolved residual components, yielding reliable error estimates.

For neural-network approximations, the framework lets a single network represent the solution over the entire space–time domain while evaluating the loss via spatial integrals at discrete time levels, avoiding full space–time quadrature.

Numerical experiments on diffusion–advection–reaction problems illustrate the stability and convergence properties of the proposed methods and the potential of residual-based error indicators to guide spatial adaptivity in transient simulations.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Patrick Vega
talks.authors: Ignacio Muga, Sergio Rojas, Kristoffer van der Zee, Patrick Vega
talks.title: Source regularization through projection in dual norms for nonconforming finite element discretizations
talks.abstract:
We propose a projection method in negative Sobolev spaces
$W^{-m,p}(\Omega)$ to regularise continuous linear functionals acting on Sobolev spaces such as $W^{m,q}_0(\Omega)$, where $m\geq 1$, $p^{-1}+q^{-1}=1$, $1<p<\infty$, and $\Omega$ is a Lipschitz domain. We focus on projections onto discrete finite element spaces $G_H$ to compute the best approximation as measured in the negative
(dual) norm. For computability reasons, we employ a discrete dual norm based on a discrete nonconforming test space
$V_H\not\subset W^{m,q}_0(\Omega)$ and a smoothing/averaging operator that provides a well-defined action of the rough functional on $V_H$. We show that this approach leads to a fully discrete nonconforming method given by a mixed problem on $V_H\times G_H$. We propose compatible pairs and therefore
obtain quasi-optimal approximation properties. Finally, we show how the presented projection method can be used to compute numerical approximations to partial differential equations with (ultra) rough data.

talks.speaker: Mr Noah Vinod
talks.title: Well-Posedness and Numerical Method for the Non-Homogeneous Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert Equation
talks.abstract:
Due to the physics of spins, the orientations of the magnetisation in a ferromagnet can influence the conductivity of the metal and vice-versa, the spins of these electrons can also influence the orientations of the
magnetisation. The Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation has historically been used to model the magnetisation of a permanent magnet, but in the context of spin-torques, a non-homogeneous term usually needs to be appended to the PDE to account for these torque effects. This motivates our study of the non-homogeneous Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation. We examine the conditions under which the PDE is well-posed and develop a finite element method that approximates these solutions.

talks.speaker: Mr Abdul Wahab
talks.title: A Mass-Conservative and Energy Dissipative Spectral IMEX Method for the Cahn-Hilliard Equation with an Adaptive Free Energy
talks.abstract: The logarithmic free-energy potential provides a thermodynamically meaningful description of phase separation but introduces severe numerical stiffness as the phase variable approaches its pure states. We develop an adaptive numerical treatment of the Cahn-Hilliard equation that retains the logarithmic derivative in the physically admissible region and locally replaces it with a polynomial derivative within narrow neighbourhoods of the singular values. This pointwise switching mechanism avoids direct clipping of the numerical solution while preserving the conservative form of the governing equation. Time integration is performed using Eyre-type implicit-explicit splitting with first-order BDF1-AB1 and second-order BDF2-AB2 discretizations. A Fourier cosine spectral formulation is employed in space to accommodate homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. Since the discrete Laplacian is diagonal in the cosine basis, the implicit update separates into independent scalar problems for the spectral modes and requires no nonlinear iteration. The zero-frequency mode is preserved exactly, yielding discrete mass conservation up to machine precision. Numerical experiments involving curvature-driven interface relaxation, spinodal decomposition, droplet coalescence, degenerate mobility, and three-dimensional pattern formation demonstrate monotone energy decay, controlled phase extrema, and consistent interfacial dynamics. Sensitivity tests further show that the computed evolution is nearly independent of the switching tolerance over a broad practical range. The method therefore provides an efficient and structurally reliable computational framework for stiff Cahn-Hilliard dynamics.
talks.affiliation: King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals

talks.speaker: Dr Yiming Ying
talks.title: Stability and Generalization of Straight-Through Estimators for Training Two-Layer Quantised Neural Network
talks.abstract:
Training neural networks with binary activations presents a computational challenge: the activation functions are discontinuous, and their derivatives
provide no useful information for gradient-based optimisation. The straight-through estimator (STE), proposed by Bengio and colleagues, addresses this difficulty by substituting a surrogate derivative. Despite its heuristic nature and huge empirical success in training quantised neural networks, its stability
and generalisation properties remains largely a mystery.

In this talk, we study the identity STE for training a two-layer binary-activation
network trained with hinge loss. Our key observation is that, in the saturated-output regime, the zero-initialised sample-wise STE recursion is exactly stochastic sub-gradient descent on a convex latent loss. This
reformulation connects a discontinuous neural-network training rule to classical convex optimisation and provides a tractable framework for analysing its stability.

We examine the geometry of coupled updates through an exact distance identity and establish approximate non-expansiveness. These properties
yield explicit algorithmic stability and generalisation bounds. Combining
them with an optimisation (convergence) bound gives an excess induced-risk rate of
$O(n^{-1/2})$ after $n^2$ updates. Under margin separability, a complementary
one-pass analysis yields the statistically optimal rate 
$O(R^2/(\gamma^2 n))$ expected excess misclassification bound for a randomised
iterate, where $R$ bounds the input norm and $\gamma$ is the separation
margin. The results illustrate how convex reformulation and update geometry
can explain the statistical behaviour of a widely used surrogate-gradient algorithm.

talks.speaker: Mr Aamir Yousuf
talks.authors: Carsten Carstensen, Neela Nataraj, Ricardo Ruiz-Baier, Aamir Yousuf
talks.title: Unconditionally stable and energy conserving discretization \\of the dynamic von K\'arm\'an equations
talks.abstract:
The dynamic von Kármán equations couple the large deflection of a thin elastic plate with an Airy stress function through a nonlinear Monge-Ampère bracket. This nonlinearity makes it difficult to construct time discretizations that are unconditionally stable, conserve energy, and admit a rigorous error analysis.
We propose a fully discrete scheme for the clamped plate that combines the nonconforming Morley finite element in space with a modified Newmark second-order time discretization. The scheme conserves energy at the discrete level and is unconditionally stable. Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem gives existence of a discrete solution, and uniqueness follows under smallness assumptions on the data and time step. Under additional smallness of the load, we prove optimal-order a priori error estimates in the piecewise energy norm, with optimal spatial rates and quadratic convergence in time.
