Numerical experiments confirm the predicted rates and show that the 2D von Kármán model closely matches 3D simulations as the plate thickness decreases.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Erchuan Zhang
talks.title: Determinant-Normalized Pad\'e Coordinates for Approximate Riemannian Cubic Splines on the Special Unitary Group
talks.abstract:
Riemannian cubic splines are intrinsic interpolants defined as critical points of the mean squared covariant acceleration. Their direct computation requires the solution of nonlinear boundary-value problems and is therefore substantially more difficult than the classical Euclidean construction. This talk develops a determinant-corrected Pad\'e coordinate scheme for the special unitary group $\mathrm{SU}(n)$. A direct application of the diagonal Pad\'e approximant of type $(2,2)$ maps $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ into $\mathrm{U}(n)$ but, when $n\geq 3$, does not generally preserve determinant one. We remove this defect by introducing a determinant-normalized Pad\'e retraction that maps exactly into $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ while retaining an $O(h^5)$ approximation to the matrix exponential.  Interlocking normalized Pad\'e coordinates then reduce the determination of the interior velocities to a block-tridiagonal linear system, in which the coordinate differential generally couples the components of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$. 

This talk is based on the joint work with Prof. Lyle Noakes (UWA).

talks.speaker: Prof Dingxuan Zhou
talks.title: Distribution regression with neural networks and linear transformers
talks.abstract:
Deep learning has been widely applied and brought breakthroughs in speech recognition, computer vision, natural language processing, and many other domains. The involved deep neural network architectures and computational issues have been well studied in machine learning. But there is much less theoretical understanding about the modelling, approximation or generalization abilities of deep learning models with network architectures. 

This talk describes the topic of distribution regression with structured neural networks where the input space for learning is the set of probability distributions with high complexity. Generalization analysis is presented when the network structure takes the forms of deep convolutional neural networks or linear transformers.

talks.speaker: Ms Yuyan Zou
talks.authors: Yuyan Zou, Luke G.Bennetts, Hailong Guo
talks.title: Mixed Unfitted finite element approximation of band structures in photonic crystals
talks.abstract: Photonic crystals are periodic dielectric structures whose optical properties are characterized by Maxwell eigenvalue problems with discontinuous material coefficients. Accurate computation of their band structures is challenging, particularly for complex inclusion geometries, where conventional finite element methods require body-fitted meshes. In this work, we develop a mixed unfitted finite element method based on the Floquet–Bloch transform for computing photonic band structures. The method employs a uniform background mesh independent of the inclusion geometry, avoiding the need for interface-fitted meshing and allowing periodic boundary conditions to be imposed through direct identification of degrees of freedom. The discrete spaces preserve the de Rham commuting relation for the shifted operator, providing a structure for establishing uniform inf–sup stability and excluding spurious eigenmodes. We further establish optimal convergence of eigenvalues and eigenspaces, with constants independent of the interface position. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method for photonic crystals with complex inclusion geometries.

talks.speaker: Prof Craig Costello
talks.title: Isogenies: hard problems for a quantum world
talks.abstract:
Elliptic curves underpin much of today’s public-key cryptography, yet a sufficiently powerful quantum computer would break the mathematical problems on which that cryptography relies. Could the same curves help us build its replacement? Shifting attention from points on elliptic curves to maps between them opens up a different mathematical landscape, and a rich source of candidates for post-quantum cryptography.

This talk will survey isogeny-based cryptography through its mathematical foundations, promising constructions and dramatic setbacks. We will see how ideas from number theory and arithmetic geometry have supplied both new cryptographic tools and unexpected ways to break them. Particular attention will go to the open problems that shape the field: finding paths through isogeny graphs, computing endomorphism rings, and understanding how much quantum algorithms can accelerate these tasks. These questions connect the security of practical protocols to fundamental gaps in our understanding of computation on elliptic curves.

The talk will offer a broad mathematical introduction to the field, its current state and the opportunities ahead. No specialist background in cryptography will be assumed.

talks.speaker: Mr Blair Butler
talks.title: Cyclic isogenies of abelian surfaces via dimension 4
talks.abstract:
Isogeny algorithms in higher dimensions have focused on $(l,...,l)$-isogenies, whose degree $l^g$ grows with the dimension. Take a principally polarised abelian surface with maximal real multiplication by a real quadratic field $K$, where $l$ splits into principal ideals $\beta$ and $\Bar{\beta}$. Any nonzero $\beta$-torsion point generates a cyclic isogeny of degree $l$ that respects the polarisation and real multiplication. These cyclic isogenies could outperform $(l,...,l)$-isogenies as the dimension grows, but they are notoriously hard to compute.
We realise cyclic isogenies out of $E_1 \times E_2$ as a block of a single tr($\beta$)-isogeny between abelian fourfolds. Recent four-dimensional $(2,2,2,2)$-chains make this practical.
This is joint work with Raul Hernandez-Gonzalez, Luciano Maino, Nicolas Swanson and Suo-Jun Tan.

talks.speaker: Mr Harry Hiatt
talks.title: Poncelet Porism in Extremal Pencils Over Finite Fields
talks.abstract: The study of Poncelet's porism is often restricted to pairs of conics in general position over the fields $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, or $\mathbb{C}$. Here, we study Poncelet's porism for three special pencils of conics where any two members are tangent in at least one point, over fields of finite characteristic. We are able to provide a complete description of the necessary conditions for the existence of Poncelet polygons for any pair of conics from any of the three families. We do so from three different but related perspectives: the stabiliser groups that fix the conics from each pencil, the underlying singular elliptic curves of each family and the polynomial Pell equations associated to each pencil and their respective Poncelet polygons.

talks.speaker: Prof Nalini Joshi
talks.title: Arithmetic dynamics of a discrete Painlev\'e equation
talks.abstract: Motivated by arithmetic dynamics on elliptic curves, and related estimates for cryptography, we consider bounds on the number of image points of a discrete Painlev\'e equation over finite fields. Our results reveal some surprising observations, which contrast sharply with the theory of discrete Painlev\'e equations over $\mathbb C$.

talks.speaker: Mr Tomas Lasic Latimer
talks.authors: Nalini Joshi, Tomas Lasic Latimer, Pieter Roffelsen
talks.title: Integrable Systems as Verifiable Delay Functions
talks.abstract: In this talk, we discuss the viability of integrable systems as a possible source of post quantum secure verifiable Delay Functions (VDFs). We will begin with a brief introduction of the theory of VDFs and current vulnerabilities to Shor's algorithm. We then discuss integrable systems over finite fields and the pros and cons of their properties from the perspective of VDFs. Finally, we conclude with an example application of a discrete Painleve equation as a VDF.

talks.speaker: Mr Yintong Luo
talks.title: Elliptic Curve Arithmetic on a Quantum Computer
talks.abstract: Shor's quantum algorithm computes the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) in polynomial time. Here, we explore how the curve model, coordinate system, and special properties of the curve affect the cost of this computation. We discuss how classical methods for elliptic curve arithmetic can be adapted to reversible quantum computation, with particular attention to the properties of addition laws and the use of affine and projective coordinates. We examine how the requirements of quantum computation change the trade-offs between arithmetic operations and storage.

talks.speaker: Dr Jun-Yong Park
talks.title: Families of Elliptic Curves over $k(t)$, $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$, $\mathbb{C}(t)$: Height Moduli, Exact Counts, Mordell--Weil Rank Jumps
talks.abstract:
The notion of height does more than order the infinite set of elliptic curves: it turns their totality into a geometric space. After a brief motivation over $\mathbb{Q}$, I will explain how this geometry connects moduli, exact counting, and Mordell--Weil rank jumps.\\

Over $k(t)$, an elliptic curve can be viewed as an elliptic surface over $\mathbb{P}^1_k$. Its Faltings height is the degree of the fundamental line bundle; on the semistable locus, this is the degree of the Hodge line bundle pulled back along the classifying map to $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,1}$. The resulting height moduli stack is of finite type and parametrizes elliptic curves of fixed Faltings height $n$, with a natural correspondence between its strata and Kodaira fibre configurations.\\

Over $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$, motivic methods, together with explicit calculations in characteristics $2$ and $3$, yield exact weighted and unweighted counts of elliptic curves of bounded height in every characteristic. The lower-order terms reflect nonsmooth-locus corrections, extra-automorphism loci, and minimality defects.\\

Over $\mathbb{C}(t)$, when restricted to elliptic surfaces with only irreducible nodal singular fibres, the Shioda--Tate formula identifies Mordell--Weil rank jumps with Picard rank jumps. At each fixed height $n\ge 2$, the intersection of the period image with Hodge loci produces analytically dense loci of Jacobian elliptic surfaces with Mordell--Weil rank at least $r$ throughout the transverse range $1\le r\le\left\lfloor\frac{10n-2}{n-1}\right\rfloor$.

talks.speaker: Dr Pieter Roffelsen
talks.title: Integrable systems over finite fields and p-curvature
talks.abstract: In this talk I will describe recent explorations of integrable systems over finite fields, focusing on Painlev\'e equations.  In the complex-analytic setting, their integrability is encoded by transcendental integrals of motion, constructed from monodromy data of associated Lax pairs. Over finite fields however, a strikingly different picture emerges: $p$-curvature of the Lax pairs gives rise to algebraic integrals of motion. I will explain this construction and some of its consequences.

talks.speaker: Mr Abraham Zhang
talks.title: Height bounds on modular polynomials for various modular functions
talks.abstract: The classical modular polynomial $\Phi_N$ characterises isogenies between elliptic curves. This is useful in cryptography, for example in isogeny-based cryptography and efficient point counting on elliptic curves. The coefficients of $\Phi_N$ are large enough that storing them is difficult, so one may want to work with the modular polynomials $\Phi_{f,N}$ for other modular functions $f$. In this talk, I will give new explicit height bounds on modular polynomials for the $j$-invariant, the cube root of $j$, and the Weber $\mathfrak f$-function. The preprint is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22214.

talks.speaker: Dr Min Chen
talks.title: Optimal domain for fundamental Gap
talks.abstract:
The first author and Clutterbuck proved the fundamental gap conjecture,
establishing a sharp lower bound on the fundamental gap of a convex Euclidean
domain with given diameter. The associated rigidity question, raised by Yau, asks
whether there exists an extremal domain attaining the sharp lower bound. Amato,
Bucur and Fragalá proved that in dimension at least two this bound is not attained
by any nondegenerate convex domain. In this paper we consider the problem of
finding the sharp lower bound on the fundamental gap for convex planar domains if a
lower bound on the minimum width is also imposed. We characterise the geometry
of the extremal domains if the imposed lower width bound is small compared to the
circumradius: these are ‘circular wedges’ given by intersecting a disk with a cone of
small angle from a distant centre.

talks.speaker: Mr Petrus Ferreira
talks.title: Thorny Questions About Non-null Lie Quadratics
talks.abstract:
Cubic splines are energy minimal interpolants important for control problems in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). An extension of cubic splines to general Riemannian manifolds are Riemannian cubics. Riemannian cubics locally minimise the energy functional \(\displaystyle \int_a^b\langle \frac{D}{dt}\dot x,\frac{D}{dt}\dot x\rangle dt\), where \(\displaystyle \frac{D}{dt}\) is the covariant derivative under the Levi-Civita connection. In bi-invariant Riemannian Lie groups such curves satisfy the pair of differential equations:
\[\dot x=T_eL_xV\]
\[\ddot V=[\dot V,V]+C.\]
Where \(C\) is an arbitrary constant and \(T_eL_x\) is the left action of the group onto it's Lie algebra. Solutions to the second equation are called Lie quadratics. When \(C\neq 0\) we call these non-null Lie quadratics. We focus our study to \(\mathfrak{so}(3)\) as it is the simplest non-trivial space these curves exist in.
\\
\\
In 1989 mathematicians attempting to form asymptotics of non-null Lie quadratics found that points colloquially labelled ``thorns" impeded their progress and have since remained mysterious. In this talk we aim to provide the audience with the first ever formal definition of thorns, briefly mention extensions to other Lie algebras and briefly explore how these points are organised. We will then provide a first ever proof of a long held conjecture regarding the apparent circular organisation of thorns.

talks.speaker: Mr Marcus Flook
talks.title: Extrinsic geometric flows of hypersurfaces immersed in complex space
talks.abstract:
In $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$, domains of holomorphy with sufficiently regular boundary can be characterised by (Levi) pseudoconvexity, which is defined by the positive-semidefiniteness of the Levi form. Inspired by research from Huisken and Klingenberg [1], we discuss results on extrinsic geometric flows of hypersurfaces immersed in complex space by symmetric functions of the eigenvalues of the Levi form. These flows are analogous to other extrinsic flows, including mean curvature flow, however with an additional degeneracy. We also discuss future directions of the work.

[1] G. Huisken, W. Klingenberg, Flow of real hypersurfaces by the trace of the Levi form, Math. Res. Lett. 6 (1999), no. 5-6, 645–661.

talks.speaker: Ms Mashniah A. Gazwani
talks.title: Surface diffusion flow of axially symmetric hypersurfaces with generalised Neumann boundary conditions
talks.abstract: In this talk, we consider evolving smooth, embedded, axially symmetric hypersurfaces whose boundaries intersect two parallel hyperplanes perpendicularly. It is assumed that the initial hypersurface is sufficiently far from the axis and has axial curvature sufficiently small in $L^2$. We prove that the solution to the surface diffusion flow with generalised Neumann boundary conditions beginning from this initial data exists for all time, remains axially symmetric and at a distance away from the axis, with the smallness condition preserved. Moreover, the evolving hypersurface converges exponentially in the $C^\infty$-topology to a cylinder with the same axis and enclosing the same volume as the initial hypersurface.This is a joint work with Prof. James McCoy.

talks.speaker: Mr Benjamin Hamblin
talks.authors: Benjamin Hamblin, Victor Calo, Klaus Regenauer-Lieb
talks.title: Ruppeiner Contact Geometry: Symmetries and Quasi-Equilibrium Invariants Over Thermodynamic Phase-Spaces
talks.abstract: We examine symmetries in a contact Lagrangian description of coupled thermodynamic systems in quasi-equilibrium. We identify a non-trivial invariant for many-channel systems by analogy with the Tolman--Ehrenfest effect of relativistic thermodynamics.  Treating different positions on the entropy manifold as virtual thermodynamic observers subject to channel-coupling potentials, we derive the relation $\zeta_i\,T_i = C$ from two independent arguments (conservation of an effective coupled energy; a field-theoretic variational principle), and compute the coupling coefficient $\zeta_i$ explicitly from the Ruppeiner curvature via a path integral on the entropy manifold.

talks.speaker: Mr Stepan Hudecek
talks.authors: Timothy Buttsworth, Artem Pulemotov, Stepan Hudecek
talks.title: Poisson equation for G2-Laplacian
talks.abstract: Riemannian manifolds whose holonomy group lies inside the exceptional Lie group $G_2$ are called $G_2$-manifolds. These manifolds have several interesting properties (they are Ricci-flat) and are of interest in geometric analysis as well as in mathematical physics and other fields. In this seminar, we will give an introduction to the theory of $G_2$-manifolds and discuss an associated non-linear Laplacian-type operator whose kernel essentially determines whether a compact manifold is $G_2$. We will present uniqueness and existence results for the Poisson’s equation of this operator on cohomogeneity-one manifolds.

talks.speaker: Mr Joseph Kwong
talks.title: The Fino--Vezzoni conjecture on homogeneous spaces
talks.abstract: One way of distinguishing between complex manifolds is by studying special metrics they admit: the most infamous are Kahler, balanced, and pluriclosed metrics. The Fino--Vezzoni conjecture asserts that a compact complex manifold admitting both balanced and pluriclosed metrics must also admit a Kahler metric. In this talk, I will explain the proof of the conjecture in the homogeneous case.

talks.speaker: Mr An Ky Duy Nguyen
talks.title: Quadratic Killing tensors on symmetric spaces
talks.abstract:
We will present some recent results on the structure of the algebra of Killing tensors on Riemannian symmetric spaces. The fundamental question (Bolsinov -Matveev-Miranda-Tabachnikov, 2018), is whether any Killing tensor field on a Riemannian symmetric space is decomposable, that is, is a polynomial in Killing vector fields. For spaces of constant
curvature, the answer is in the positive, as has been known for quite some time. The same is true for the complex projective space (Eastwood, 2023). For other rank one symmetric spaces, the answer is almost always in the
negative (Matveev-Nikolayevsky, 2024). We show that for several classes of symmetric spaces, all quadratic Killing tensors are decomposable. This is a joint project with my PhD supervisors Y.Nikolayevsky (La Trobe University, Australia) and V.Matveev (University of Jena, Germany).

talks.speaker: Dr Yuri Nikolayevsky
talks.title: Orthogonal coordinates and separation of variables on symmetric spaces
talks.abstract:
I will present two results on geometrically distinguished coordinate systems on Riemannian symmetric spaces. 

The first one states that a symmetric space admits local orthogonal (diagonal) coordinates if and only if it is a product of space forms. The ``if'' direction is clear. The non-existence of orthogonal coordinates on $\mathbb{C}P^m$ and $\mathbb{C}H^m$ for $m \ge 2$ has been established by [Gauduchon, Moroianu, 2020] and then extended to other symmetric spaces \emph{of rank one} of non-constant curvature by [Bolsinov, Dullin, Matveev, Nikolayevsky, 2026]. 

The second result states that the Hamilton-Jacobi equation on an \emph{irreducible symmetric space of compact type} $M$ admits a separation of variables if and only if $M$ is either a round sphere or the complex projective space with the Fubini-Study metric. The ``if'' direction follows from [Kalnins, Miller, 1986] and [Boyer, Kalnins, Winternitz, 1985]. The proof of the ``only if'' direction requires the above theorem on orthogonal coordinates and results from the theory of quadratic Killing tensors on symmetric spaces.

talks.speaker: Mr Max Orchard
talks.title: Closed geodesics on three-dimensional Lie groups
talks.abstract: Geodesics are among the most fundamental objects in Riemannian geometry, with closed geodesics being of particular interest. However, detecting when geodesics are closed is difficult in general, and the problem of classifying all closed geodesics on a given Riemannian manifold is challenging even under strong symmetry assumptions. In this talk, I will focus on three-dimensional Lie groups equipped with arbitrary left-invariant metrics; in this situation, the geodesic equation reduces to a first-order ODE on the Lie algebra known as the Euler--Arnold equation. I will discuss how this reduction can be used to analyse the existence and structure of closed geodesics in this setting. This is joint work with Timothy Buttsworth and Stephen Preston.

talks.speaker: Dr Virinchi Rallabhandi
talks.authors: Bernardo Araneda, James Lucietti and Virinchi Rallabhandi
talks.title: The classification problem for toric self-dual Einstein 4-manifolds
talks.abstract: In this talk I'll discuss the classification problem for self-dual, Einstein 4-manifolds with toric symmetry. When the curvature constant is positive, it is known that the only such manifolds are $S^4$ and $\mathbb{CP}^2$ with their canonical metrics, while in the Ricci-flat case a hyper-Kähler structure results. In contrast, the negatively curved setting is far less constrained. It is known that any Killing vector field on a self-dual Einstein manifold defines a local conformal Kähler structure. Furthermore, the local form of these metrics is known - and in fact can be determined through a single, axis-symmetric, harmonic function on $R^3$. However, a global analysis of the solutions is lacking. In this talk, I'll present the results of our paper where we proved that if the conformal Kähler structure associated to one of the torus Killing fields is global and extends to an ALE manifold with no additional fixed points, then the corresponding self-dual Einstein manifold is precisely given by an infinite class of multipole solutions constructed by Calderbank, Pedersen and Singer.

talks.speaker: Prof Gerd Schmalz
talks.authors: Martin Kolar, David Sykes, Gerd Schmalz
talks.title: Rigid spheres and Bochner-Kähler manifolds
talks.abstract: This is an update on a 2024 AustMS talk on Bochner-Kähler manifolds studied through their correspondence with spherical Sasakian manifolds (rigid spheres). This yields a universal formula for their Kähler potentials, a host of examples, and a classification, according to their symmetries.

talks.speaker: Dr James Stanfield
talks.authors: Elia Fusi, Ramiro Lafuente, and James Stanfield
talks.title: Homogeneous generalised Ricci flows.
talks.abstract:
The generalised Ricci flow is a coupling of the Ricci flow with the heat equation on closed 3-forms, and arises naturally in mathematical physics, and complex geometry. For instance, the pluriclosed flow, a popular flow of non-Kaehler Hermitian metrics can be viewed as a generalised Ricci flow.

In this talk, we discuss some recent results obtained in the homogeneous setting. In particular, we prove that the flow exists for all times and converges to a self-similar solution on a large class of solvable Lie groups. We also show some surprising instability results on compact Lie groups, disproving a conjecture of Garcia-Fernandez and Streets.

The proof relies on an extension of Lauret's method of moving brackets and real geometric invariant theory to the setting of homogeneous generalised geometry. We expect this framework to be very powerful in answering further questions about the homogeneous flow.

This is based on joint work with Elia Fusi and Ramiro Lafuente.

talks.speaker: Mx Marcos Martinez Wagner
talks.title: A splitting theorem for Einstein manifolds with symmetries
talks.abstract:
In this talk, I will give a brief overview of a theorem I recently proved: every connected negative-Einstein manifold with cocompact symmetries splits isometrically as a Riemannian product $H \times K$, where $H$ is homogeneous and $K$ is compact.

This confirms a conjecture of B\"ohm and Lafuente. As a consequence, we obtain a new proof of the 1975 Alekseevskii conjecture, which states that every homogeneous negative-Einstein manifold is isometric to a simply connected solvable Lie group endowed with a left-invariant Riemannian metric.

talks.speaker: Dr Glen Edward Wheeler
talks.title: Ideal lemniscates and butterflies
talks.abstract: We study critical points of the length-penalised ideal energy, which combines the squared arclength derivative of curvature with a penalty on length. Adding this length term produces a rich family of stationary planar curves. In joint work with Shinya Okabe, we prove the existence, for every positive penalty parameter, of infinitely many geometrically distinct smooth closed immersed critical points with turning number zero. These include lemniscate-type and butterfly-type families. I will explain the variational construction using symmetric arcs, the selection mechanism that ensures smooth closure, and the role of boundary-layer analysis and Fresnel phases. Numerical illustrations reveal the geometry of these families and motivate questions about their conjectural relationship to self-similar solutions of the free ideal flow.

talks.speaker: Mr Marcus Wong
talks.authors: Nathan Duignan, Naoki Sato, Marcus Wong
talks.title: Classifying invertible k-plectic structures on $\mathbb{R}^n$
talks.abstract:
We look at a generalisation of symplectic geometry: multisymplectic geometry. A key trick in the proof of Darboux’s theorem is that there is only one equivalence class of non-degenerate $2$-forms on $\mathbb{R}^n$. A natural question to ask is if this also holds for k-forms on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Ryvkin (2019) says no and gave a classification. 

We can refine this question to look at $k$-forms with a specific condition, invertibility. In this talk, we classify the equivalence classes of invertible $k$-forms on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

talks.speaker: Mr Henry Wood
talks.title: Ricci Flows and Bracket Flows on Twisted Principal Bundles
talks.abstract: To study invariant Ricci flows on twisted principal bundles, we formulate the bracket flow, an associated flow that describes the evolution of the structure constants. Using this technique, we prove Type III estimates for Ricci flows on twisted principal bundles with a circle base and nilpotent fibres. Furthermore, we show that on the universal cover, these normalised Ricci flows subconverge in the pointed smooth Cheeger–-Gromov topology to a solvsoliton metric on a simply connected solvable Lie group.

talks.speaker: Dr Andreia Chapouto
talks.authors: Andreia Chapouto, Simão Correia, João Pedro Ramos
talks.title: Gauge transform for the Korteweg-de Vries equation and well-posedness below the $H^{-1}$-scale
talks.abstract:
In this talk, we consider the low regularity well-posedness problem for the Korteweg-de Vries equation (KdV) on the real line. Aiming to bridge the regularity gap between the scaling critical space $H^{-\frac{3}{2}}$ and the known optimal well-posedness in $H^{-1}$ in $L^2$-based Sobolev spaces, we consider rough data in Fourier-Lebesgue spaces. Via infinite normal form reductions and exploiting algebraic cancellations, we introduce a new gauged KdV equation, equivalent to the original one at high regularity, but better behaved for rough solutions, below the $H^{-1}$-scale. Our method is easily adapted to other equations with quadratic derivative nonlinearities, such as the dispersion generalized BO equations, and thus it is totally independent of the KdV completely integrable structure. 
This talk is based on joint work with Simão Correia (IST, U. Lisboa) and João Pedro Ramos (IMPA).

talks.speaker: Miss Rongshan Chen
talks.title: Heat-wave semigroup estimates and the compressible Navier-Stokes Equations
talks.abstract: In this talk, we will report some recent progresses regarding the interplay between the harmonic analysis and the compressible Navier-Stokes (CNS) equations. Bases on the parabolic-hyperbolic nature of the CNS, we launched the study of space-time estimates for heat-wave semigroup  by using recent harmonic analysis developments. Moreover, we apply the new estimates to obtain sharp global well-posedness in the critical Besov spaces. To achieve the latter goal, we have proposed a new CNS framework, which fully exploits the inherent structure of the equations and successfully applies the aforementioned estimation techniques, ultimately obtaining the optimal range of p within 6 dimensions.

talks.speaker: Mr Puti Dai
talks.title: Local Well-posedness for the Extended Schr\"{o}dinger-Benjamin-Ono System
talks.abstract:
We study the well-posedness problem for the extended Schr\"{o}dinger-Benjamin-Ono system (eSBO) on the real line. This system couples a Schr\"{o}dinger field $u$ with a Benjamin-Ono type field $v$, including a term of the form $dx(v^2)$. This latter term, just as in the case of the Benjamin-Ono equation, causes the system to become quasilinear and intractable via Picard iteration.
I will attempt to sketch the outline of the proof of local well-posedness in $H^{s+\frac 12}(\mathbb R)\times H^{s}(\mathbb R)$ for any $s\geq 0$. More specifically, we follow the framework introduced by Molinet and Pilod in 2010 for the Benjamin-Ono equation, but with some differences.

talks.speaker: Mrs Minoli Fernando
talks.title: Computing harmonic-measure distribution functions of regions on the surface of the sphere.
talks.abstract:
Harmonic-measure distribution functions, or h-functions, encode, for each positive number r, the probability that a particle undergoing Brownian motion in a region first reaches the boundary within the given distance r of its starting point. The study of h-functions draws on the fields of complex analysis, probability, and computational and numerical methods. While these functions have been studied
extensively for planar regions, much less is known about their behaviour for regions lying on curved surfaces.

I will discuss how to calculate h-functions of regions on the surface of the unit sphere using both analytical and numerical methods. I examine a range of geometries, including regions formed either by deleting line segments along great or small circles, or by deleting circular portions of the sphere. I also investigate how the behaviour of h-functions changes when the starting point of the Brownian particle is moved to different locations on the sphere. The examples reveal several intriguing points, particularly about how the form and asymptotics of the h-function vary with the shape of the boundary components and the position of the starting point relative to the boundary. This is a joint work with Christopher Green, Lesley Ward, Takashi Sakajo, and Koya Sakakibura.

talks.speaker: Dr Justin Forlano
talks.authors: Andreia Chapouto, Justin Forlano, Thierry Laurens
talks.title: The intermediate nonlinear Schrödinger equation
talks.abstract: In this talk, I will discuss recent results regarding the intermediate nonlinear Schrödinger equation (INLS). Analytically, INLS is a one-dimensional completely integrable nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a cubic derivative nonlinearity and is $L^2$-critical. A limiting form of INLS is the continuum Calogero-Moser equation (CCM), which is also completely integrable. Interestingly, CCM keeps the Hardy space $L^2_+$ invariant, and, under this assumption, tools from complete integrability have recently resolved the well-posedness problem for CCM in $L^2_+$. I will discuss progress on the well-posedness for INLS and CCM (not relying on complete integrability), outside of the Hardy space and in low-regularity. Our approach combines a gauge transformation, bilinear Strichartz estimates and a refined decomposition for smooth solutions. This is based on joint work with A. Chapouto (CNRS, Monash) and T. Laurens (UW-Madison).

talks.speaker: Dr Terry Harris
talks.title: Divergence set for the wave equation in higher dimensions
talks.abstract:
I will discuss the following result: If $u$ solves the wave equation in $\mathbb{R}^{4+1}$ with initial data $u(\cdot,0) = u_0(\cdot) \in H^s$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,0) = u_1(\cdot ) \in H^{s-1}$, where $0.5 < s \leq 0.55$, then $u(x,t) \to u_0(x)$ and $\partial_tu(x,t) \to u_1(x)$ pointwise as $t \to 0$, for all $x$ outside an exceptional set of Hausdorff dimension at most $6-4s$. In a very small range of $s$, this verifies a conjecture of Barcel\'o, Bennett, Carbery, and Rogers. More generally,  a partial improvement to the exceptional set bound in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is obtained for $n \geq 4$ and $1/2 < s < n/4$.

This is joint work with Xiumin Du and Jianhui Li.

talks.speaker: Miss Xuejing Huo
talks.title: Sharp estimates for certain operators related to Schr\"odinger operators with inverse-square potential
talks.abstract:
Let
	\[
	\mathcal L_a=-\Delta+\frac{a}{|x|^2},
	\qquad -\frac{(n-2)^2}{4}\le a<0,
	\]
	in dimension \(n\ge3\), and set
	\[
	\sigma:=\frac{n-2}{2}-\frac12\sqrt{(n-2)^2+4a}.
	\]
	In this talk, we will present sharp estimates for the Schrödinger flow and imaginary powers associated with \(\mathcal L_a\) at the endpoint \(p=p_0=n/(n-\sigma)\). More precisely, for \(\gamma>0\), \(\gamma\ne1\), and \(\beta=\gamma n(1/p_0-1/2)\), we will show that
	\[
	(I+\mathcal L_a)^{-\beta/2}e^{i\tau\mathcal L_a^{\gamma/2}}
	\]
	maps \(L^{p_0,1}(\mathbb R^n)\) to \(L^{p_0,\infty}(\mathbb R^n)\), with operator norm bounded by \(C(1+|\tau|)^{n(1/p_0-1/2)}\). We will also present the corresponding endpoint estimate for the imaginary powers \(\mathcal L_a^{i\alpha}\), with operator norm bounded by \(C(1+|\alpha|)^{n(1/p_0-1/2)}\).

talks.speaker: Mr Nicola Baglioni
talks.title: Integrable deformations via auxiliary fields
talks.abstract: In this talk a will present a recent approach to the study of integrable Quantum Field Theories (QFTs) in two spacetime dimensions. In particular I will focus on a class of stress tensor deformations of some conformal models (e.g. the Principal Chiral Model) that preserves the integrability of the seed theory, in the sense of the existence of a Lax connection. An infinite family of these deformations can be studied with the aid  of auxiliary fields that one can couple to the undeformed theory. Some of these deformations, like the celebrated TTbar deformation, are believed to survive quantisation and in the past few years have offered important insights in the study of the space of Integrable QFTs, with surprising connections to quantum gravity and string theory.

talks.speaker: Prof Murray Batchelor
talks.title: The Riemann zeta function in quantum light-matter dynamics
talks.abstract: The quantum Rabi model describes a two-level system coupled to a harmonic oscillator and is a fundamental model of light-matter interaction. We show that its dynamics can be arranged so that the spin coherence is determined exactly by the completed Riemann $\xi$-function. A finite-energy oscillator state constructed from the Jacobi theta function then makes the Riemann zeros appear as exact dephasing points in the quantum evolution. The construction also gives a physical interpretation of the functional equation and extends to the full time evolution, where the dephasing events occur along a closed phase-space trajectory with an exact revival.

talks.speaker: Prof Philip Broadbridge
talks.title: Evolution of non-oscillatory field modes in expanding FLRW universe.
talks.abstract:
In a dark energy $\Lambda$ -dominated universe, the expansion may contribute an effectively negative mass to the covariant scalar Klein-Gordon field that is minimally coupled to the metric.
Each dynamical mode eventually transitions oscillatory-to-repulsive. Runaway modes may originate in the mass dominated cosmological epoch if their repulsive-to-oscillatory transition does not occur before $\Lambda$ dominates. Canonical quantisation leads to an infinite number of Fock particulate modes plus a finite number of runaway modes for which there is no vacuum state of lowest energy and no number operator that commutes with the Hamiltonian. Because the runaway modes have increasing but finite classical degrees of freedom, we are free to choose the cyclic representation of the Heisenberg algebra that follows from Euclidean field theory after a Wick rotation in the complex t-plane.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Evgeny Buchbinder
talks.title: Heterotic Flux Vacua with a Small Superpotential
talks.abstract:
Though heterotic string theory on a smooth Calabi-Yau manifold is phenomenologically attractive, the stabilisation of moduli remains an underdeveloped topic. In my talk, I will discuss heterotic CY compactifications with NS-NS three-form flux in view of moduli stabilisation and investigate whether the value of the flux superpotential
evaluated at supersymmetric minima can be small. A non-vanishing flux superpotential induces a tree-level scalar potential for complex structure moduli, and controlled moduli stabilisation requires that the value of the flux superpotential be sufficiently small to compete with non-perturbative effects. I will present two no-go theorems regarding supersymmetric vacua with small superpotential in moduli space. I will also present an analysis in regions of moduli space not forbidden by the no-go theorems, where the period structure is known. In general, the small values of the flux superpotential are not easy to obtain, however, 
in certain examples values compatible with moduli stabilisation can be found.

talks.speaker: Mr Arcadia Fegebank
talks.title: Massive gauge models for higher-spin supermultiplets in three dimensions
talks.abstract: Gauge-invariant models for massive higher-spin fields are of interest for a variety of reasons, including recent attempts to use such models to describe rotating black holes. While much work has been done in the non-supersymmetric case, there is a gap in the literature for models of higher-spin massive gauge supermultiplets. This talk will review the first construction of such models. In particular, we shall describe the process of dimensionally reducing the massless supersymmetric models in four dimensions to massive models in three dimensions endowed with a central charge. It will be shown that the central charge is responsible for the mass generation.

talks.speaker: Mr Cengiz Gazi
talks.authors: Cengiz Gazi, Jan de Gier, Peter Taylor, Rhys Bowden
talks.title: Differential-difference equation for blockchains and asymptotic results
talks.abstract:
Differential-difference equations appear vastly in mathematical physics such as in lattice dynamics and integrable systems. In this talk, we present a differential-difference equation which arises as a Functional Law of Large Numbers limit of a Markovian model for a blockchain mining process. This equation describes deterministic time dynamics of blockchain heights in the large miner limit. 

Our first result is that solutions of this equation converge uniformly, within a co-moving frame, to a limiting profile in the large height limit. Utilising an asymptotic computation, due to Brunet and Derrida (1997), we present an explicit expression for the position of the travelling front, which exhibits a leading order logarithmic Bramson correction in time. For a finite number of miners, we further present a correction to the travelling speed which is logarithmic in the number of miners. Finally, by application of a result due to Ablowitz and Zeppetella (1979), we identify that, for a specific choice of the travelling speed, the Painlev\'e integrable, travelling wave solution of the Fisher-KPP equation with drift accurately matches our limiting profile. Our results are supported by numerical simulations.

talks.speaker: Prof Jan De Gier
talks.title: Matrix product classical and quantum non-equilibrium stationary states
talks.abstract:
We discuss an out-of-equilibrium generalisation of matrix product operators to implement duality transformations in one-dimensional boundary-driven Markov processes on lattices. In contrast to local dualities associated with generalised symmetries, here the duality operator intertwines two Markov processes via generalised exchange relations and realises the out-of-equilibrium duality glob-
ally. We construct these operators exactly for the symmetric simple exclusion process with distinct out-of-equilibrium boundaries. In this case, out-of-equilibrium boundaries are dual to equilibrium boundaries satisfying Liggett’s condition, implying that the Gibbs–Boltzmann measure captures out-of-equilibrium physics when leveraging the duality operator.

talks.speaker: Dr Jessica Hutomo
talks.authors: Martin Cederwall, Jessica Hutomo, Sergei Kuzenko, Kurt Lechner, Dmitri Sorokin
talks.title: Non-linear chiral 4-form gauge field theories in ten dimensions
talks.abstract: In this talk, we will discuss the general structure of non-linear gauge theories of a chiral 2-forms in D=6 and chiral 4-forms in D=10 spacetime dimensions. While the corresponding action in D=6 is governed by a single independent field-strength invariant and can be formulated as a stress-tensor deformation of the free theory, the D=10 case is considerably more intricate, involving 81 independent invariants constructed from the self-dual five-form field strength. We will show that the deformation structure familiar from lower dimensions does not generally extend to D=10, where the so-called root-TTbar flow equations involve both stress-tensor invariants and additional higher-order field-strength structures.

talks.speaker: Dr Joseph McGovern
talks.title: Geometrically probing interacting gauge theories
talks.abstract:
Gauge theories flow to conformal field theories in the infrared. A particularly constrained class of theories - Gauged Linear Sigma Models (GLSM)- may flow to special CFTs that describe nonlinear sigma models with Calabi-Yau target spaces. 

Turning this around, tools from Calabi-Yau geometry (like mirror symmetry and topological string theory) can be used to shed light on a novel GLSM that we study. We uncover a new class of GLSMs that flow to Calabi-Yau sigma models, distinguished by the presence of a cubic superpotential.

talks.speaker: Prof Makoto Narita
talks.title: $C^0$-inextendibility of spatially homogeneous spacetimes in string theory
talks.abstract: We investigate the $C^0$-inextendibility of cosmological singularities within the Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton-axion (EMDA) theory, contributing to the mathematical verification of the Strong Cosmic Censorship (SCC) conjecture. The modern geometric study of $C^0$-inextendibility, pioneered by Sbierski, was initially applied to Schwarzschild spacetimes and Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetimes, and subsequently extended to anisotropic vacuum Kasner solutions. According to the BKL conjecture, generic cosmological singularities are expected to be dominated by velocity-terms in the field equations near the boundary, making Kasner-like dynamics highly relevant. Incorporating these insights, we extend Sbierski's framework to accommodate the rich structure of low-energy string effective actions with coupled scalar, pseudo-scalar and electromagnetic fields. We prove that the past boundaries of some spatially homogeneous and anisotropic solutions in EMDA theory cannot be continuously extended as Lorentzian manifolds. Our results show the validity of the SCC conjecture in a broader class of gravitational theories.
talks.affiliation: National Institute of Technology, Okinawa College

talks.speaker: Mr Ainsley Nicoll
talks.title: Discrete Lindblad Systems
talks.abstract:
In this talk we define a class of operators which we call 'discrete Lindblad systems.' The purpose of these operators are to generalise the Lindblad Master Equation, studied in quantum statistical 
mechanics, to a discrete setting in which we can use the language of integrable vertex models. We then demonstrate in an example how techniques from integrable vertex models can be used to find an exact steady state solution to the discrete system and how this solution then descends to a steady state solution of the associated continuous time Lindblad master equation.

talks.speaker: Dr Madeline Nurcombe
talks.authors: Alexander Molev, Madeline Nurcombe, Eric Ragoucy
talks.title: Casimir elements for orthosymplectic Lie superalgebras
talks.abstract: Casimir elements are elements of the centre of the universal enveloping algebra of a Lie (super)algebra. They are of interest in representation theory, as their eigenvalues may be used to classify irreducible representations, particularly for finite-dimensional Lie (super)algebras, and in physics, where they can correspond to conserved quantities such as total angular momentum. In a previous paper (arXiv:2507.22738), Molev and I constructed Segal--Sugawara vectors for affine orthosymplectic Lie superalgebras; these vectors play a similar role to Casimir elements in the affine case. In this talk, I will discuss our work with Ragoucy (arXiv:2607.06926) on the Harish-Chandra images of these Segal--Sugawara vectors, and the resulting construction of Casimir elements for finite-dimensional orthosymplectic Lie superalgebras.

talks.speaker: Mr Joshua Pinelli
talks.authors: Evgeny Buchbinder, Darren Grasso, Sergei Kuzenko, Joshua Pinelli
talks.title: Heat kernel approach to nonlinear electrodynamics and non-compact duality-invariant couplings
talks.abstract:
The one-loop effective action (OLEA) encodes the leading quantum corrections to the dynamics of a system of elementary particles. In this talk, I will discuss the logarithmically divergent term (the ``induced action’’) of the OLEA obtained by integrating out quantum vector fields. In particular, we focus on two theoretical models:

(i) A general class of nonlinear electrodynamics (NLED) theories in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime. Working in the weak-field regime, we compute the leading contributions to the heat kernel. In the case of conformal NLED, we also discuss causality as a necessary and sufficient condition for convergence.

(ii) Non-compact duality-invariant couplings of $n$ Abelian gauge fields to complex scalar fields in a gravitational background. This model is Weyl invariant and possesses the maximal non-compact duality group $\mathsf{Sp}(2n, {\mathbb R})$. Although both symmetries are anomalous in the quantum theory, they should be respected by the induced action.

In each case, quantisation yields non-minimal differential operators, for which standard heat kernel techniques are not immediately applicable. To address this challenge, we employ a Fourier-based method, generalised to curved backgrounds using Synge’s world function and the parallel displacement propagator. This covariant construction allows us to compute the heat kernel asymptotics through a DeWitt expansion and a Volterra series representation.

talks.speaker: Mr Parth Raina
talks.authors: Michele Galli, Christian Kennedy, Parth Raina, Gabriele Tartaglino-Mazzucchelli
talks.title: Superform approach to equivariant localization in supergravity
talks.abstract: Equivariant localization has proven to be a powerful technique for evaluating on-shell supergravity actions on supersymmetric backgrounds admitting a U(1) isometry. A key step in this technique is the construction of an equivariantly closed polyform whose top-degree component corresponds to the supergravity lagrangian. Although such polyforms have been identified in a wide range of supergravity theories, a general and systematic explanation for their origin has been lacking. In this talk, I will describe a superspace mechanism that systematically produces off-shell equivariant polyforms on supersymmetric backgrounds from closed superforms. In particular, I will illustrate this construction in 4D N = 2 conformal supergravity.

talks.speaker: Mr Damodar Rajbhandari
talks.title: Bosonic Ghost Correlators: A Case Study
talks.abstract:
We study a two-dimensional bosonic ghost conformal field theory with central charge c = 2, a widely used in superstring theory and a recipe for the Wakimoto free-field realisations. The fusion rules between ghost primaries can be analytically computed using Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov technology which generates infinitely coupled differential equations. 

Using Belavin–Polyakov–Zamolodchikov-like technology, we computed certain four-point correlators under specific conditions on affine charges and observed logarithmic singularities. This aligns with the 2015 algebraic result of David Ridout and Simon Wood which confirmed that the bosonic ghost system is a logarithmic conformal field theory. Additionally, we conjecture that some four-point correlators are expressed in terms of a generalised hypergeometric function 3F2.

talks.speaker: Dr Pieter Roffelsen
talks.title: On monodromy of monodromy surfaces
talks.abstract: In enumerative geometry, monodromy groups capture the symmetries of enumerative problems, a topic revitalised by Harris's influential 1979 paper on the subject. In this talk, I will discuss some elementary enumerative problems regarding monodromy surfaces. The corresponding monodromy groups can be identified with groups of combinatorial, Galoisan and integrable-systems origins, leading in particular to the solution of an open problem in the theory of Painlev\'e equations.

talks.speaker: Dr Jake Stirling
talks.title: New duality-invariant models for nonlinear supersymmetric electrodynamics
talks.abstract:
Duality-invariant theories possess several interesting properties, with the most famous example being Maxwell electrodynamics in a vacuum. The condition of $\mathsf{U}(1)$ duality invariance is equivalent to the requirement that the Lagrangian solves the so-called self-duality equation. In the supersymmetric setting, one deals with a superfield analogue of the self-duality equation. Generating solutions to the self-duality equation is difficult due to its nonlinear nature. 

In this talk, we delve into the auxiliary superfield formalism, a methodology capable of deriving solutions to the self-duality equation. Following this, we present a new family of $\mathsf{U}(1)$ duality-invariant models for nonlinear $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric electrodynamics coupled to supergravity. It includes the Cribiori-Farakos-Tournoy-van Proeyen supergravity-matter theory for spontaneously broken local supersymmetry with a novel Fayet-Iliopoulos term without gauged $R$-symmetry.

talks.speaker: Mr Luke Wen
talks.title: Representation theory of $W_{3,k}$ at the non-admissible levels
talks.abstract: Vertex operator algebras (VOAs) lie at the intersection of mathematics and conformal field theory. An important family is provided by $W$-algebras, which are closely connected with affine Lie algebras and Wess–Zumino–Witten models. In this talk, I will focus on the principal $W$-algebra $W_3^k$ at the non-admissible levels $k+3=\frac{2}{2m+1}$, where $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$. I will discuss the construction of explicit singular vectors and the resulting necessary polynomial constraints on the highest weights of modules over its simple quotient. The main tools are principal quantum Hamiltonian (Drinfeld–Sokolov) reduction, free-field realisations, screening operators, and Jack and skew Jack symmetric functions.

talks.speaker: Ms JIAYUE YUAN
talks.authors: Ian Marquette, Jiayue Yuan, Yao-Zhong Zhang
talks.title: Algebraic structure and representations for Hamiltonians from confluent supersymmetric quantum mechanics
talks.abstract: We study the algebraic structure of Hamiltonians obtained from confluent supersymmetric quantum mechanics (SUSYQM). In this construction, a Jordan chain is used when the factorization energies coincide. Starting from a solvable Hamiltonian with known ladder operators, we construct new ladder operators for the transformed system and study their action on the physical states. An important point is that the state at the confluent energy must be treated separately from the other transformed states. For a physical seed, this produces additional zero modes of the ladder operators and can split the physical spectrum into separate invariant sectors. We relate this structure to the corresponding polynomial algebra and illustrate the construction using the infinite square well and the harmonic oscillator. We first discuss the second-order confluent case and then consider the extension to a Jordan block of arbitrary length.

talks.speaker: Ms Yuyang Zhou
talks.authors: Jan de Gier, Richard Kenyon, Michael Wheeler, Yuyang Zhou
talks.title: The five vertex model on a rectangle
talks.abstract: We derive a determinantal expression for the inhomogeneous asymmetric five vertex model in a rectangular geometry with arbitrary boundary conditions at the bottom and top. Standard non-intersecting lattice path, or free fermion, approaches are not applicable and the determinantal form thus is not immediate.

talks.speaker: Mr Tim Bourke
talks.title: Calculus Without Limits
talks.abstract:
The "Calculus Without Limits" research project at the Australian National University ran two pilot projects during 2026 with groups of ANU first year Mathematics students centred around two 90 minute workshops on "Indian Sequences and Series".  These workshops focussed on first year level sequences and series topics, drawing the material from the Indian "Yuktibhasa", which was written by a member of the Kerala School of Astronomy and Mathematics in the southern state of Kerala in India around 1530 and so has rightly been called "the first textbook of calculus".

The workshops, and the project more broadly, sought and are seeking to study the effect on students' learning of presenting commonly taught topics drawn from a less well known culture and source.  The focus is on students' attitudes to mathematics and their own levels of confidence and interest before and after the workshops.

The project is transdisciplinary, divided up into three interwoven, interrelated "streams" - 1. Undergraduate Calculus Education, 2. Equitable and Accessible Mathematics, and 3. Cross-Cultural Influences in Mathematics.

In 2027, the project will continue with two major focuses:

1. Extending the work done with the two workshops in 2026 to design, build, test, advertise, and utilise an ANU "Indian Calculus" Escape Room in 2027, once again studying ANU Matheamtics student attitudes before and after the event;

2. Further researching "Cross-Cultural Influences in Mathematics" with a specific focus on claims by a number of authors that the work of the Kerala School may have been transmitted to European mathematicians and scientists who later presented and utilised very similar ideas - including limits, sequences and series, Taylor series and series convergence.

talks.speaker: Mrs Jo-ann Larkins
talks.title: Reassessing Assessment
talks.abstract:
Traditional assessment norms within mathematics are being challenged by technology capable of both producing fully worked solutions and bypassing invigilation. This questions our ability to assure that our assessment truly reflects the student learning and skills acquisition we are credentialing them for. We need to immediately reimagine what the future of assessment looks like against a rapidly changing landscape. But for many of us that’s a daunting prospect and we don’t know where to begin.
Drawing on my experience as teaching-focused academic and Teaching Champion whose research uses assessment transformation as a framework for re-thinking assessment to generate meaningful evidence of learning, we’ll explore some starting points for rethinking assessment design in our units and courses. We’ll move beyond content and skills to explore how we can harness our understanding of the culture of mathematics to more authentically and creatively assess our students.

talks.speaker: Dr Fu Ken Ly
talks.authors: Linda Galligan, Leanne Rylands, Raquel Salmeron, Fu Ken Ly, Joshua Peate, Michael Brickhill, Sophie Kennedy
talks.title: Mathematics Learning Support in Australian Universities: A National Update
talks.abstract:
Almost two decades ago, MacGillivray’s national review on mathematics and statistics learning support argued that such support should be recognised as a core component of university teaching and learning. Since then, participation in university support has broadened, fewer degrees have mathematics prerequisites, and student backgrounds have become increasingly diverse.
\\

A recent national audit examined mathematics preparation and learning support across Australian universities. A 2023 desktop audit of 42 institutions was followed by consultations and interviews across 40 universities during 2023–2025. The study mapped mathematics and statistics learning centres, bridging and enabling programs, workshops, peer learning and online support, and examined how provision varies between institutions.
\\

Results of the audit will be presented, providing an update on MacGillivray's review. Consequences of the findings for the Australian mathematics sciences community will be discussed, including how mathematics departments and learning-support specialists might contribute to more coherent and sustainable support across Australian universities.

talks.speaker: Dr Vladimira Seckarova
talks.title: Beyond Getting the Answer: Supporting Mathematical Reasoning in the Age of Generative AI
talks.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can help students write code and produce computational solutions without necessarily understanding the methods they use or the results they obtain. This presents a challenge for mathematics and statistics educators, particularly in large first-year units: how can students be supported to use AI productively while remaining responsible for their analytical decisions?

This contribution describes teaching developments across two consecutive first-year data science units at Monash University. In 2025, weekly in-class project stand-up meetings with the teaching team were introduced to support students working on group projects. While these meetings appeared to improve cooperation, they did not sufficiently address students’ understanding of the analytical methods used in their projects.

In 2026, ungraded, paper-based comprehension checks were introduced in class in both units. These involve direct questions about the material and open-ended questions requiring students to explain their reasoning. Students can use AI and other resources to prepare and discuss their answers as a group. During each check, however, they explain their answers to a member of the teaching team without access to digital devices or other resources. The aim is to make students’ understanding visible and encourage them to explain their reasoning, rather than simply produce an answer or working code.

Following the introduction of the comprehension checks, we observed improvements in students’ project analyses and discussions during the weekly stand-up meetings. Students were better able to explain their analytical choices, interpret model results and suggest improvements. They were also progressing further through the modelling process, with individual students exploring multiple models rather than struggling to complete a single model.

This experience illustrates how AI can support programming while students retain human agency in deciding how to analyse their data, evaluating results and determining what to do next. It raises broader questions about how mathematics educators can make students’ reasoning visible and preserve students’ active role in problem-solving when computational solutions are increasingly easy to generate.

talks.speaker: Mr Donald Shearman
talks.title: Diagnose. Support. Succeed.
talks.abstract:
Universities face growing challenges supporting diverse student cohorts entering disciplines with varying levels of assumed mathematical knowledge. While traditional diagnostic testing identifies skill gaps, it often offers limited pathways for scalable remediation. This talk presents an integrated model combining adaptive diagnostic testing with targeted, self-paced learning resources to effectively support students transitioning into tertiary mathematics.
We examine how adaptive diagnostics efficiently pinpoint strengths and gaps across prerequisite concepts using personalized question pathways, minimizing student testing burden. Key focus areas include knowledge map design, diagnostic data interpretation, and delivering actionable insights to both students and educators. Identified gaps are addressed through aligned self-paced resources that allow students to revisit foundational concepts, practice core skills, and track progress independently.
By linking diagnostic testing directly to tailored remediation pathways, institutions shift from basic student classification toward a developmental model that fosters mathematical readiness, confidence, and agency. Drawing on practical examples, the session addresses key considerations around scalability, student engagement, instrument validation, and the evolving role of adaptive systems alongside artificial intelligence.
Ultimately, this presentation aims to stimulate discussion on building responsive, evidence-based systems that help students bridge the gap between assumed and actual mathematical knowledge.

talks.speaker: Dr Hayden Tronnolone
talks.title: Two Years of Oral Assessment in First-Year University Mathematics Classes
talks.abstract: Interactive oral assessments provide a means of assessing students’ verbal communication skills while also exploring their conceptual understanding, beyond the procedural understanding common in first-year mathematics classes. This assessment type can be readily adapted to different cohorts across teaching locations, including online students, while also providing a relatively secure form of assessment. While forms of oral assessment have been used in higher-level mathematics classes, the large enrolment numbers often found in first-year cohorts have acted as a barrier to their adoption. We present a format for interactive oral examinations used for the past two years in a first-year, first-semester mathematics class at Flinders University (South Australia) with enrolments of up to approximately 300 students. The oral assessments comprised ten-minute conversations with students at the end of the semester, with an emphasis on conceptual understanding and justification of methods used. It was found that this assessment type could be run efficiently and helped to avoid the skewed final grade distribution observed previously. Surveys run pre- and post-assessment showed that students felt apprehensive about this assessment type while also recognising the benefits it provided. The responses show a shift in student attitudes around the impact of artificial intelligence on assessment, with increasing agreement that oral assessment strengthens academic integrity. The oral examinations revealed a gap in student understanding, both in their ability to communicate verbally and in general conceptual understanding, that is potentially impacting their success in future studies, and we discuss attempts to address this through in-class activities. Analysis of the survey data and grade distributions suggests that oral examinations provide an authentic and reliable assessment format in the presence of artificial intelligence.

talks.speaker: Dr Victor Villalba
talks.title: Designing scalable STACK assessment in first- and     second-year mathematics: Lessons from ENG1090 and MTH2010
talks.abstract:
STACK enables students to enter mathematical expressions rather than select
answers from predetermined options, while using computer algebra to assess
mathematical equivalence and provide targeted feedback. This presentation
reflects on the design and implementation of STACK quizzes in two engineering
mathematics units at Monash University: ENG1090, a large first-year foundation
mathematics unit, and MTH2010, a second-year unit in multivariable calculus.

ENG1090 has approximately 1,150 students and covers topics ranging from algebra
and trigonometry to vectors, calculus and differential equations. A typical
three-question quiz therefore generates about 3,450 individual responses.
MTH2010 has approximately 230 students. Each weekly STACK quiz contains two
questions based directly on the material covered in the applied classes,
providing students with an opportunity to consolidate that week's work and
receive immediate feedback.

The presentation will discuss the practical principles that guided the
development of these questions: parameter randomisation, testing mathematical
equivalence, identifying common misconceptions through Potential Response
Trees, writing useful feedback, and maintaining consistent marking across many
question variants. It will also consider the quality-assurance work required,
including automated screening of parameters, systematic testing of deployed
variants, and checking for unintended alternative answers.

The experience suggests that STACK can support frequent and scalable
assessment while reducing repetitive marking. However, its effectiveness
depends less on automation itself than on careful mathematical design,
rigorous testing, close alignment with classroom activities, and an
appropriate balance between computer-marked work and human assessment of
reasoning and communication.

talks.speaker: Dr Ting-Ying Chang
talks.title: Making Analysis Themed, Humorous and Satisfying
talks.abstract:
To complement existing lectures and tutorials for MATH2023 Analysis at the University of Sydney, the Learning Hub (Mathematics) introduced Supplementary Learning Tutorials that reimagine rigorous mathematical worksheets as playful, narrative-driven puzzles.

Each themed activity guides students through mathematical problems towards a final meta-puzzle that enables independent answer-checking. These shared challenges encourage discussion, collaboration and problem-solving, while creating memorable reference points for revisiting concepts in later weeks.

Drawing on positive student feedback, this presentation explores how playful, self-checking activities can complement formal teaching while fostering engagement, confidence and mathematical understanding.

talks.speaker: Dr Alice Devillers
talks.title: WA Junior Olympiad
talks.abstract:
I will give an overview of the local high school maths competition (WAJO) that has been occurring at UWA since 1999 (but the organising committee includes people from a variety of backgrounds, not just UWA staff members).
This competition is unique in its set up: a traditional individual component, followed by a team component consisting of questions of increasing difficulty, all on a single topic.

talks.speaker: Dr Sean Gardiner
talks.title: Ten years of the Simon Marais Mathematics Competition
talks.abstract: The Simon Marais Mathematics Competition (SMMC) is an international undergraduate-level contest designed to encourage creative mathematical problem-solving. Distinctive features of the competition include the option for students to compete in pairs, and the inclusion of an unsolved open problem in one of the papers each year. This talk looks back on the first ten years of the SMMC through the problems it has posed and the choices behind its design, exploring how the competition’s emphasis on collaboration, creativity, and curiosity can engage students with research-style mathematics beyond the undergraduate curriculum.

talks.speaker: Dr David Kohan Marzagão
talks.authors: David Kohan Marzagão and Josh Murphy
talks.title: Rep-tiles, Consensus, and other interactive mathematical objects
talks.abstract:
Several university-level and research mathematics can be represented via intuitive (and fun) interactive mathematical objects. These are often used for engagement of current students but also the general public. 


The Connections Project, hosted at King's College London, is one of those informal collections of interactive objects, created in partnership with universities in Europe and South America. Some of our more computer-sciency objects have webpages and interactive demos on top of physical pieces: \url{https://connections.computer}. 

In this presentation, I will showcase some of our recent work, including on tiling problems and on opinion dynamics on graphs. Furthermore, I wanted to share some funding avenues we explored in the past to hopefully allow us to find ways for new UK-Australia partnerships.

talks.speaker: Dr Geoffrey Pearce
talks.title: Modular Origami and Maths for Gifted Secondary Students
talks.abstract: Modular origami involves assembling individually folded paper ‘modules’ to build decorative 3-dimensional structures. These structures can usually be modelled with graphs, and very often a given model will exhibit interesting symmetry properties in its colouring or structure. In this talk I will discuss ways I have used modular origami as the basis of a short lecture course with the aim of introducing gifted Year 11 and 12 students to concepts in group theory and graph theory, and pure maths more generally.

talks.speaker: Dr Kamilla Rekvényi
talks.title: Your Stereotypical Mathematician: Mathematics Outreach on Instagram and Beyond
talks.abstract: In this talk, I will share my experiences of communicating mathematics through my Instagram account, @mathswithkala. From unexpected applications of mathematics to humorous takes on stereotypes, I will discuss how short-form content can make mathematics more accessible and relatable. I will also reflect on the challenges of communicating mathematics accurately to non-specialists and the importance of visibility, particularly for women in mathematics.

talks.speaker: Ms Rachel Rachel Theunissen
talks.title: The Australian Mathematics Competition and beyond
talks.abstract: The Australian Mathematics Trust (AMT) is widely known for running the Australian Mathematics Competition (AMC) in over 30 countries. In this session we will explore the AMC and the many other competitions offered by the AMT. This will include when the competitions typically run and a look at the type of problems posed in each competition.

talks.speaker: Dr Andy Tran
talks.title: Mathematical Problem Solving Program
talks.abstract: The Mathematical Problem Solving Program (MaPS) is offered to motivated high school students to explore mathematics beyond the school curriculum. Established in 2020, the program is run by the School of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Sydney and has continued to evolve over the years. In this talk, we will introduce the structure of the core program, which combines fortnightly notes, online classes and problem sets. We will also explore additional activities including in-person events and research-style projects. We will share our experiences and lessons learned from developing and running the program and we hope that this talk will be useful for educators and outreach organisers interested in developing enrichment opportunities for school-aged students.

talks.speaker: Mr Attawut Wongpradit
talks.title: Designing Difficulty: Adaptive Tromino Tiling Puzzles for Cognitive Engagement
talks.abstract: Puzzles can be powerful tools for cognitive training, but only if people keep playing them, and adherence depends on getting the difficulty right. In this talk we present a family of physical puzzles based on deficient board tilings, in which players cover a deficient grid (i.e. missing one or more squares) using standard trominoes together with a non-standard ``alien'' piece. We show the different design mechanisms that we have developed for adjusting difficulty: changing the shape of the alien piece, varying the number of holes, and altering the shape of the board. Since difficulty has no single definition, we discuss several measures that can serve as proxies for it, such as the number of solutions and computational solving time, along with the limitations of each metric. Finally, we share early feedback from participants and describe how the project will investigate the effect of difficulty level on participant adherence.

talks.speaker: Prof Yihong Du
talks.title: The fractional Fisher-KPP equation with free boundaries
talks.abstract: In this talk, I'll discuss a free boundary problem with fractional diffusion, as a model for species spreading in a one dimensional setting. This model is a natural extension of some existing local and nonlocal free boundary models, where the diffusion term is given by the classical Laplacian (for local diffusion), or by an integral operator generated by a continuous integrable kernel function J(x) (for nonlocal diffusion), and their propagation dynamics has been rather well understood when the growth function is of Fisher-KPP type. Due to the difficulties caused by the singularity and non-integrability of the associated kernel function of the fractional Laplacian, and the lack of general enough regularity results for operators extending the standard fractional Laplacian, such an extension has been open for many years now. In this talk, I'll report some recent successes on this question, and explain some of the difficulties blocking the progress, as well as the new ingredients that enabled the breakthrough. This talk is based on joint work with Huyuan Chen (Shanghai) and Wenjie Ni (UNE).

talks.speaker: Prof Ben Andrews
talks.authors: Ben Andrews, Min Chen, Tianci Luo, Yong Wei, Rong Zhou
talks.title: Gauss curvature flows in curved backgrounds
talks.abstract: The Gauss curvature flows, in which convex hypersurfaces move by the power $\alpha>0$ of their Gauss curvature, are well understood for $n$-dimensional hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$:  They shrink to points in finite time, and become spherical in shape if $\alpha>\frac{1}{n+2}$, and ellipsoidal if $\alpha=\frac{1}{n+2}$.  Our new result extends this to Riemannian backgrounds:  The same conclusion holds, provided there exists a convex function on the region enclosed by the hypersurface -- in particular, this is true for convex hypersurfaces in manifolds of positive sectional curvature or in Hadamard manifolds, and several other settings of geometric interest.  On the other hand, if no such function exists then the solution exists for all time and does not contract to a point.

talks.speaker: Dr Andreia Chapouto
talks.authors: Andreia Chapouto, Benjamin Harrop-Griffiths, Guopeng Li, Tadahiro Oh, Tengfei Zhao
talks.title: The shallow-water limit of the intermediate long wave equation
talks.abstract:
The intermediate long wave equation (ILW) models the propagation of an internal wave at the interface of a stratified fluid of finite depth, providing a natural connection between the deep-water regime (= the Benjamin-Ono regime) and the shallow-water regime (= the Korteweg-de Vries regime). In this talk, we will discuss recent developments in the latter regime. Exploiting the dispersive and completely integrable nature of ILW, we will see how to establish shallow-water convergence of $L^2$-solutions, through a perturbative normal form approach and weakly uniform equicontinuity. Moreover, this limit is singular: on the real line, the solution map jumps from not being $C^2$ to becoming analytic in the limit.
This talk is based on joint works with Benjamin Harrop-Griffiths, Guopeng Li, Tadahiro Oh, and
Tengfei Zhao

talks.speaker: Prof Florica Corina Cirstea
talks.title: Elliptic equations with Hardy potentials and gradient-dependent absorption
talks.abstract:
Under sharp conditions, we present the existence and refined asymptotic behaviour near zero for all positive radial solutions to elliptic equations of the form 
$$ \mathbb L_{\rho,\lambda}(u)=\Delta u+ (2-N-2\rho)\, \frac{x\cdot \nabla u}{|x|^2}+ \frac{\lambda}{|x|^2}u=|x|^{\theta}\,u^q\, |\nabla u|^m\quad \mbox{in } \Omega\setminus\{0\},
$$
where $\Omega=B_R(0)$ for suitable $R>0$ and 
$N\geq 2$. The dynamics of such solutions is very rich and complicated since 
$\rho, \lambda,\theta\in \mathbb R$ are arbitrary, with $ m>0$, $q\geq 0$ and $\kappa=m+q-1>0$. 
We identify all profiles near zero (and at infinity via a modified Kelvin transform) under optimal conditions, depending on how $\Theta:=(\theta+2-m)/\kappa$ relates to $0$ or the roots 
$\Theta_\pm$ of $t^2+2\rho t+\lambda$ when $\lambda\leq \rho^2$. For each profile, we advance new methods that unearth the higher order terms in the asymptotic expansion, illuminating the influence of the operator $\mathbb L_{\rho,\lambda}$ and the absorption not visible just from the leading term. Our refined asymptotics is new even when $m=0$ and $\rho=(2-N)/2$.

talks.speaker: Dr Justin Forlano
talks.title: Invariant Gibbs dynamics for the nonlinear Schrödinger equations on the disc
talks.abstract:
In 1983, Zakharov posed a question regarding the numerical observations that solutions to nonlinear dispersive
PDEs possess a “returning property”: solutions return close to their initial data after a long time. Explaining
this phenomenon has partly motivated the program of constructing invariant Gibbs dynamics for nonlinear
dispersive PDEs, which presents considerable analytical and probabilistic difficulties. Nonetheless, there has
been dramatic progress in this study for equations posed on (flat) tori; a canonical example being the nonlinear
Schrödinger equation (NLS), studied in this context by Bourgain, McKean, Tzvetkov, and Deng-Nahmod-Yue. In particular, Tzvetkov (2006) initiated the study of Gibbs dynamics for NLS on other compact manifolds, such as the unit disc with radial symmetry. On the disc, he proved almost sure global well-posedness for sub-quintic nonlinearities, and Bourgain-Bulut (2014) provided weak solutions for all powers. With Y. Wang (Univ. Birmingham) we completed this program by constructing a strong global-in-time solution theory for NLS on the disc with respect to the Gibbs measure for all power type-nonlinearities.

talks.speaker: Prof Zihua Guo
talks.title: Strichartz estimates for the Schrodinger equation on the one-dimensional torus
talks.abstract:
we prove the sharp Strichartz estimates for the Schr\"odinger equation on the one-dimensional torus. The proof was found with the assistance of AI. Surprisingly, the proof mainly uses p-adic harmonic analysis tools, with only a little number theory and without incidence geometry at all. This talk will
introduce p-adic harmonic analysis and highlight its advantages compared to the Euclidean harmonic analysis. This is a joint work with Yangkendi Deng, Chenjie Fan, Shaoming Guo, Yongming Luo.

talks.speaker: Prof Emmanuel Kengne
talks.title: The problematic role of mathematics in analytical studies devoted to nonlinear dispersive media
talks.abstract: Analytical studies of nonlinear dispersive media face deep mathematical challenges because the interaction between nonlinearity (which steepens waves and can cause finite-time singularity or blow-up) and dispersion (which spreads wave packets out according to frequency) resists universal closed-form solution.
