On the other hand, gaps in mathematical knowledge lead many non-mathematician researchers to perceive mathematics and their own fields of research as entirely separate disciplines, which prevents them from correctly applying mathematical logic when studying problems that involve mathematical modeling. Such shortcomings generally lead to erroneous results when attempting to find analytical solutions to these problems. In our presentation, we demonstrate how the incorrect use of logical operators---such as "AND," "OR," implication, and equivalence---can distort the results of an analytical study. To illustrate the negative effects of gaps in mathematical knowledge on scientific results, we will examine (i) the case of pulse propagation in optical media, the dynamics of which are governed by the complex nonlinear Shynaray-IIA equation and (ii) the case of the modulational instability phenomenon.

talks.speaker: Dr Kwok-Kun Kwong
talks.title: Higher order isoperimetric inequalities and rigidity for surfaces in $\mathbb R^n$
talks.abstract:
In this talk, I will present a hierarchy of sharp higher-order isoperimetric inequalities for compact surfaces in Euclidean spaces of arbitrary codimension, generalising classical results of Carleman, Sachs, Chakerian, and Li–Schoen–Yau. These inequalities involve higher derivatives of the boundary curve and the mean curvature vector of the surface, and are obtained using higher order Wirtinger inequalities. 

The equality cases exhibit interesting rigidity properties in higher codimension, including non-flat and non-circular equality cases. At lower orders, their Fourier modes can be decomposed into circles lying in mutually orthogonal planes, while this property no longer holds at higher orders. I will also present a characterisation of higher-order equality cases through a factorisation of the unit tangent map into planar rotations.

This is joint work with Xu-Qian Fan.

talks.speaker: Dr jihye lee
talks.title: The ABP method and Geometric inequalities
talks.abstract: The Alexandrov-Bakelman-Pucci (ABP) method is a powerful tool in the study of partial differential equations and geometric inequalities. In this talk, I will discuss how the ABP method can be used to establish geometric inequalities, beginning with its application to the classical isoperimetric inequality. I will then present some extensions of this approach to Riemannian manifolds under various curvature assumptions.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Ji Li
talks.title: Optimal lifting of Levi-degenerate hypersurfaces and applications to the Cauchy–Szeg\"o projection
talks.abstract:
We study the Cauchy–Szeg\"o projection on a class of Levi-degenerate model hypersurfaces in \(\mathbb C^2\). We lift their horizontal vector fields to left-invariant vector fields on a stratified nilpotent Lie group and use this lifting to obtain a Taylor expansion on the original hypersurfaces. We then discuss Schatten class membership of commutators of the Cauchy–Szeg\"o projection, including a Besov space characterization for \(p>4\) and a rigidity result for \(0<p\leq4\).

This is based on the joint work with Der-Chen Chang, Alessandro Ottazzi and Qingyan Wu, in  Adv. Math. 2026.

talks.speaker: Dr Zhuo Ma
talks.authors: Yihong Du, Zhuo Ma, Zhi-Cheng Wang
talks.title: Precise propagation profile for a monostable free boundary problem in time-periodic media
talks.abstract:
We study the long-time dynamics of the following problem:
\[
u_t-du_{xx}=f(t,u), \qquad x\in[g(t),h(t)],
\]
where $f(t,u)$ is periodic in $t$ and monostable in $u$ for fixed $t$, and  $[g(t), h(t)]$ represents the population range of an invasive species with density $u(t,x)$. The free boundaries $x=g(t)$ and $x=h(t)$ evolve subject to a ``preferred population density" condition at the habitat edges, which allows the population range to both expand and shrink. We prove that there is a unique time-periodic semi-wave associated to this problem, and the solution u(t,x) converges to this semi-wave as $t\to\infty$, which extend the corresponding results for autonomous environments to time-periodic settings. Previously, such sharp results were proved for a free boundary model only when $f$ is autonomous ($f=f(u)$), while in the time-periodic case, only a less precise result was obtained under an extra strong KPP condition on $f$. A key feature of our result is that no KPP condition is imposed on $f$, which played an essential role in the proof of the existing results in the time-periodic setting.

talks.speaker: Dr Abdul Majid
talks.title: Stability Analysis and Surrogate Modeling of Elastic Rods
talks.abstract: This work presents a combined analytical and data-driven framework for studying the stability of elastic rods and strips. The stability behavior is first investigated using a linear stability analysis of the governing equations around equilibrium configurations. A perturbation approach is then employed to characterize the onset of instability and the resulting oscillatory modes. Particular attention is given to the dependence of these modes on geometric, material, and loading parameters. The analytical results provide a basis for understanding the transition from stable to unstable configurations and the associated dynamic response. To enable efficient exploration of the parameter space, high-fidelity solutions are generated from the underlying model. These solutions are subsequently used to train a neural-operator-based surrogate model that learns the mapping between system parameters and stability characteristics. The surrogate model provides rapid predictions of the oscillatory response without repeatedly solving the full governing equations. The proposed framework combines physical modeling with machine learning to efficiently capture complex stability behavior.
talks.affiliation: The Institute of Business Administration Karachi

talks.speaker: Prof James McCoy
talks.title: Contraction of convex and near-convex hypersurfaces in the sphere
talks.abstract:
We study closed hypersurfaces evolving by smooth, symmetric, strictly increasing, convex speeds that are one-homogeneous functions of the principal curvatures.  We prove that every smooth, closed, strictly convex initial hypersurface contracts in finite time to a point that, after rescaling, is a round sphere. This gives the convex-speed counterpart to Claus Gerhardt’s spherical roundness theorem in the sphere, whose argument for nonlinear speeds relies on strict concavity.  The main new ingredient is a roundness estimate based on the quotient of the speed function and the harmonic
mean curvature. 

We also establish a quantitative convexification result driven by the positive ambient curvature: if the initial hypersurface is `slightly non-convex' then, under a uniform
admissibility condition and an explicit curvature size bound, the solution becomes strictly convex after an explicitly-determined positive time and consequently contracts to a round point.  This result is new even for the mean curvature flow. For surfaces in $\mathbb{S}^3$, the corresponding convexification result holds for arbitrary smooth, symmetric, strictly increasing, one-homogeneous speeds, without any convexity or concavity assumption.

talks.speaker: Mr Devesh Rajpal
talks.title: Uniqueness of Lp Minkowski problem near the affine exponent
talks.abstract: We prove dimensional $C^0$ estimates for solutions of the $L_p$ Minkowski problem in the entire supercritical range. This implies a spectral gap of the Brunn-Minkowski operator for $L_p$ Minkowski solutions. Furthermore, following methods from Ivaki-Milman and Du's results, this allows us to prove uniqueness of the $L_p$ Minkowski problem in the supercritical range near the affine exponent $p = -n-1$ and importantly without any symmetry assumption.

talks.speaker: Dr Haotian Wu
talks.title: Ważewski's retraction method
talks.abstract: We explain how Ważewski's retraction method can be used to construct solutions to nonlinear PDEs. Our main example is a rigorous construction of the degenerate neckpinch singularities in Ricci flow due to Angenent, Isenberg and Knopf.

talks.speaker: Dr Nan Wu
talks.title: The Lowener-Nirenberg Problem on Lipschitz Domains
talks.abstract:
We study asymptotic behaviors of solutions to the Loewner-Nirenberg problem in general Lipschitz domains 
and establish optimal asymptotic expansions in terms of the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff convergence. 
We further establish the quantitative estimates for such Gromov-Hausdorff convergence, 
and prove the equivalence to the classical optimal asymptotic expansion under appropriate boundary regularity.

talks.speaker: Ms Joshua Zavone
talks.authors: Joshua Zavone, supervised by Florica-Corina Cirstea
talks.title: Existence and full asymptotic expansion for singular non-linear elliptic equations
talks.abstract:
We consider the behaviour of positive local solutions (near the origin in $\mathbb{R}^N$) of the following singular non-linear elliptic equation: $$
\Delta u-(N-2+2\rho)\frac{x\cdot\nabla u}{|x|^2}+\lambda\frac{u^\tau|\nabla u|^{1-\tau}}{|x|^{1+\tau}}=\frac{u^q}{|x|^2},
$$ 
for arbitrary real parameters $\rho,\lambda,\tau,q$ subject to $0\leq\tau < 1$ and $q>1$. The possible first order behaviours as $x\to 0$ have already been completely classified into a list of asymptotic profiles, and this talk presents significant refinements of these profiles for radial solutions. By new methods, adapted to each profile separately, we obtain both the existence of radial solutions, and a precise refinement of the first order behaviour into a full asymptotic expansion of the solutions (with arbitrarily many terms). For profiles with infinitely many radial solutions, these solutions can now be distinguished by the presence of an arbitrary coefficient in the full expansion (which may only appear well after the first term).

talks.speaker: Ms Xiaohui Zhang
talks.authors: Yihong Du, Wenjie Ni, Xiaohui Zhang, Meng Zhao
talks.title: A Free Boundary Model for the Spatial Spread of West Nile Virus
talks.abstract:
Reaction-diffusion free boundary models provide an effective framework for describing the spatial spread of infectious diseases. In this work, we propose a new free boundary model for the spatial spread of West Nile virus (WNv) of mosquito-bird transmission. We assume that the range boundary is moving according to a preferred population density assumption, which means that the densities of infected birds and infected mosquitoes at the moving range boundary are positive.
	
We first establish the global existence and uniqueness of solutions. We then characterize the long-time dynamics of the model according to the basic reproduction number $R_0$. When $R_0<1$, the infected region vanishes asymptotically. When $R_0>1$, the infected region expands indefinitely, and the populations converge to a unique positive equilibrium. To further investigate the spreading dynamics, we study the associated semi-wave problem and prove the existence and uniqueness of a semi-wave solution, which determines the asymptotic spreading speed of the virus.

talks.speaker: Mr Qiyu Zhou
talks.title: Convexity, Cylindrical Estimates, and Surgery for High-Codimension Mean Curvature Flow with One Spacelike Codimension
talks.abstract: In this talk, I will present new convexity and cylindrical estimates for high-codimension mean curvature flow with one spacelike codimension. These results are inspired by the argument of Haslhofer--Kleiner, but use a different and more flexible approach that extends naturally to the high-codimension setting considered here. I will explain the main ideas behind this generalisation and discuss ongoing work towards a corresponding surgery theory. This is a joint work with Ben Andrews

talks.speaker: Mr Gustav Kjaerbye Bagger
talks.title: Norm-Euclideanity in cyclic fields
talks.abstract: Consider a cyclic number field of prime degree p. For a fixed degree, there are only finitely many such fields which are norm-Euclidean. The cases p=2 and 3 have been completely determined, but elsewhere only large upper bounds on their discriminants are known. In this direction, I will present some recent work substantially improving these bounds via an explicit Burgess-type criterion. I will also outline how one could use this result to completely resolve other small prime cases.

talks.speaker: Mr Saunak Bhattacharjee
talks.title: Equidistribution at the level of primes and upper bounds on $L$-functions at the edge of the critical strip.
talks.abstract: In this talk, we discuss how equidistribution of coefficients at primes can lead to improved upper bounds for certain $L$-functions at the edge of the critical strip. Let $L(s,f)$ be an $L$-function given by the Dirichlet series $\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{a_n}{n^s}$ and suppose its coefficients at primes $a_p$ are equidistributed. Combining this with the zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function, we obtain non-trivial cancellation in oscillatory prime sums of the form $\sum_{p\le x}a_pp^{it}$ for suitable ranges of $t$.  As applications, we establish new upper bounds for the $L$-function associated with non-CM elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ as well as for their symmetric power $L$-functions.
talks.affiliation: University of New South Wales Canberra

talks.speaker: Prof Florian Breuer
talks.title: Parity of fundamental units of real quadratic fields
talks.abstract: Let $d \equiv 5 \bmod 8$ be square-free and consider the real quadratic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$. If the fundamental unit of $K$ reduces to 1 modulo the prime above 2 then we call $d$ an Eisenstein discriminant. A conjecture of Stevenhagen predicts that about $1/3$ of all discriminants (square-free and $5 \bmod 8$) are Eisenstein. In this talk, I will outline some results in this direction, including joint work with James Punch computing Eisenstein discriminants up to $10^{11}$.

talks.speaker: Mr Peter Campbell
talks.title: Prime Plus a Non-Square-Free Integer: An Elementary Approach
talks.abstract: Can every integer greater than 24 be written as the sum of a prime and a positive integer that is not square-free? Lee and O'Clarey recently conjectured that this is always possible, establishing the result conditionally on the generalised Riemann hypothesis. In this talk, I will present an elementary approach to the problem based on congruences and the least prime not dividing a given integer. This reduces the question to finding sufficiently small primes in arithmetic progressions. I will discuss the unconditional results arising from this approach and the role of explicit estimates for primes in arithmetic progressions.

talks.speaker: Ms Shashi Chourasiya
talks.title: Ingham's zero density for Dirichlet L-functions
talks.abstract: In $2015$, Ramaré gave an explicit zero-density estimate for Dirichlet $L$-functions, based on ideas related to Ingham’s first zero-density estimate. In this talk, we consider Ingham’s second zero-density estimate in the setting of Dirichlet $L$-functions. We discuss how the original argument can be adapted to this setting and present an explicit version of the resulting zero-density estimate. We also describe some of the estimates required in carrying out the argument explicitly.
talks.affiliation: University of New South Wales Canberra

talks.speaker: Dr Lewis Combes
talks.title: Lifting ethereal Bianchi modular forms
talks.abstract: Ethereal modular forms are those that appear in mod p cohomology at a given level, but not in characteristic 0. Nevertheless, they can often be lifted to characteristic 0 by increasing the level. In this talk, we will discuss interesting examples of ethereal forms, some general theorems on lifting, and analyse data that suggest lifting may hold in general for favourable ranges of parameters.

talks.speaker: Mr Chandler Chase Corrigan
talks.title: Transformation formulae for Modular forms
talks.abstract: In this talk, we discuss an analogue of the van der Corput B-process for trigonometric sums twisted by Hecke eigenvalues of newforms of arbitrary weight and nebentypus.  We give some applications of these results to subconvexity estimates.

talks.speaker: Dr Adrian Dudek
talks.title: Counting Isomorphism Classes of I-Graphs
talks.abstract: The Petersen graph has many generalisations. We will look at the generalised Petersen graphs, as well as a further extension known as the I-graphs. We state and prove precisely, in the asymptotic limit, the proportion of I-graphs that are isomorphic to generalised Petersen graphs, thus quantifying the size of this generalisation. Our results rely on the estimation of sums over tuples satisfying various coprimality conditions along with some other techniques from analytic number theory.

talks.speaker: Dr Kevin Fergusson
talks.title: Partitions into k-th Powers
talks.abstract: An asymptotic estimate is obtained for the number of partitions of the positive integer n into unequal k-th powers, with each k-th power exceeding m. The estimate holds uniformly with respect to integers m such that $m = o(n^{1/(1+k)})$, as n becomes arbitrarily large.

talks.speaker: Mr Pasidhu Matthew Maseuge Fernando
talks.authors: Gustav Kj \ae rbye Bagger and Matthew Fernando
talks.title: Primitive Normal Progressions in Finite Fields
talks.abstract: Primitive and normal elements are fundamental objects in finite field theory. There is an extensive literature on the existence of m consecutive primitive elements in $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ where q is a prime power. A generalisation is to consider arithmetic progressions with a given non-zero common difference, requiring all terms to be primitive and at least one term to be normal. Lemos, Neumann and Ribas obtained concrete results for m=2,3 and asymptotic results for larger m. In this talk, I present further work on the m=4 case, substantially improving their bound. This is joint work with Gustav Bagger.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Alexandru Ghitza
talks.title: Number fields with small discriminant
talks.abstract: We discuss some strategies for finding totally real number fields with small discriminant in degrees where exhaustive searches are impractical.

talks.speaker: Mr Dhruv Gupta
talks.authors: Alexandru Ghitza, Dhruv Gupta, Max Kortge
talks.title: Volcanoes that never erupt: a two-torsion obstruction
talks.abstract:
Graphs of $\ell$-isogenies between ordinary elliptic curves over finite fields are very well structured: their connected components are all $\ell$-volcanoes (loosely speaking, one can say that they look like volcanos). Now, fixing $k$ to be a positive integer, the inverse problem seeks to find the primes $p$ for which a given volcano can occur over $\mathbb{F}_{p^k}$ (such primes we call $k$-explosive). Every volcano has infinitely many $1$-explosive primes, but for larger $k$, it becomes impossible to find explosive primes for certain volcano shapes.

In this talk, I will give an intuitive walkthrough of a non-existence theorem for $2$-volcanoes. The proof begins with a splitting criterion for finite abelian groups, which we will apply to class groups of imaginary quadratic orders. I will explain how information about elements of order two and four can force the relevant extensions to split, and how this produces an obstruction to realising a prescribed volcano. Following the argument, we will see why the arithmetic of the crater and the power of two dividing the extension degree constrain the volcano’s depth.

This is joint work with Alexandru Ghitza and Maximilian Kortge.

talks.speaker: Mr Bowan Hafey
talks.title: Theta series for surjectivity of the Global Siegel operator
talks.abstract: Theta series attached to lattices in a quadratic space define Siegel modular forms with level. The level is determined by the lattice. The Siegel operator gives a way of taking theta series of a certain degree to theta series of a lower degree. We describe how the arithmetic of theta series as modular forms can be used to prove the surjectivity of the Global Siegel operator for squarefree level and small weight — extending results of Böcherer and Ibukiyama. This is joint work with Chengjing Zhang and Alex Ghitza.

talks.speaker: Mr Maximilian Kortge
talks.authors: Alex Ghitza, Dhruv Gupta, Max Kortge
talks.title: The hitchhiker's guide to isogeny graphs
talks.abstract:
Over a finite field, one can construct a graph whose vertices are elliptic curves and whose edges are isogenies between them. These graphs have fascinating structure, in particular volcanoes for ordinary curves. But what happens when we venture into higher dimensions? Replacing elliptic curves with abelian varieties reveals a wealth of new structure, bringing new challenges. \\
In this talk, I will begin with the familiar territory of elliptic curves before exploring what lies beyond, culminating in our recent work describing the degree-$\ell$ isogeny graphs of ordinary abelian varieties isogenous to the power of an elliptic curve. And, with any luck, you'll leave knowing where your towel is.

talks.speaker: Mr Miles Koumouris
talks.title: Explicit models for algebraic modular forms
talks.abstract:
Algebraic modular forms exhibit many properties
that their classical cousins enjoy, including
having a graded ring structure, and a natural
notion of integrality and mod p reduction. But
models for this structure have not been made
explicit. By exploring the fascinating
representation theory of quaternionic and special
orthogonal groups, we present explicit ring
structures for algebraic modular forms attached
to these groups, and discuss when formation of
modular forms commutes with mod p reduction.
This is joint work with Chengjing Zhang.

talks.speaker: Ms Giulia Pelizzari
talks.title: On the growth of the Dedekind zeta function of a number field
talks.abstract:
The growth of the Riemann zeta function is a central topic in analytic number theory. What happens when one passes from $\mathbb{Q}$ to general number fields?

In this talk, I will discuss the motivation for studying the growth of the Dedekind zeta function of a number field and highlight some recent progress.

talks.speaker: Mr James Punch
talks.title: Burgess-strength bounds for sums of quadratic characters modulo a prime
talks.abstract:
Consider the quadratic character modulo a prime $p$, and sum it over integers in the interval $[M,M+N)$ for some positive integers $M$ and $N$. It is of interest in many number-theoretic problems to give an upper bound on the modulus of this sum.

A trivial bound is $N$; the P\'olya-Vinogradov inequality gives $\sqrt{p}\log{p}$. Burgess established that we can take (asymptotically) $N^{1-1/r}p^{(r+1)/(4r^2)+\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$. For computational problems, we need an explicit version of this bound; one was provided by Booker in 2006.

In this talk, I will sketch a modest improvement to Booker's result. My result takes into account the value of $M$, and improves as $M$ increases; I am not aware of any other result of this type.

talks.speaker: Miss Manna Riddhi
talks.title: Quadratic inverse large sieve conjecture
talks.abstract: Given a set of integers $A$, which is a subset of $[1, N]$, the large sieve and the larger sieve inequalities give upper bounds for the cardinality of $A$ from information about how many residue classes $A$ occupies modulo each prime $p$.  For instance, if a set $A$ occupies about $\alpha p$ residue classes modulo each prime $p$, the larger sieve gives the bound $N^{\alpha}$ for the size of $A$. If we consider the case of the squares up to $N$, we find that this bound is sharp. The inverse conjecture for the large sieve states that if the set $A$ is close to the size $N^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and exhibits this type of behaviour modulo each prime $p$, then it consists of the squares or any other dense quadratic structure. In this talk, I will discuss the history of this conjecture and some recent results which provide evidence towards this conjecture.
talks.affiliation: University of New South Wales Canberra

talks.speaker: Dr Nikita Shulga
talks.title: Generalizations of three-gap theorem
talks.abstract: The famous three-gap theorem, also known as the Steinhaus conjecture, tells us that $n$ points on a circle placed at angles $\theta, 2\theta, 3\theta,\ldots, n\theta$ have at most three distinct distances between pairs of points in adjacent positions around the circle. While this one-dimensional result was proven in 1950s, the natural multidimensional generalizations are only known in dimensions $d=2$ and $d=3$. In this talk, I will discuss recent progress in multidimensional gap theorems and present a new result that holds in all dimensions.

talks.speaker: Mr Simon Thomas
talks.authors: Simon N. Thomas, Adrian W. Dudek
talks.title: Asymptotic estimates for sums involving $\omega(n)$.
talks.abstract: Let $\omega(n)$ denote the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$. Sums of the form $\sum_{2\le n\le N}\frac{z^{\omega(n)}}{\omega(n)^k}$, where $z>0$ and $k\in \mathbb{N}$, have recently been used to obtain improved zero-density estimates. In this talk, I'll discuss how the Selberg-Delange method can be used to obtain asymptotic estimates for these sums.

talks.speaker: Mr Ameya Tilgul
talks.title: Spacing Statistics of $S$-unit Sequences
talks.abstract: Spacing statistics describe the local distribution of a sequence modulo 1, and provide a way of measuring how closely its behaviour resembles that of random points. In this talk, I will discuss the spacing statistics of sequences that arise from S-units. In particular, I will focus on how concepts from the theory of Diophantine equations can be used to study these local statistics.

talks.speaker: Prof Timothy Trudgian
talks.title: B is for Breakable
talks.abstract:
Consider consecutive primes, say 13 and 17. Look at the smallest factor of each number between these primes. These factors are 2, 3, 2, each of which is smaller than the gap of 4 (between 17 and 13). Erd\H{o}s conjectured that it should be `rare’ for prime gaps $(p_{n}, p_{n+1})$ to be packed to the gunwales with numbers having such `small’ prime factors.

Tao and Gafni proved this conjecture in 2025. I shall discuss further work, which is joint with Mike Mossinghoff, where we coin a term that explains the title --- you’re welcome!

talks.speaker: Mr Sebastian Tudzi
talks.title: Lucky Numbers: A sieve that mimics the primes
talks.abstract: Lucky numbers are the survivors of a variant of the sieve of Eratosthenes, one that deletes numbers by their position, rather than their value. Despite this purely combinatorial origin, they share many features with the primes, including the same asymptotic density. This talk introduces the basic structure of lucky numbers, explains which prime-like properties come from sieving alone and describes how lucky numbers interact with some arithmetic functions.
talks.affiliation: University of New South Wales Canberra

talks.speaker: Mr Watcharakiete Wongcharoenbhorn
talks.title: Variance of Some Multiplicative Functions Over Random Polynomials
talks.abstract:
Let $g\in \{\mu^2, \tau\}$ be a multiplicative function, and let $\mathcal{F}_k(H)$ 
be a family of integral polynomials of degree $k\geqslant 1$ with coefficient size at most $H$ in 
absolute value. It is expected that
\[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n\leqslant N} g(f(n))=P_f(\log N)+\Delta(N),\]
for a suitable polynomial $P_f$ with coefficients depending on $f$, and $\Delta(N)=o(P_f(\log N))$.
To our knowledge, these asymptotic behaviors remain open when $k\geqslant 3,4$ for $g=\tau, \mu^2$ respectively.  
    In this talk, we will discuss our approach to estimating the variance of the error term $\Delta(N)$:
\[\frac{1}{\#\mathcal{F}_k(H)}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}_k(H)} \left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n\leqslant N} g(f(n))-P_f(\log N)\right|^2,\]
uniformly over $\mathcal{F}_k(H)$. We establish asymptotic formulae for certain ranges of height $H=H(N)$.
talks.affiliation: University of New South Wales Canberra

talks.speaker: Mr Chris Zeng
talks.title: Moduli spaces in algebraic geometry
talks.abstract:
In this talk, we will motivate and introduce the notion of moduli spaces in algebraic geometry. We will then describe a series of ideas with striking consequences in number theory. 
This will motivate open problems about moduli with a strong geometric flavour.
In particular, a geometric problem related to moduli theory and the Shafarevich conjecture will be discussed. This will be developed in parallel to the arithmetic case, in which the Shafarevich conjecture is equivalent to Mordell/Faltings' Theorem, which states there are finitely many solutions to a very large class of Diophantine equations.

talks.speaker: Mr Chengjing Zhang
talks.title: Maslov index and metaplectic groups
talks.abstract: In the literature, metaplectic groups are usually defined using the Stone--von Neumann theorem, and thus depend on some auxiliary data. In this talk, I will introduce an axiomatic definition of the Maslov index, and use it to define the metaplectic groups. This construction also works over division algebras, and explains the existence of splittings of reductive dual pairs in the theory of theta correspondence.

talks.speaker: Dr Sebastian ZUNIGA-ALTERMAN
talks.title: Averages of arithmetic functions and sets with sieve structure
talks.abstract:
We study some averages of arithmetic functions of a certain class, essentially generalising the divisor function, which involve the support of a sequence with sieve structure.
We are inspired by the Erdös divisor bound on polynomials (1951) as well as by Wolke's and Shiu's results in the early 70's. We discuss the smoothest conditions that one can consider for obtaining such bounds and derive some applications.

talks.speaker: Dr Scott Boivin Lindstrom
talks.authors: Andrew Calcan, Jordan Collard, Alberto De Marchi, Scott B. Lindstrom
talks.title: Resolvent Moreau Identities and Gabay Duality
talks.abstract: Daniel Gabay showed that when we use the alternating direction method of multipliers to solve a convex primal problem, we are implicitly using the the Douglas--Rachford method to solve a convex dual problem. We can exploit this duality to prove many things about ADMM, and Gabay's framework is also the platform for various performance improvement schemes that take advantage of the discrete time dynamical system admitted by the Douglas--Rachford operator. In this talk, I will (1) describe how we can use Gabay's duality to study ADMM even for nonconvex problems; (2) show examples where we can use Gabay's duality to show that ADMM's iterates cycle or are chaotic for very natural problems; and (3) explain how we can use Gabay's duality in designing algorithms that show better promise.

talks.speaker: Dr Lele (Joyce) Zhang
talks.title: Adaptive Incentive Optimization for Airport Ride-Hailing Rebalancing: An MPC–Stackelberg Framework
talks.abstract:
Airport ride-hailing systems exhibit spatial supply–demand imbalances caused by asynchronous temporal variation in airport and urban demand and decentralised driver relocation. We formulate the vehicle rebalancing problem as a closed-loop Stackelberg optimisation framework in which a transportation network company (TNC) selects bidirectional positive incentives and driver movements evolve according to evolutionary dynamics. Behavioural uncertainty is addressed through online estimation of driver response sensitivity, while the model predictive control (MPC) horizon is adapted according to parameter-estimate stability.
Relocation externalities are internalised through a shadow-pricing term for sustainable operating cost (SOC). Because the resulting optimisation problem must be solved repeatedly, we develop a Shifted Contextual Bayesian Optimisation (CBO) scheme that exploits temporal structure by reusing compatible historical evaluations and shifted subsidy trajectories across decision epochs.
The framework is evaluated in seven full-day simulations parameterised using data from Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport. Adaptive optimisation consistently improves TNC performance relative to a non-adaptive benchmark in terms of positive payoff gains for both the TNC and drivers, while SOC internalisation reduces subsidy-induced relocation by 3.1%–34.5% and total external costs by 3.6%–47.3%. With only 40% of the evaluation budget, Shifted CBO attains at least 95% of the paired pooled-best improvement in 76.9% of optimisation subproblems, compared with 43.6% under memoryless Bayesian optimisation. The results show that the proposed formulation provides an effective computational framework for adaptive spatial rebalancing under behavioural uncertainty, externalities, and repeated optimisation.

talks.speaker: Dr Thi Hoa Bui
talks.title: Low Rank Nonlinear Integer Programming
talks.abstract:
In this talk, we study a class of mixed-integer optimisation problems that exhibit an underlying low-rank structure. We show that this structure can be exploited to establish that optimal solutions of the continuous relaxation lies in a low-dimensional face of the convex hull of feasible mixed-integer points. This geometric insight motivates a more refined branch-and-bound framework that focuses the search on a substantially smaller region of the feasible space. The resulting relaxations are solved using a Frank–Wolfe algorithm over the convex hull of mixed-integer feasible points, rather than over the standard continuous
relaxation. Linear minimisation subproblems are handled directly by a mixed-integer linear optimisation solver, which serves as the linear minimisation oracle. This approach avoids the need for dedicated cutting plane
schemes to approximate the convex hull.

talks.speaker: Mr Andrew Calcan
talks.title: From dynamical systems to practical optimisation algorithms via duality theory
talks.abstract:
Optimisation algorithms are a cornerstone of modern computing, although developing principled new methods and understanding their behaviour can be challenging. This is particularly true for algorithms involving multiple interacting sequences of intermediate updates. While these methods can be difficult to analyse directly, we show that their behaviour can often be captured by relatively simple continuous-time dynamical systems. We utilise a novel algorithmic duality theory to connect these dynamical systems to a popular class of powerful optimisation algorithms. Using insights gained from continuous-time dynamics, we investigate how appropriate extrapolation techniques and discretisations can be used to develop novel optimisation methods. 

We further utilise our duality theory to analyse the behaviour of a proposed algorithm and obtain convergence guarantees in a standard setting. Several numerical experiments demonstrate our method's convergence behaviour and computational performance.

talks.speaker: Dr Bethany Caldwell
talks.authors: Regina Burachik, Yalcin Kaya, Walaa Moursi, Matthew Saurette
talks.title: The Douglas–Rachford algorithm for inconsistent problems
talks.abstract: The Douglas–Rachford algorithm has been successfully employed to solve convex optimization problems, or more generally find zeros of monotone inclusions. Recently, the behaviour of these methods in the inconsistent case, i.e., in the absence of solutions, has been a topic of interest as these problems appear regularly but can be difficult to analyse. We give a result for the strong convergence of the shadow sequence of the Douglas–Rachford algorithm in the possibly inconsistent case when one of the operators is uniformly monotone and 3* monotone but not necessarily a subdifferential. We also provide numerical experiments comparing the performance of the Douglas–Rachford algorithm for inconsistent finite- and infinite-dimensional linear-quadratic problems with the Peaceman–Rachford algorithm and Dykstra's projection algorithm.

talks.speaker: Mr Jordan Collard
talks.title: Quadratic Convergence of Lyapunov Surrogate Extrapolation for Nonconvex Feasibility
talks.abstract: In this talk, we examine a Lyapunov surrogate extrapolation method and establish its quadratic convergence for the nonconvex feasibility problem of finding a point in the intersection of a hyperplane and the graph of a smooth function. The setting generalises the classical circle-line problem in two dimensions, a standard model problem in the study of projection methods such as the Douglas--Rachford method. We outline the key geometric ideas underlying the proof and conclude with numerical results illustrating the behaviour of the method.

talks.speaker: Dr Neil Dizon
talks.authors: N. D. Dizon, Q. Y. Huang, V. Jeyakumar, G. Li, C. Tammer
talks.title: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimisation: From Two-Stage to Multi-Objective Decisions
talks.abstract: This talk presents recent advances in Wasserstein distributionally robust optimisation, focusing on two-stage and multi-objective decision-making under distributional ambiguity. First, we develop exact semidefinite and second-order cone programming reformulations for two-stage problems with convex quadratic and piecewise affine recourse under different uncertainty structures. We also investigate multi-objective stochastic convex optimisation, introducing notions of distributionally robust efficiency and establishing exact semidefinite programming reformulations for weighted-sum scalarised problems under suitable structural conditions. Applications in production–transportation, multitask regression, and portfolio optimisation illustrate the computational tractability and practical relevance of the proposed approaches.

talks.speaker: Dr Srecko Durasinovic
talks.authors: S. Durasinovic, P. Azzi, J-B. Lasserre, V. Magron, O. Mula
talks.title: Leveraging Christoffel-Darboux Kernels to Strengthen Moment-SOS Relaxations
talks.abstract: The classical Moment-SOS hierarchy allows one to approximate the global minimum of a polynomial optimization problem through semidefinite relaxations of increasing accuracy. For many optimization problems, however, moving to higher relaxation orders quickly becomes computationally prohibitive. While this difficulty is commonly addressed by exploiting structural properties such as symmetry or sparsity, we explore a complementary direction: strengthening a low-order relaxation using information contained in its own pseudo-moment solution. To this end, we leverage Christoffel-Darboux kernels to identify regions that are compatible with the current pseudo-moment information and use them to construct additional polynomial constraints. We propose two mechanisms: the first, denoted $H1$, is based on successive global Christoffel restrictions, while the second, denoted $H2$, combines marginal Christoffel information with an available local solution. For $H1$, we establish a uniform separation property for successive pseudo-moment solutions and geometric convergence of the fixed-order bounds on a particular subclass of knapsack problems. Moreover, for specific Boolean quadratic problems, we derive an explicit $H2$ selection rule and establish conditions under which the resulting marginal constraints preserve all global minimizers. Numerical experiments on dense and sparse nonconvex quadratically constrained quadratic programs show that the resulting strengthened low-order relaxations can significantly improve the initial bounds, sometimes attaining exactness, while remaining substantially cheaper than solving higher-order relaxations.

talks.speaker: Mr Hugo Fellows-Smith
talks.title: Malfatti's Dice: How much of a shape's area can you fill with k disjoint squares?
talks.abstract:
In 1803, Malfatti asked how to pack three circles (of variable size) into a triangle to maximise their total area. Nearly two centuries later, Zalgaller and Los proved that the greedy strategy is always optimal: placing the largest available circle three times will fill a larger fraction of the triangle than any other method. Melissen subsequently asked if this was true for any number of circles, and if greedy circle packings are optimal for filling more than just triangles. I study the same phenomenon, but replacing circles with axis-aligned squares. I will show two results on packing squares into rectangles and right triangles respectively, where the greedy packing satisfies a majorization property over all other packings.

The approach replaces the fixed-number-of-squares packing problem by a family of convex-score packing problems. Karamata's inequality tells us that the greedy packing is optimal for all of these problems if and only if the Melissen-type conjecture is true for every k. Passing each convex-score problem to its linear-programming dual leaves an apparently impossible optimisation over distributions. However, an ansatz, suggested by the self-similarity of the greedy packing, reduces it to an integral equation with a nice solution. My results show the greedy packing is optimal for a large subset of the convex-score problems, which leads me to offer a slightly weaker conjecture than Melissen's.

talks.speaker: Dr Yingkun (Queenie) Huang
talks.authors: Q. Y. Huang, N. D. Dizon, N. Jeyakumar, V. Jeyakumar
talks.title: Robust machine learning for classification and feature selection under data uncertainty
talks.abstract: We introduce an efficient machine learning method based on robust Support Vector Machines (SVMs) that simultaneously classifies data and selects relevant features whilst accounting for data uncertainty. Based on Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, we develop computationally feasible robust SVM models along with efficient second-order cone programming methods using an integrated application of tools from convex non-smooth analysis and difference-of-convex optimization. Our computational results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that these robust SVMs identify relevant features whilst achieving higher classification accuracies than the conventional (non-robust) SVM models, especially for datasets with more features than instances.

talks.speaker: Dr Janosch Rieger
talks.title: Galerkin approximations to the space of convex bodies by polytopes in nondegenerate V-representation
talks.abstract:
We introduce finite-dimensional approximations to the space of convex bodies based on polytopes in vertex representation. For a prescribed set of directions, the admissible point configurations form a polyhedral convex subcone of the Euclidean vector space, described by a finite
system of linear inequalities. The interior of this cone contains only nondegenerate representations, in which all
parameter points are distinct vertices of the represented polytope. We study the geometry of the parameter cone, redundancies in its defining inequalities, and natural projections of convex bodies onto the resulting polytope spaces. We derive quantitative approximation estimates in terms of how densely the prescribed directions cover the unit sphere and construct nested Galerkin sequences whose
approximation error converges locally uniformly to zero. Finally, we use these approximation properties to establish the convergence of finite-dimensional approximations of constrained global optimization problems in the space of convex bodies.

talks.speaker: Dr Lindon Roberts
talks.title: Adaptive Sampling Trust Region Optimization for Derivative-free Stochastic Functions and Deterministic Constraints
talks.abstract: Motivated by problems from simulation-based optimization, we consider the problem of minimizing a stochastic, black-box objective subject to deterministic nonlinear constraints. In this setting, we only have access to stochastic estimates (and no derivatives) of the objective, but we assume access to exact function and gradient evaluations for the constraints. We extend an adaptive sampling variant of a model-based derivative-free optimization algorithm to this setting, and establish almost sure convergence of an SQP-based algorithm, and present numerical results on a stochastic activity network problem. This is joint work with Nicole Felice and Sara Shashaani (North Carolina State University).

talks.speaker: Mr Santanu Soe
talks.authors: Santanu Soe, Matthew K. Tam, V. Vetrivel
talks.title: GRAAL for variational inequalities revisited: sharp parameter range and adaptive step sizes
talks.abstract: This paper revisits the Golden Ratio Algorithm (GRAAL) of Malitsky (Math. Program. 184, 383--410, 2020) for monotone variational inequalities. The original analysis of GRAAL restricts the convex-combination parameter $c$ to $1<c\leq\varphi$, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ is the golden ratio. Through a new Lyapunov analysis, we show that this range of $c$ can be extended to $1<c<3$. Further, a two-dimensional linear counterexample shows that this parameter range is sharp. In particular, for every $c\geq3$ and every positive constant step size, the iterates of GRAAL can be unbounded. Building on this analysis, we propose a simpler version of the adaptive GRAAL (aGRAAL) that requires neither a line search nor a prescribed upper bound on the step sizes, and demonstrate its convergence for locally Lipschitz cost operators over the same parameter range. For both methods, we establish an $O(1/N)$ ergodic gap bound and, under a residual-based error bound condition, prove the R-linear convergence of the adaptive iterates. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to compare the proposed strategies with existing ones.

talks.speaker: Mx Rory Stevens
talks.title: Applying Operator-Splitting Methods to the Wavelet Feasibility Problem
talks.abstract: Operator-splitting methods are a class of optimisation method that have demonstrated flexibility in solving various problems in signal processing, agnostic of their convexity. In my honours thesis, I focused on benchmarking applications of operator splitting methods, such as Douglas-Rachford and CRM, to the one-dimensional and two-dimensional wavelet feasibility problem. The wavelet feasibility problem is a natural example of a non-convex and high-dimensional optimisation problem. It has applications to signal processing, with the two-dimensional wavelet problem feasibility being especially useful for images. While working on this project, I also successfully applied an experimental extension of the Lyapunov Surrogate Method to the wavelet feasbility problem. This extension was successful in improving on established results for the one-dimensional wavelet feasibility problem, and providing results for the two-dimensional wavelet feasibility problem. It also provided insight into how the Lyapunov Surrogate Method performs on high-dimensional non-convex problems.

talks.speaker: Mr Liam Walsh
talks.authors: Scott Lindstrom, Vera Roshchina, Liam Walsh
talks.title: Prescribing the facial dimensions of a convex body and its polar
talks.abstract: The primal signature $\mathcal{S}(C)$ of a convex set $C$ records the dimensions of its nonempty faces. In 2025, Roshchina and Tun{\c c}el showed that arbitrary primal signatures can be realised; in other words, for any finite subset $I$ of the nonnegative integers, there exists a convex set $C$ whose primal signature $\mathcal{S}(C)$ is equal to $I$. In this talk, we discuss a constructive approach to the following related problem: for any finite subsets $I$ and $J$ of the nonnegative integers with $0\in I\cap J$ and $\max I = \max J =:n $, does there exist a convex set $C$ whose primal signature $\mathcal{S}(C)$ is equal to $I$ and whose polar signature $\mathcal{S}(C^\circ)$ is equal to $J$? Our proposed solution uses strictly convex functions that have a prescribed subdifferential at one point, are smooth elsewhere, and agree to first order with a radial quadratic function on the boundary of their domain. After rescaling, their epigraphs may replace small spherical caps of an $n$-ball with the effect of inserting exactly one  dimension into the polar signature while leaving the primal signature unchanged. A pair of mutually polar inner and outer bounds to the $n$-ball guarantee that at least $2(n-1)$ such modifications can be made to either the primal or the polar set and, as a consequence, at least $n-1$ integers can be added to either the primal or polar signature of an $n$-ball to form the desired signatures $I$ and $J$. This construction may shed light on an answer to the broader question of ``what information about polar facial structure can be inferred from the primal?''. Answers to this question may have implications for the design and analysis of optimisation algorithms which exploit primal and polar facial structure, such as facial reduction and primal-dual interior point methods for conic linear programs.

talks.speaker: Prof Wei-Chang Yeh
talks.title: A Finite Markov Chain Analysis of the Simplified Swarm Optimisation Update Rule
talks.abstract: Simplified swarm optimisation updates each decision variable independently by partitioning the unit interval into four segments, of widths $c_g$, $c_p$, $c_w$ and $c_r$, which respectively copy from the global best, copy from the individual best, retain the current value, and resample uniformly. Because the update is coordinate-wise and memoryless given the incumbents, the population process is a finite Markov chain whose sampling kernel does not depend on the objective function. The objective enters only through incumbent updates; since incumbent values are monotone and finitely valued, every trajectory decomposes into finitely many frozen phases on which the kernel is exact rather than approximate. Within a phase we obtain closed forms. The spectral gap is exactly $1 - c_w$, independent of dimension, alphabet size and the other three widths, while the stationary distribution depends only on the ratios of the remaining three, so convergence speed and convergence location are governed by disjoint parameters. On coordinates where the two incumbents disagree, the stationary bias is $(c_g - c_p) / (c_g + c_p + c_r)$, vanishing exactly at $c_g = c_p$. Tracking the age since the last improvement yields a relaxation curve interpolating two distinct effective mutation rates, from which the retention width emerges as a built-in adaptive escape mechanism rather than as wasted effort.

talks.speaker: Mr Stephen Zhang
talks.title: Global Exponential Convergence of Two-Layer Linear Network Training
talks.abstract:
We prove global exponential (linear) convergence with an explicit rate in the rich scaling for wide two-layer linear networks trained with smooth
Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz predictor losses. Gradient flow in the factors closes exactly in terms of a finite-dimensional Bures flow of the neuron law covariance, in which the predictor dynamics are preconditioned by hidden covariance blocks.
Mean-field conservation laws provide uniform spectral lower bounds on the hidden preconditioning blocks when the initial covariance satisfies a spectral support gap condition.
This condition encompasses positive definiteness while still allowing for singular initializations.
For an initial covariance $\Sigma_0 = \sigma^2 \text{Id}$, the loss converges to the global minimum with linear rate at least $4\sigma^2\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the PL constant. We establish stability of this rate under finite-width sampling, as well as global convergence of factor gradient descent for an explicit stepsize interval depending on smoothness, the initial loss, and conserved spectral margins.
Our argument extends layerwise to deep linear ResNets, subject to a residual-path bound.
In the case of heavy-ball momentum, training dynamics close instead over positions and velocities in terms of a lifted phase covariance.
Linear convergence holds under an explicit condition on the energy and damping, specifying a window of admissible dampings. For two-scale white initializations, this interval is nonempty for sufficiently large position scales, with a fixed initial loss gap and velocity covariance. Numerical experiments illustrate the covariance geometry and compare the predicted and observed rates.

talks.speaker: Mr Luke Attrill
talks.authors: Luke J. Attrill, Timothy M. Garoni
talks.title: The clumsy coupon collector's problem
talks.abstract:
We consider a generalisation of the classical coupon
collector's problem, in which at each time step a collector either
receives a new copy of a randomly chosen coupon, or loses all their
previously collected copies of that coupon. We consider the amount
of time it takes this ``clumsy'' coupon collector to obtain the
full set of $m$ coupons. We establish limit theorems as $m\to\infty$
for the clumsy coupon collection time, and describe the large $m$
asymptotics of its mean and variance. We identify three regimes,
depending on how the probability of a clumsy update, $p$, 
scales with $m$. If $p=o(1/m)$, we obtain a Gumbel limit theorem,
as is the case for the classical coupon collector. If $p=\omega(1/m)$,
we instead show weak convergence to an exponential random variable.
In the critical case, $p=c/m$, we give a full characterisation
of the limiting distribution in terms of a birth-death process.
We also describe the asymptotics of the mean and variance in these three regimes.

talks.speaker: Mr Dila Bhandari
talks.title: Sequential Analysis and AI Approach for Forecasting Tourism demand and Economic Growth
talks.abstract:
For developing economies, tourism is a key driver of economic growth, employment generation, and foreign exchange earnings. Perfect tourism demand forecasting is therefore crucial for sustainable development planning and informed policymaking. This paper forecasts tourism demand using a time series modeling approach of tourism statistics data from 2005 to 2022, incorporating the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. ARIMA and SARIMA models are applied after testing for stationarity and seasonality, with model selection guided and forecast performance evaluated using RMSE, MAE, and MAPE. The results show that an ARIMA (0,1,2) model provides the best fit for annual tourist arrivals, outperforming alternative ARIMA and exponential smoothing specifications. Forecasts signify a gradual and partial recovery of tourism demand, with arrivals stabilizing below pre-pandemic levels in the medium term. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating seasonality and structural shocks in tourism demand modeling. Reliable demand forecasts support efficient resource allocation, infrastructure planning, and risk management, thereby directly contributing to SDG 8 (target 8.9) and promoting sustainable tourism development.
Keywords: SARIMA, ARIMA, South Asia, Forecasting Accuracy Metrics, SDG 8.

talks.speaker: Dr Boris Buchmann
talks.title: Laws of the Iterated Logarithm for Self-normalised L\'{e}vy Processes at Zero
talks.abstract:
We develop tools and methodology to establish laws of the iterated logarithm (LILs) for small times (as $t\downarrow0$) for the \textquotedblleft
self-normalised" process $(X_{t}-at)/\sqrt{V_{t}}$, $t>0$, constructed from a
L\'{e}vy process $(X_{t})_{t\geq0}$ having quadratic variation process
$(V_{t})_{t\geq0}$, and an appropriate choice of the constant $a$. We apply
them to obtain laws of the iterated logarithm when $X_{t}$ is in the domain of attraction of the normal
distribution as $t\downarrow0$, when $X_{t}$ is symmetric and in the Feller
class at 0, and when $X_{t}$ is a strictly $\alpha-$stable process. When
$X_{t}$ is attracted to the normal distribution, an important ingredient in
the proof is a Cram\'{e}r-type theorem which bounds above the distance of the
distribution of the self-normalised process from the standard normal
distribution.
\\
\emph{This talk is based on joint work with Ross A. Maller, Australian National University, and dedicated to late David M. Mason, University of Delawere.}\\

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Conrad Burden
talks.authors: Conrad J. Burden and Robert C. Griffiths
talks.title: The Feller diffusion interpreted as the limit of a coalescent point process
talks.abstract:
The Feller diffusion $\big(X(\tau)\big)_{\tau \in [0, t]}$ is a continuous state stochastic process defined by the generator 
\[
{\cal L} = \tfrac{1}{2} x \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} +  \alpha x \frac{\partial}{\partial x}, \qquad x \ge 0,\; \alpha \in \mathbb{R}. 
\]
This process was introduced by Feller as the continuum analogue of a classical branching process, primarily with
the intention of modelling the growth of a population of statistically independently reproducing individuals. 

I will summarise the results of our recent paper~\cite{BurdenGriffiths26} in which the Feller diffusion is interpreted as the limit of a coalescent point process in which the density of the node height distribution is 
skewed towards zero.  A number of recent results pertaining to scaling limits of branching processes will be reviewed and reinterpreted as properties of the Feller diffusion arising from this limit.  Topics covered include a limiting form of Bernoulli-sampling appropriate for samples drawn from infinite continuum populations and methods for studying 
the coalescent properties of the $k$-sampled Feller diffusion, in which the sample size is pre-specified.   

\begin{thebibliography}{9}

\bibitem{BurdenGriffiths26} Burden, C. J. and Griffiths, R. C. (2026). The Feller diffusion as the limit of a coalescent point process.  Theor. Popul. Biol.  171, 47--58.

\end{thebibliography}

talks.speaker: Dr Marco Carfagnini
talks.title: Berry-Heisenberg random waves
talks.abstract: In the 70s, Berry argued that in the high-energy limit wave functions locally look like random superpositions of independent plane waves, having all the same wavenumber. He introduced a Gaussian random field whose sample paths are generalized Laplace eigenfunctions. The aim of this talk is to present a similar model for the sub-Laplacian on the Heisenberg group, which is the analogue of the Euclidean space in sub-Riemannian geometry. It combines ideas from PDE, representation theory, and stationary random fields.

talks.speaker: Dr Illia Donhauzer
talks.title: Asymptotics of multifractal products of spherical random fields
talks.abstract:
The talk will present multifractal random measures on spheres $S^d$ constructed using multifractal products of random fields. We present new limit theorems for multifractal products of spherical fields and conditions for the non-degeneracy of the limiting measure. We also focus on studying multifractal properties of the limiting measure and calculate its Rényi function under conditions that are expressed in terms of second-order moments in the geometric Gaussian scenario. Compared to earlier results, the obtained limit theorems hold under general mixing conditions that allow for considering multifractal products of fields from a wide class and deriving random measures with flexible multifractal
properties.

talks.speaker: Dr Jie Yen Fan
talks.authors: Jie Yen Fan, Kais Hamza, Fima Klebaner, Ziwen Zhong
talks.title: Estimation of rates in population-age-dependent processes by means of test functions
talks.abstract: We consider the problem of estimation of parameters in the general age and population-dependent models. The individual parameters (birth and death) depend not only on the age of the individual but also on the whole population composition. We assume that we observe only ages of living individuals, and using dynamical evolution equations we derive new estimators of rates based on the use of test functions. A remarkable finding is that we can estimate age-dependent birth rates even though we don't observe the mother's age at the time of birth by using time-dependent test functions.

talks.speaker: Dr Laurence Field
talks.title: Two-dimensional Brownian motion: interplay of topology and boundary conditions
talks.abstract: Two-dimensional Brownian motion, even as a very well-studied process, remains a fruitful source of ideas and methods for analysing conformal mappings and conformally invariant random processes. We will present some recent results which exemplify this interplay in the case of nontrivial topologies interacting with various choices of boundary conditions. These illuminate some extensions of the classical theory of canonical conformal mappings and also more modern topics in random geometry.

talks.speaker: Dr Jing Fu
talks.authors: Jing Fu, Bill Moran, Jos\'e Ni\~no-Mora
talks.title: Weakly-Coupled Restless-Bandit Models: Exponential Convergence in Probability
talks.abstract: We study a finite time horizon Markov decision process (MDP) consisting of several groups of multi-action finite-state restless bandit processes, which are identical within each group. The bandit processes into different groups can be rather different. The bandit processes are subject to multiple weakly coupled constraints on their state and action variables. In contrast to prior studies that considered only a few specific policies/algorithms, here, we study the behaviours of the general stochastic process and, most importantly, the design of policies that guarantee its convergence to an ideal trajectory as the problem size increases. We prove that, for any policy in a rather general class, the resulting stochastic process converges in probability to a deterministic process as the system size (measured by the number of bandits) tends to infinity, at an exponential rate. Unlike the previous proofs, our exponential convergence does not rely on any non-degeneracy assumptions. It follows that the chosen policy asymptotically approaches optimality (with exponentially diminishing probability of suboptimality) in the size dimension if and only if the deterministic process coincides with optimality.

talks.speaker: Prof Timothy Garoni
talks.authors: Timothy M. Garoni and Aram Perez
talks.title: Berry-Esseen Bounds for High-Temperature Ising Models
talks.abstract: We consider the nearest-neighbour Ising model on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and establish sharp results for the normal approximation of the magnetisation throughout the high-temperature regime. In particular, we establish optimal Berry--Esseen bounds between the magnetisation in an arbitrary finite region and a Gaussian with the corresponding finite-volume variance. These results hold for finite-volume Gibbs measures with arbitrary boundary conditions, as well as for the infinite-volume Gibbs measure. We also determine sharp rates of convergence of the magnetisation in a finite box to a Gaussian with variance given by the infinite-volume susceptibility. For this fixed Gaussian target, we show that, in dimensions $d\ge3$, periodic boundary conditions yield strictly faster convergence than free boundary conditions. Our approach uses Stein's method to quantify the normal approximation error by analysing the semigroup of the continuous-time Ising heat-bath dynamics.

talks.speaker: Dr Xi Geng
talks.title: Optimal tail estimates for differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion
talks.abstract:
In this talk, we discuss optimal lower tail estimates for solutions to differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion in both Young's and rough regimes. 

In Young's regime, we discuss a striking fact that a uniformly elliptic system with $C_b^\infty$-coefficients could fail to have Gaussian lower tail in general, while this is always true for periodic systems in dimension two. 

In the rough regime, we discuss a sharp Weibull-type lower tail estimate for systems that satisfy a geometric non-commutativity condition. This partly confirms a conjecture of Boedihardjo-Geng 2024 on the genericness of the well-known Cass-Litterer-Lyons estimate for such systems. 

This is based on joint work with H. Boedihardjo (Warwick) and S. Wang (SISSA).

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Clara Grazian
talks.title: Bayesian Semiparametric Regression for Dependent Data: An Application to Long Memory
talks.abstract: We consider Bayesian semiparametric regression models in which the distribution of the errors is allowed to change with the predictor. A common assumption in semiparametric regression is that the error distribution is independent of the predictors, but this can be restrictive when the variability, skewness, or other features of the response change across the covariate space. We therefore model the conditional error distribution through a flexible kernel stick-breaking mixture model, while imposing a conditional mean-zero constraint to identify the regression parameters. To allow for dependence across the error terms, inference is based on a product of marginal conditional densities, treated as a pseudo-likelihood function. We then give conditions for consistency of the marginal pseudo-posterior distribution for the regression parameters. We finally apply the proposed framework to estimation of the memory parameter through log-periodogram regression. In this setting, dependence among periodogram ordinates at low frequencies induces dependence among the regression errors, whose marginal distribution may also vary with frequency.

talks.speaker: Mr Ashley Hanson
talks.title: Capacity reallocation in loss networks
talks.abstract: We consider a network, where each node is a city and each edge is a physical link of fixed capacity (or bandwidth) between a pair of cities. Between any two cities in the network, customers can communicate, and we refer to the communication path in this network as a route. A direct route only uses one physical link. A transit route uses multiple physical links, which corresponds to a route where the two communicating cities are not directly connected by a physical link. Each route in the network is allocated a logical capacity, which is the maximum number of communications possible on that route at any time. The logical capacity of a route respects the capacity of each physical link the route uses. A communication request on a given route is lost if the logical capacity has been reached. In this research, we analyse the case where the logical capacity of each route is static and then compare the results with those for the case where it is dynamic.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Simon Harris
talks.authors: Simon C. Harris, Samuel G. G. Johnston, Juan Carlos Pardo
talks.title: Behaviour Near Explosion in Continuous-Time Galton-Watson Trees
talks.abstract:
In this talk, we will explore the behaviour of continuous-time Galton-Watson trees whose offspring distribution has heavy tails such that the population size \emph{explodes} in a finite time. 
Specifically, we consider offspring generating functions of the form 
$f(s) = s - (1-s)^\alpha L(1-s)$
where $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $L:[0,1] \to [0,\infty)$ is slowly varying at zero. 

Conditional on explosion at time $T$, at each  earlier time $t < T$ there is a unique particle $\xi_t$ alive at time $t$ who is an ancestor of all but finitely many of the particles alive at the explosion time. We call this particle the \emph{`spine to explosion'}.  Births off the spine to explosion admit a Poissonian description, where they become both more frequent and larger as $t \uparrow T$.  

Under an appropriate space-time rescaling, % leading up to the explosion time,
the population size process near explosion converges in finite-dimensional distributions to a stationary continuous-state branching process with immigration whose branching mechanism is subcritical and whose immigration mechanism corresponds to spine to explosion birth events. 
This limiting process has a Gamma($\alpha, 1$) stationary distribution and a Markovian time reversal, with an associated coalescent structure governed by a stochastically time-changed Beta($2-\alpha, \alpha$)-coalescent. This essentially describes the genealogies of samples of particles selected uniformly at random near explosion.

talks.speaker: Mr Shahid Khan
talks.title: Testing Diagonal Anisotropy]{Testing Diagonal Anisotropy Based on Single Realisation of Spherical Random Field
talks.abstract:
Spherical data appear in various applications, including cosmology and the Earth sciences. A standard statistical model for such data employs isotropic spherical random fields. The isotropy assumption may be unrealistic for many real-world datasets. Also, in various applications such as cosmology, only a single realisation of the field is observed, making isotropy impossible to assess through repeated sampling. 
This work considers an alternative anisotropic model, referred to as diagonal anisotropy. To test isotropy against diagonal anisotropy, we develop score and cumulative-sum-type tests. Their asymptotic properties and Monte Carlo-based alternatives suitable for moderate sample sizes are established. The performance of the proposed methods is illustrated by numerical studies via applications to simulated data and to actual Planck cosmic microwave background radiation observations. The tests are also applied to three Planck SMICA cosmic microwave background radiation maps and demonstrate how results can vary for different data releases and map construction procedures.

The talk is based on joint research with Andriy Olenko, LaTrobe University, Melbourne.

talks.speaker: Prof Fima Klebaner
talks.authors: Fima Klebaner, with Jeremy Baker, Pavel Chigansky and Peter Jagers
talks.title: On the  Establishment of a mutant.
talks.abstract:
How long does it take for an initially advantageous mutant to 
establish itself in a resident population,  and what does the
population composition look like then? We approach these questions in
the framework of the so called Bare Bones evolution model (Klebaner et al. in J. Biol. Dyn. 5(2):147–162, 2011)
that provides a simplified approach to the adaptive population
dynamics of binary splitting cells. As the mutant 
population grows, cell division becomes less probable,
and it  may in fact turn less likely than that of residents. 

Our analysis rests on the assumption of the process starting from
resident population, with sizes proportional to a large carrying
capacity, $K$. Actually, we assume carrying capacities to be
$a_1K$ and $a_2K$ for the resident and the mutant
populations, respectively, and study the dynamics for $K\to\infty$. We
find conditions for the
mutant to be successful in establishing itself  alongside the
resident. The time it takes turns out to be  proportional to $\log
K$. We introduce the time of establishment through the  asymptotic behaviour 
of the stochastic nonlinear dynamics describing the evolution, and
show that it is indeed $(1/\log \rho)\log K$, where $\rho$ is twice
the probability of successful division of the mutant at its
appearance. Looking at the composition of the population, 
at times $(1/\log \rho)\log K +n, n = 0, 1, 2 \ldots$, we find that
the densities (i.e. sizes relative to carrying capacity) of  
both populations follow closely the corresponding two dimensional
nonlinear deterministic dynamics  that starts at  
{\it a random point}. We characterise this random initial condition
in terms of the scaling limit of the corresponding 
dynamics, and the limit of the properly scaled initial binary splitting process of the mutant. 
These findings complement the ``random shift'' theory for Bare Bones model given in Barbour  et al.  in  Adv. Appl. Probab. 47(4):1190–121, 2015.

talks.speaker: Mr Pavel Krupskiy
talks.title: Parsimonious Factor Models for Asymmetric Dependence in Multivariate Extremes
talks.abstract:
Modelling multivariate extreme events is essential when extrapolating beyond the range of observed data. Parametric models that are suitable for real-world extremes must be  flexible - particularly in their ability to capture  asymmetric dependence structures - while also remaining parsimonious for interpretability and computationally  scalable in high dimensions. Although many models have been  proposed, it is rare for any single construction to satisfy all of these requirements. For instance, the popular 
H\"{u}sler–Reiss model is limited to symmetric dependence structures. In this manuscript, we introduce a class of ad-
ditive factor models and derive their extreme-value limits. This leads to a broad and tractable family of models characterised by a manageable number of parameters. These models naturally accommodate asymmetric tail dependence and allow for non-stationary behaviour. We present the limiting models from both the componentwise-maxima and Peaks-over-Thresholds perspectives, via the multivariate extreme value and multivariate generalized Pareto distributions, respectively. Simulation studies illustrate identifiability properties based on existing inference methodologies. Finally, applications to summer temperature maxima in Melbourne, Australia, and to four air pollutants in Milan, Italy, demonstrate improved fit compared with the 
H\"{u}sler–Reiss model as well as some of the most common asymmetric models.

talks.speaker: Dr Dennis Leung
talks.authors: Kiarash Nikoo, Liqian Zhang and Dennis Leung
talks.title: Sharp bounds on the variance of U-statistics
talks.abstract: We have developed new upper and lower bounds on the variance of U-statistics of any rank that are, surprisingly, uniformly sharper than a pair of analogous bounds established in the original paper on U-statistics by Hoeffding (1948), and in important ways. To the best of our knowledge, our bounds are new to the literature, but a prototype of our upper bound has been hinted in the recent literature on Berry-Esseen bounds for the normal approximation of complete U-statistics. As an additional application, we have applied our new result to improve an existing Berry-Esseen bound on incomplete U-statistics with Bernoulli sampling, when the computational budget is much smaller than the sample size.

talks.speaker: Dr Kevin Lu
talks.title: Discrete dividends after maturity adjust the stock and strike prices
talks.abstract: The standard method to price European calls on a discrete dividend-paying stock is to  subtract the present value of the dividends from the initial stock price in the Black-Scholes formula. However, when there are dividends after maturity, this is inconsistent with the model. Within the escrowed dividend model, we highlight an extension of the Black-Scholes formula in which those  dividends after maturity adjust both the stock price and strike price, allowing for calls over all maturities to be priced in a model-consistent way. As a related application to American calls with a single dividend before maturity, we establish a neglected case where  it is always optimal to early exercise and derive an extension of the Roll-Geske-Whaley formula when there are dividends after maturity, including fully characterising the optimal exercise policy.

talks.speaker: Mr Anant Mathur
talks.title: A Collinearity Test Statistic for Hypothesis Testing in High-Dimensional Generalized Linear Models
talks.abstract: We propose a simple collinearity statistical test for nested model comparison in generalized linear models, with p predictors and sample size n. We show that the collinearity test applies without modification to a wide range of asymptotic relationships between p and n, including the difficult high-dimensional case of p > n. The collinearity test is simple to apply and compute and, unlike some of its competitors, requires neither the solution of a set of nonlinear equations, nor the nonconvex optimization of a partial penalized likelihood. We provide a few numerical examples comparing the test with the classical Wald and likelihood ratio tests. The results suggest that the test enjoys high statistical power across a range of asymptotic regimes and has the highest power when the alternative hypothesis is sparse.

talks.speaker: Prof Terence Mills
talks.title: John Maynard Keynes and Probability
talks.abstract: John Maynard Keynes (1883-1946) was one of the most famous economists of the twentieth century. The phrase "Keynesian economics" is often used. It is not so well known that, at Cambridge University, Keynes studied mathematics, not economics. Indeed one of his earliest publications was "A treatise on probability" which was published in 1921. In this presentation, I will outline his life and his imaginative work on probability.

talks.speaker: Mr Adair Antonio da Silva Neto
talks.authors: Adair Antonio da Silva Neto, Xi Geng, Haiyi Wang, Weijun Xu
talks.title: Favourable islands and eigenfunction decay in the parabolic Anderson model on the hyperbolic plane
talks.abstract:
We study the parabolic Anderson model
$$
	\partial_{t} u = (\Delta + \xi)u, \qquad u(0, \cdot) = 1,
$$
on the hyperbolic plane, where $\xi$ is spatial white noise and the product is defined by renormalisation. We construct the global solution from Dirichlet semigroups and determine its almost-sure long-time growth
$$
	\lim_{ t \to \infty } \frac{\log u(t, o)}{t^{3}} = \frac{4}{27 I^{2}},
$$
where $I$ is the sharp constant in the two-dimensional Euclidean Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality $\lVert f \rVert_{4}^{4} \leq \frac{2}{I} \lVert \nabla f \rVert_{2}^{2} \lVert f \rVert_{2}^{2}$. The growth reflects a competition between exponentially many distant regions in which the noise may be unusually favourable, and the cost of transporting mass to such a region. I will explain how distant favourable islands drive the lower bound, and how the exponential decay of high-energy eigenfunctions gives the matching upper bound. This is based on joint work with Xi Geng, Haiyi Wang, and Weijun Xu.

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Andriy Olenko
talks.title: On spherical anisotropic random fields.
talks.abstract:
General properties of spherical anisotropic random fields will be discussed.  We introduce several classes of anisotropic random fields and present a geometric–spectral classification of second-order anisotropy on the sphere. This framework enables a description of feasible isotropic and anisotropic models and their structural properties. We also examine three classes of composite transformations of isotropic random fields and investigate how these transformations generate and characterise anisotropy. The results provide new insights into the interplay between geometry, spectral representations, and anisotropic behaviour of random fields on the sphere.

The talk is based on joint results with C.Durastanti (Sapienza Universita di Roma, Italy) and S. Khan (La Trobe University, Australia):

Durastanti, C., Khan, S., Olenko, A. (2026). Exploring the Structure of Anisotropic Random Fields on the Sphere. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32538

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Milena Radnovic
talks.title: Finite Groups of Random Walks in the Quarter Plane
talks.abstract:
We discuss a long standing open problem formulated by Malyshev of finding effective, explicit necessary and sufficient conditions in the closed form to characterize all random walks in the quarter plane with a finite group of the
random walk.

talks.speaker: Dr Soudabeh Shemehsavar
talks.authors: Soudabeh Shemehsavar, Graeme Hocking, Ross Maller
talks.title: Stochastic Flight-Path Modelling of Bird Collision Risk at Wind Turbines in Arid Australia
talks.abstract: Wind energy developments pose a collision risk to birds, yet estimating that risk requires models that capture how birds actually move. We present a hybrid probabilistic framework that combines stochastic flight-path models with field data to quantify bird collision risk at wind turbines. Species-specific flight parameters for migratory and resident birds were estimated from direct observations and radar data collected in an arid outback region of Australia.
