Using simulation, we estimated the probability that a bird enters the turbine rotor-sweep area and the expected number of collisions, accounting for both turbine characteristics and variability in flight behavior. Our results indicate that migratory birds with high directional persistence generally face a lower collision risk than resident birds under comparable conditions. By linking individual movement behavior to turbine-level risk, the framework provides a transparent, species-specific basis for environmental impact assessment and for informing turbine siting and mitigation decisions.

talks.speaker: Prof Tomoyuki Shirai
talks.title: Zeros of random power series with stationary Gaussian coefficients
talks.abstract: It is well known that the zeros of a random power series with independent standard complex Gaussian coefficients form a determinantal point process with the Bergman kernel of the unit disk. As a natural generalization of this model, we consider random power series whose coefficients form a centered, stationary complex Gaussian sequence. We study the zero sets of these Gaussian analytic functions and analyze the asymptotic behavior of the mean zero density near the circle of convergence.

talks.speaker: Mr Gleb Smirnov
talks.title: Deep belief networks are exact
talks.abstract:
Sigmoid belief networks are simple generative models from machine learning. They generate a random vector 
in $\{-1,1\}^n$ layer by layer. Each layer is drawn from the previous one using logistic probabilities. Sutskever and Hinton (2008) showed that these networks can approximate any
distribution on $\{-1,1\}^n$ as closely as we like. 
They asked whether they can represent every distribution exactly. We answer yes, for all strictly positive distributions. The proof combines the Sutskever-Hinton construction with Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. 
I will explain the argument and what remains open.

talks.speaker: Dr Caroline Wormell
talks.title: Sampling pseudospectrum for data-driven matrices
talks.abstract:
Many complex systems can be reduced to their key components through spectrally decomposing matrices that capture their dynamics. These matrices can in turn be constructed from data, often by least-squares fitting: common examples of this idea include Dynamical Mode Decomposition and variants, subspace identification and eigenvalue realisation algorithms. Typical outputs of these algorithms include a set of isolated eigenvalues capturing persistent emergent patterns in the system. However, there is no objective way to assess which of these discrete eigenvalues are artefacts of finite data error, and which are reflections of a fully sampled operator.
In this talk I present a sampling pseudospectrum $P(\lambda)$, that provides probabilistic information on the behaviour of finite-data eigenvalues in the complex plane, and an estimator $\hat P(\lambda)$, which can be obtained by reprocessing our finite data sample. The estimator, which is computationally efficient to implement, allows us to test statistically for the location of the true eigenvalues. This gives us a rigorous and very general way to assess whether the patterns we extract from finite data are likely to be signal or noise.

talks.speaker: Dr Kazutoshi Yamazaki
talks.authors: Kei Noba, José Luis Pérez, Kazutoshi Yamazaki, Qingyuan Zhang
talks.title: Continuous-time multi-armed bandits under random intervention times
talks.abstract: This paper examines multi-armed bandits with J independent arms in which actions are taken at random discrete times. When an arm is operated, it must remain active for a renewal inter-arrival time. For arms evolving as a Lévy process, we provide an explicit characterization of the Gittins index, known to yield an optimal strategy. Furthermore, when the inter-arrival times are exponential and the arms evolve as a spectrally negative Lévy process, a reflected spectrally negative Lévy process, or a diffusion process, the Gittins index is explicitly characterized in terms of the scale function or diffusion characteristics, respectively. Convergence analysis and numerical experiments are performed to support the theoretical results.

talks.speaker: Mr Qingyuan Zhang
talks.authors: Zbigniew Palmowski, Kazutoshi Yamazaki, Qingyuan Zhang
talks.title: Exit problems and stationary distributions for self-similar Markov processes with partial resetting
talks.abstract: We study a self-similar Markov process subject to stochastic partial resetting. At the arrival times of an independent Poisson process, the current position is multiplied by a fixed factor c in (0,1). We solve the one- and two-sided exit problems for the resulting process and prove that, under certain conditions, it has a unique stationary distribution, which we characterize through its moments. Explicit expressions are obtained for processes without positive jumps (one-sided exit) and with continuous paths (two-sided exit). Examples, including Brownian motion and positive self-similar Markov processes obtained from Brownian motion with drift via the Lamperti transform, are studied in detail.

talks.speaker: Ms Katharina Arms
talks.title: Representation Gaps, Diagrams and Cryptography
talks.abstract: The linear decomposition attack threatens cryptographic protocols constructed over groups or monoids with low-dimensional linear representations. This talk will present diagram monoids, such as the Temperley--Lieb monoid, and their representation gaps, defined as the smallest dimension of a non-trivial representation. We identify exponential growth in these gaps, which is an initial indicator of suitability for cryptographic protocols withstanding the linear decomposition attack.

talks.speaker: Miss Shurui(Super) CAO
talks.title: Tambara–Yamagami diagrams beyond groups
talks.abstract:
Tambara–Yamagami categories combine a finite group with one extra object. We develop a diagrammatic calculus and study extensions to finite semigroups. The original fusion rules force a group, but restricting the square of the extra object to a group ideal gives new categories whose objects need not have duals. I will explain the construction through small examples and briefly discuss the affine extension, using diagrams on an annulus.

This is joint work with Daniel Tubbenhauer.

talks.speaker: Mr Yuxuan Cheng
talks.title: Deformed graded skew Specht module of affine type A and C
talks.abstract: We construct the graded skew Specht module of the KLR algebra of type $A^{(1)}_e$ and $C^{(1)}_e$ using the seminormal representation theory of the deformed cyclotomic KLR algebras, recently developed by Mathas. We prove that this construction of skew Specht module is isomorphic to the universal skew Specht module that was defined by Muth using the Garnir relation. Under a special assumption, we explicitly  realize Muth's skew cyclotomic KLR algebra by some idempotent truncations.  Together with the theory of seminormal form, this gives us a skew version of branching rules. This is then used in a "truncated" crystal graph which leads to a classification of simples of the skew cyclotomic KLR algebras and some results on graded decomposition numbers.

talks.speaker: Mr Daniel Dunmore
talks.authors: Daniel Dunmore, Anna Romanov, Victor Zhang
talks.title: Lusztig–Vogan Categories of Equal Rank 2
talks.abstract: Lusztig–Vogan categories are module categories over the category of Soergel bimodules. They categorify the principal block of the Lusztig–Vogan module over the Hecke algebra. Just as the Hecke algebra carries information about representations of complex semisimple Lie algebras via the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture, the Lusztig–Vogan module analogously carries information about admissible representations of real reductive groups. Throughout this talk, we will gently introduce algebraic tools that we have developed for the purpose of studying these categories. We will present a concrete demonstration of our techniques in the equal rank 2 setting.

talks.speaker: Mr Tasman Fell
talks.title: Representation Theory and p-Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials
talks.abstract: Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials are known to control decomposition numbers in various categories of representations of algebraic groups. In this talk I will discuss $p$-Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials and their relation to representation categories in prime characteristic. At the end I will discuss and demonstrate how they can be computed.

talks.speaker: Mr Ethan Fursman
talks.title: W-Algebra Representations and Reduction Functors
talks.abstract: Affine W-algebras are algebraic objects which play a central role in modern representation theory. They are constructed from affine vertex algebras using a cohomological functor known as quantum Hamiltonian reduction, or simply ‘reduction’. From the representation theory of W-algebras, one may use reduction functors to study and construct representations of related objects like affine Lie algebras. Unfortunately, few tools exist for working with reduction functors explicitly. In recent work with David Ridout and Justine Fasquel (arXiv:2605.19708), we have developed tools in the rank 1 case, for $$V^k(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$$. This allows us, amongst other things, to understand how certain important families of modules are mapped by the reduction functor in this setting. After reviewing these results, I will discuss some on-going work and preliminary results extending this to a wider family of modules.

talks.speaker: Dr Edmund Xian Chen Heng
talks.authors: Kevin Coulembier, Edmund Heng, Calvin Pfeifer
talks.title: There are more symmetries than you might think
talks.abstract:
We often exploit symmetries to understand and solve problems in mathematics (and beyond). I’d like to convince you that certain transformations that are not invertible are still sufficiently powerful to be called symmetries. In other words, there are more symmetries than just the usual symmetries captured by groups.

In this talk, I will discuss the application of this general idea in the context of representation theory of algebras, and how these more general symmetries can be applied to answer homological algebraic problems. This will be based on recent joint works with Kevin Coulembier and Calvin Pfeifer.

talks.speaker: Mx James Jensen
talks.title: McKay quivers of Hopf algebras
talks.abstract: The McKay quiver associated to a finite group $G$ and a $\mathbb{C}G$-module $V$ is a directed graph encoding how tensor products with $V$ decompose as direct sums of simple modules. By relaxing direct sums to Jordan-Hölder decompositions, this construction makes sense for modular group representations and even modules over finite-dimensional Hopf algebras.  In this talk, I discuss graph-theoretic properties of these generalized McKay quivers and their connection to properties of the underlying Hopf algebra and module.

talks.speaker: Dr Sam Jeralds
talks.title: Reduction rules in representation theory
talks.abstract: In algebraic combinatorics or representation theory, reduction rules give equalities between some quantity (a dimension, a multiplicity, etc) to a similar quantity arising from a "smaller" source. To develop and apply reduction rules, we first need to understand (1) when such reductions can be applied, and (2) to what smaller case we can reduce to. In this talk, we'll give an overview of many such reduction rules in representation theory, along with their common source in geometric representation theory, with specific focus on recent results giving reduction rules for Demazure module characters.

talks.speaker: Mr Peter Karapalidis
talks.title: Representation theory of rank 2 W-algebras at integral levels
talks.abstract:
Vertex operator algebras are algebraic objects that are of broad interest across the mathematics and physics literature. Notably, they serve as a rigorous axiomatisation of two-dimensional conform field theory. W-algebras are a specific class of VOA from whose representation theory one can study that of other related objects such as affine Lie algebras. Unfortunately, what general techniques exist to study this representation theory fail when the level of the W-algebra has small enough denominator.

In this talk, I will discuss the representation theory of the W-algebra $W_k(\mathfrak{sp}_4,f_{subreg})$ at integer levels $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq -1}$. In particular, I will present the classification of its irreducible modules, and then discuss some preliminary results concerning its reducible but indecomposable modules.

talks.speaker: Dr Dilpreet Kaur
talks.title: Conjugacy Classes and Irreducible Representations of a Finite Group
talks.abstract: It is a well-known fact that for a finite group $G,$ the number of conjugacy classes is the same as the number of irreducible inequivalent representations of $G.$ However, there is no known bijective map between these two sets. In this talk, we discuss the connection between various properties of conjugacy classes and irreducible representations of a finite group. This talk is based on my joint work with Amit Kulshrestha, Anupam Singh, Sushil Bhunia, and Saikat Panja.

talks.speaker: Mr Finn Klein
talks.title: Towards a "modular modular branching rule" for symmetric groups
talks.abstract:
The One Tree Island (OTI) functor $\Phi$, introduced (in the symmetric group setting) by Hone, Pauwels, Sherman, Yacobi,
Zhang and the speaker, restricts a representation of $S_n$ to
$S_{n-p}\times C_p$ and semisimplifies the $C_p$-action. It commutes with the categorical $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_p$-action on $\bigoplus_n \operatorname{Rep}_k S_n$ and decategorifies to $e^p$ on the mod-$p$ Grothendieck group. In ongoing work with Tao Qin (MPIM Bonn), we study the composition multiplicities $[\Phi(D^\lambda): D^\mu]$ modulo $p$, where $\lambda \vdash n$ and $\mu \vdash n-p$ are $p$-regular partitions and $D^\lambda, D^\mu$ are the corresponding simple modules. Understanding these multiplicities would give a ``modular'' (mod $p$) version of Kleshchev's modular branching rules.

In this talk, we will explain some (but not all) of the irreducible constituents of $\Phi(D^\lambda)$ via a combinatorial game on two copies of the crystal graph.
We also present new findings on Jordan blocks of even size appearing in $\Phi(D^\lambda)$, which currently lie beyond the explanatory reach of the crystal rules.

talks.speaker: Dr Yixuan Li
talks.title: Real Group Interpretation of Certain Affine Springer Fibers
talks.abstract: It is Cartan’s discovery that there is a complex projective variety structure on a compact Lie group $K$ (e.g. $U(n)$) modulo a maximal torus $T$. Indeed, let $G$ be the complexification of $K$ (e.g. $GL(n,\mathbf{C}$), the inclusion from $K$ to $G$ induces a diffeomorphism from $K/T$ to the flag variety $G/B$. There are also loop group versions of this result, where the affine grassmannian of $G$ is diffeomorphic to the manifold of based real algebraic loops in $K$. Donaldson gave a gauge theoretic interpretation of this fact as an example of Kobayashi-Hitchin correspondence. In this talk we seek to generalize this further to certain affine Springer fibers, leaving the gauge theory interpretation as an ongoing open direction.

talks.speaker: Mr Dominic Matan
talks.title: The Sarkisov program for mildly noncommutative surfaces
talks.abstract: The minimal model program tells us that to classify varieties of a given dimension we should first find some best representatives in each birational class. These representatives need not be unique, so the next question is how they relate to one another. For Mori fibre spaces, the Sarkisov program answers this: any two in the same birational class are connected by a sequence of elementary birational maps called Sarkisov links. In this talk, we will see how this extends to terminal orders on surfaces, which are mildly noncommutative analogues of smooth surfaces. As an application, we will construct division algebras over function fields of surfaces with the smallest possible $\mathbb{C}$-automorphism group.

talks.speaker: Mr Joseph Newton
talks.title: Lie algebras in the Verlinde category
talks.abstract: In this talk, I will describe a combinatorial approach to studying algebraic structures in the semisimple Verlinde category. This can be used to obtain a complete classification of simple Lie algebras of length at most 3 in this category, along with some incomplete computational results for higher lengths. I will discuss the various ways in which these Lie algebras can be constructed, and highlight several cases which give counterexamples to conjectures regarding semisimple symmetric tensor categories in positive characteristic.

talks.speaker: Mr Jacques du Plooy
talks.title: Cyclic subgroups of type A Hecke algebras
talks.abstract: The Iwahori-Hecke algebra of type $A$ at a $p$-th root of unity $q$ is a characteristic zero analogue of the symmetric group algebra of order $n$ in characteristic $p$. Many constructions in characteristic $p$ rely on the existence of a cyclic subgroup of order $p$ inside the symmetric group. We construct a well-behaved analogue of the group algebra generated by a $p$-cycle in $H_n(q) $ when $n\ge p$ and apply this to  the construction of interesting functors which commute with non-degenerate categorical Heisenberg actions, including on $\bigoplus\limits_{n=0}^\infty H_n(q)-mod$.

talks.speaker: Dr Christopher Raymond
talks.authors: Christopher Raymond j.w. Dimitar Grantcharov and David Ridout
talks.title: Inverse hamiltonian reduction and infinite-dimensional weight spaces
talks.abstract: Inverse hamiltonian reduction is a new method for constructing modules over vertex operator algebras (VOAs). In particular, it gives a way of constructing the simple objects and modular data for nonsemisimple and nonfinite generalisations of modular tensor categories that play a role in physics. One interesting feature is that this method naturally builds simple weight modules with infinite-dimensional weight spaces. Using the correspondence between affine VOAs and finite simple Lie algebras, it builds analogous modules for the latter also, and gives tools for their analysis. This talk will introduce the inverse hamiltonian reduction method and discuss recent progress in its application to representation theory.

talks.speaker: Prof David Ridout
talks.title: Representations of affine vertex operator algebras and W-algebras
talks.abstract: Vertex algebras occupy an increasingly important place in modern representation theory and mathematical physics.  Some of the most accessible examples are based on affine Kac--Moody algebras.  These affine vertex algebras, along with their W-algebras, have beautiful representation theories.  In particular, they admit module categories that are tensor, braided and often even modular (but usually non-finite and non-semisimple).  This talk will discuss some of what is known and try to explain how much we still don't know.

talks.speaker: Miss Tanisha Talekar
talks.title: Combinatorics of Bridgeland stability conditions on 2-CY categories
talks.abstract: Certain Bridgeland stability conditions on the 2-CY category of type $A$ induce a convex order on the root system of the underlying quiver. These stability conditions can also be realised geometrically as configurations of points in the Euclidean plane, giving rise to combinatorial structures such as pseudoline arrangements and also complexes of pointed-pseudotriangulations. Independently, convex orders give rise to certain subword complexes, and in this talk we will establish a correspondence between the two simplicial complexes. We also expect (work in progress) to show that this correspondence holds for degenerate cases.

talks.speaker: Prof Ole Warnaar
talks.title: The CMPP conjecture
talks.abstract: An important class of representations of affine Lie algebras are the standard or integrable highest weight modules. Finding bases for standard modules is generally a difficult problem that is still open in many cases. Recently, Capparelli, Meurman, Primc and Primc (CMPP) introduced a beautiful new combinatorial `model' that, conjecturally, sheds new light on the problem of finding bases for standard modules. In this talk I will describe some of the work of CMPP as well as extensions pertaining to affine Lie superalgebras.

talks.speaker: Mr Bailey Whitbread
talks.title: A Deligne-Simpson problem
talks.abstract: There is an old problem about matrices called the Deligne–Simpson problem. This talk is about a younger geometric version. With Masoud Kamgarpour, we solve this problem in all open cases, by exploiting a connection between connections and braids.

talks.speaker: Mr Victor Zhang
talks.title: Diagrammatic Lusztig--Vogan categories
talks.abstract: The Kazhdan--Lusztig conjecture (1979) relates the decomposition numbers of complex semisimple Lie algebra representations in terms of a special change of basis in the Hecke algebra. In a subsequent proof of the conjecture, a complete diagrammatic language was developed for the categorification of the Hecke algebra, the category of Soergel bimodules, following the effort of various people throughout the 2000s and 2010s. The theory of real reductive Lie groups carries a result analogous to the KL-conjecture by Lusztig and Vogan (1983), that the Lusztig--Vogan modules over the Hecke algebra capture composition multiplicities of $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-modules. We will motivate these diagrammatic tools in mathematics and present the beginnings of a diagrammatic theory for a categorification of these Lusztig--Vogan modules.

talks.speaker: Prof Luca Scarpa
talks.authors: Andrea Di Primio, Andrea Papini, Luca Scarpa
talks.title: Stochastic phase-separation driven by transport noise
talks.abstract:
We propose a stochastic Cahn--Hilliard model driven by transport noise in order to describe phase-separation phenomena occurring in mixtures of turbulent fluids. The model is analysed in its thermodynamically-relevant framework, namely employing a singular Flory--Huggins potential and a possibly degenerate mobility, and the noise is considered both in It\^o and Stratonovich form. As a first-step investigation, we establish well-posedness of the system in two and three spatial dimensions and its thermodynamical consistency. Several further developments are also discussed.
The works presented in the talk are based on joint collaborations with Andrea Di Primio (Scuola Normale Superiore, Pisa, Italy) and Andrea Papini (University of Gothenburg, Sweden).

talks.speaker: Dr Marco Carfagnini
talks.title: sub-Riemannian random waves on $\mathbb{S}^{3}$
talks.abstract:
It is known that, after rescaling, random superposition or spherical harmonics converges to a random field on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The limiting field, introduced by Berry in the 70s, consists of generalized random eigenfunctions for the Laplace operator. 

In this talk, we consider a sub-Riemannian structure on $\mathbb{S}^{3}$ and study the limiting behavior of superpositions of random eigenfunctions for a degenerate spherical operator. We prove that the limiting field is the Berry-Heisenberg random field on the Heisenberg group $\mathbb{H}$, introduced by the first author.

talks.speaker: Dr Andreia Chapouto
talks.authors: Andreia Chapouto, Jiawei Li, Tadahiro Oh
talks.title: Pathwise well-posedness of stochastic nonlinear wave equations with multiplicative noises
talks.abstract:
Over the last decades, the well-posedness issue of stochastic dispersive PDEs with multiplicative noises has been extensively studied. However, this study was done primarily from the viewpoint of Ito solution theory, and pathwise well-posedness remained completely open. 
In this talk, I will present the first pathwise well-posedness results for stochastic nonlinear wave equations (SNLW) with multiplicative white-in-time/coloured-in-space noise. Here, we combine the operator-value controlled rough paths adapted to dispersive flows, together with random tensor estimates, and the Fourier restriction norm method adapted to controlled rough paths.

talks.speaker: Dr Justin Forlano
talks.title: Almost sure global well-posedness for the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation
talks.abstract: I will discuss a recent result on the almost sure global well-posedness for the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation (BBM) with random initial data. We prove that BBM is almost surely globally well-posed in the full probabilistically well-posed range. This improves on a previous result of the author which established this only in a logarithmically negative regularity. To break through this logarithmic regularity barrier, I will discuss a new globalisation argument which combines (i) the I-method, (ii) the low-high argument from Bona-Tzvetkov (2007), and (iii) a refined first-order expansion for solutions.

talks.speaker: Dr Xi Geng
talks.title: Global well-posedness of parabolic Anderson model on surfaces
talks.abstract: In this talk, we discuss a simple elementary proof of the global well-posedness of the singular parabolic Anderson model with white noise potential on a 2D Riemannian manifold without using the theory of regularity structures or paracontrolled calculus. Our approach is in spirit close to the approach of Hairer-Labb\'e in 2015 in the Euclidean case. The main novel point is the use of super-exponential weights and multi-scale product estimates, which allows one to handle the situation where the underlying space has exponential volume growth. This is based on ongoing joint work with A. da Silva Neto (University of Melbourne), H. Wang (Peking University) and W. Xu (Westlake University).

talks.speaker: Assoc Prof Quoc Thong Le Gia
talks.authors: Quoc Thong Le Gia, Ben Goldys, Holger Wendland
talks.title: Approximation of the stochastic Allen-Cahn equations on the unit sphere with radial basis functions
talks.abstract:
We develop and analyse meshless radial-basis-function approximations for deterministic and stochastic Allen--Cahn equations on the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{n}$. The spatial discretization is constructed using spherical radial basis functions generated by positive definite kernels. Approximation properties for the associated trial spaces and Ritz projection are established and used to derive spatial error estimates for the semi-discrete problem.

For the deterministic equation, we introduce a fully discrete convex-splitting scheme. The implicit treatment of the cubic term yields a strongly monotone and coercive nonlinear algebraic problem at every time step. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the method converges with spatial order $h^{\nu}$ and first-order temporal accuracy.

We then consider the stochastic Allen--Cahn equation with additive Wiener noise. Regularity estimates for the stochastic solution are established under appropriate Sobolev and moment assumptions. The corresponding radial-basis-function semi-discretization is shown to converge in the mean-square sense
with spatial order $h^{\nu}$. Finally, a convex-splitting Euler--Maruyama method is analysed, yielding the strong convergence rate $O(h^{\nu}+\tau^{1/2})$.

Numerical experiments on scattered points on the sphere illustrate the theoretical convergence behaviour and demonstrate the practical applicability of the proposed method.

talks.speaker: Prof Beniamin Goldys
talks.title: Maximum Principle for stochastic Ginzburg-Landau equation in 2D
talks.abstract:
The Maximum Principle is a fundamental and powerful tool in the analysis of partial differential equations (PDEs). However, it generally fails for systems of PDEs and is rarely satisfied by stochastic PDEs, even in the scalar case.
In this talk, we consider the two-dimensional stochastic Ginzburg–Landau equation driven by transport noise (GL), a parabolic stochastic system with nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and polynomial nonlinearities. We show that this system satisfies a Maximum Principle. We also establish  $C^{2+\alpha}$ spatial regularity of its solutions, a result that is of independent interest.
Our main motivation comes from the fact that, in the large-drift limit, solutions to GL approximate the motion of random vortices arising in superconducting fluids.

talks.speaker: Prof Erika Hausenblas
talks.authors: Erika Hausenblas, Debopriya Mukherjee, Chunxi Jiao
talks.title: Stochastic Non-Darcy Transport in Porous Media with Concentration-Dependent Mobility
talks.abstract:
In this talk, we introduce a single-phase, two-component miscible
displacement model for enhanced oil recovery in porous media. An injected
solvent mixes with the resident oil and changes the viscosity of the
mixture. Consequently, the fluid mobility depends on the solvent
concentration.

Let $\mathcal U\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded domain with Lipschitz
boundary $\partial\mathcal U$, representing the porous medium, and let
$[0,T]$ be the time interval of the displacement process. We denote by
$c$ the solvent concentration, by $p$ the pressure, and by
$\kappa(c)$ the concentration-dependent mobility. In the simplest case,
\[
\kappa(c)=\frac{K}{\mu(c)},
\]
where $K$ is the permeability of the porous medium and $\mu(c)$ is the
viscosity of the mixture.

The flow is described by a nonlinear coupled elliptic--parabolic system.
The pressure satisfies an elliptic equation with source--sink term $g$,
whereas the solvent concentration satisfies a stochastic
transport--diffusion equation. More precisely,
\begin{align}
	\mathrm{d}c(t)
	&=
	\Bigl[
	r\Delta c(t)
	+\operatorname{div}\bigl(
	\kappa(c(t))c(t)\nabla p(t)
	\bigr)
	\Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t
	+\Sigma(c(t))\,\mathrm{d}W(t),
	\label{eq:concentration}
	\\
	-\operatorname{div}\bigl(
	\kappa(c(t))\nabla p(t)
	\bigr)
	&=g(t).
	\label{eq:pressure}
\end{align}
These equations are supplemented with the no-flux boundary conditions
\begin{align}
	\nabla c(t)\cdot n&=0
	&&\text{on }\partial\mathcal U,
	\label{eq:boundary-c}
	\\
	\kappa(c(t))\nabla p(t)\cdot n&=0
	&&\text{on }\partial\mathcal U,
	\label{eq:boundary-p}
\end{align}
and the initial condition
\begin{equation}
	c(0)=c_0.
\end{equation}

We first establish the existence of a solution to the stochastic system.
We then explain how the proof strategy can be extended to a more general
nonlinear model in which the Laplacian is replaced by a nonlinear
diffusion operator, such as the $q$-Laplacian, and Darcy's law is replaced
by a nonlinear Darcy law. Finally, we present numerical simulations
illustrating the effect of the stochastic forcing on the dynamics.

talks.speaker: Dr Chunxi Jiao
talks.authors: Chunxi Jiao, Agus Soenjaya and Thanh Tran
talks.title: Two thin-film limits of stochastic Landau Lifshitz equations
talks.abstract: The competition between exchange energy and magnetostatic energy in a thin-film domain can lead to different asymptotic regimes of magnetisation dynamics. In the absence of noise, the limiting equations have previously been derived from the Gilbert form of the Landau-Lifshitz equation, by taking advantage of $L^2$ estimates for time derivatives. As expected, the same limits follow from the equivalent Landau-Lifshitz form, which opens a door to an extension to the stochastic case. We show that under suitable spatial structure and intensity scaling of the noise, a sequence of weak martingale solutions of 3D stochastic Landau-Lifshitz equations converges in law to a stochastic harmonic map heat flow in the over-damped regime, and to a stochastic inertial Landau-Lifshitz equation in the weak-damping wave regime. This talk is based on joint work with Agus Soenjaya (TU Wien) and Thanh Tran (UNSW).

talks.speaker: Dr Debopriya Mukherjee
talks.authors: Debopriya Mukherjee, Zdzislaw Brzezniak, Sandip Roy
talks.title: Wellposedness and the existence of a random attractor for a stochastic nonlinear damped Schr\"odinger equation
talks.abstract: We study the long-time behaviour of the defocusing stochastic nonlinear damped Schr\"odinger equation on $\mathbb{R}^d$  with additive noise in the energy-subcritical regime. Under the restrictions $\frac12\leq \sigma<\frac{2}{d-2}$ for $d\in{3,4,5}$ and $\frac12\leq\sigma<\infty$ for $d\leq2$, we first establish existence and uniqueness of global mild solutions in the natural Strichartz space. Our approach is based on a stationary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck transformation, deterministic and stochastic Strichartz estimates, a Banach fixed-point theorem, and a perturbation technique. Using the stationary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process and the global well-posedness, we establish the existence of a random dynamical system  in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$.  Next, we establish its weak continuity with respect to initial data, which plays a crucial role (as an alternative of compact embeddings) in the proof of asymptotic compactness of the RDS. We then combine dissipative estimates with an energy method to prove the existence of bounded random absorbing sets and asymptotic compactness, overcoming the lack of compact Sobolev embeddings on the unbounded domain.

talks.speaker: Dr Kihun Nam
talks.authors: Yining Ding, Kihun Nam, Jiaqiang Wen
talks.title: Quadratic Mean-Field BSDEs and Exponential Utility Maximisation
talks.abstract: We study a class of real-valued mean-field backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) with generators of quadratic growth in the control variable and the mean-field term. For bounded terminal conditions satisfying suitable structural regularity, we establish existence and uniqueness under two complementary quadratic regimes; the uniformly continuous path-dependent case additionally requires a uniform quadratic bound on the normalised generator. Our approach for these results combines Malliavin calculus with refined BMO and stability estimates. Motivated by a mean-field exponential utility maximisation problem, we further extend our framework to terminal conditions without imposing continuity or Markovian structure on the terminal condition. Under a suitable smallness condition on the oscillation of the terminal value around its mean, we establish existence and uniqueness in an explicitly specified small solution class. We then apply to a mean-field exponential utility maximisation problem.

talks.speaker: Prof Max Nendel
talks.authors: Max Nendel; Ariel Neufeld; Kyunghyun Park; Alessandro Sgarabottolo
talks.title: Scaling limits of multi-period distributionally robust optimization problems
talks.abstract: We examine the scaling limit of multi-period distributionally robust optimization (DRO) problems via a semigroup approach.\ Each period involves a worst-case maximization over distributions in a Wasserstein ball around the transition probability of a reference process with radius proportional to the length of the period, and the multi-period DRO problem arises through its sequential composition. We show that the scaling limit of the multi-period DRO, as the length of each period tends to zero, is a strongly continuous monotone semigroup on $\mathrm{C_b}$.\ Furthermore, we show that its infinitesimal generator is equal to the generator associated with the non-robust scaling limit plus an additional perturbation term induced by the Wasserstein uncertainty.\ As an application, we show that when the reference process follows an It\^o process, the viscosity solution of the associated nonlinear PDE coincides with the value of continuous-time robust optimization problems under parametric uncertainty.

talks.speaker: Mr Adair Antonio da Silva Neto
talks.authors: Marco Carfagnini, Adair Antonio da Silva Neto, Xi Geng
talks.title: Fluctuation Asymptotics for the Parabolic Anderson Model on the Heisenberg Group
talks.abstract: The Parabolic Anderson Model is a stochastic heat equation known for its intermittent behaviour and nontrivial long-time fluctuations. While the discrete setting is by now well understood, much less is known in the continuum. In this talk, we investigate the model on the Heisenberg group and analyse the variational problem determining the fluctuation constant. The results reveal how the sub-Riemannian structure and noncommutative geometry influence the asymptotic behaviour of the solution.

talks.speaker: Dr Akash Ashirbad Panda
talks.authors: Akash Ashirbad Panda, Xiaobing Feng, Madepalli Sekharu
talks.title: Gaussian Approximation of Small Jumps in Lévy-Driven Stochastic Heat Equations: Strong and Fully Discrete Error Analysis
talks.abstract:
We study the strong numerical approximation of a semilinear stochastic heat
equation driven by multiplicative infinite-activity L\'evy noise. The L\'evy
process is decomposed into small- and large-jump components: the large jumps
are retained explicitly, while the cumulative effect of the small jumps is
approximated by a variance-matched Gaussian term. Particular attention is
given to the strong error introduced by this Gaussian replacement and its
dependence on the truncation parameter.

We further develop a fully discrete approximation based on an exponential
Euler method in time and finite elements in space, and derive mean-square
error estimates that separate the contributions from the small-jump
approximation, temporal discretization, and spatial discretization. For
stable-like L\'evy measures, the analysis provides explicit convergence rates
and suitable relations between the truncation, time-step, and mesh
parameters. Numerical experiments illustrate the influence of the small
jumps and support the theoretical convergence behavior.

talks.speaker: Dr Upanshu Sharma
talks.authors: Frederic Legoll, Lara Neureither, Upanshu Sharma
talks.title: Nonlinear phase-space constrained Langevin dynamics
talks.abstract: Sampling probability measures on submanifolds is an important task in molecular dynamics. This is typically achieved by either imposing either soft constraints, encoded via a scale separation parameter, or hard constraints, enforced through Lagrange multipliers, on stochastic differential equations. In this talk I present recent results on the soft-constrained Langevin dynamics. A central difficulty here is that the Langevin dynamics evolves on the phase space, while typical constraints of interest are only imposed on the spatial variables. This talk will discuss an appropriate choice for corresponding phase-space constraints and derives the soft-constrained limit as the soft-constraint parameter tends to zero.

talks.speaker: Dr Ho Man Tai
talks.authors: Ho Man Tai, Paolo Guasoni and Emmet Lawless
talks.title: Consumption and investment in stochastic environments
talks.abstract: In this talk, we discuss the optimal consumption-investment problems in incomplete markets, where the investor aims to maximise a general utility from consumption over an infinite time horizon. We introduce different approaches of how the optimal strategies can be characterised.

talks.speaker: Dr Zhou Zhou
talks.title: Existence of Markov relaxed equilibria for time-inconsistent control in continuous time
talks.abstract: We consider time-inconsistent stochastic control problems in continuous time and investigate the existence of intra-personal Markov relaxed equilibrium strategies. We equip the space of relaxed strategies with the stable topology of Young measures and establish the stability of value functions and their derivatives under Young-measure convergence of strategies. We then construct a set-valued best-response map with nonempty, compact, and convex values and apply the Kakutani–Fan–Glicksberg fixed-point theorem to establish the existence of a relaxed equilibrium. Finally, we extend our analysis to establish the existence of time-consistent relaxed equilibrium strategies for time-inconsistent mean-field games.

talks.speaker: Mr Huateng Zhu
talks.title: Convergence analysis of stochastic Leray-Lions equation
talks.abstract:
We analyse a divergence form stochastic differential equation featuring a Leray-Lions flux function that satisfies standard Carath\'eodory, growth, monotonicity, and coercivity conditions.
    We consider two types of noise: multiplicative Lipschitz continuous noise and a transport noise.
    Our approach utilises the gradient discretisation method, a generic framework encompassing various numerical schemes such as conforming and nonconforming finite element methods, hybrid mimetic mixed methods, and hybrid high order methods.
    For both types of noise, 
    we propose a stable generic scheme,
    prove that scheme solutions  converge to a strong solution in the probabilistic sense.

talks.speaker: Mr Daniel Bruwel
talks.authors: Daniel Bruwel, Keeley Hoek, Ashvni Narayanan, Jonathan Spreer
talks.title: Using Transformers to Generate 3-Manifold Triangulations
talks.abstract: Randomly gluing tetrahedra almost never produces a 3-manifold: for 10 tetrahedra, we found no closed manifolds among a billion random gluings. We train GPT-2-style transformers on dehydration signatures of 3-sphere triangulations and find that they generate valid triangulations at very high rates and closed manifolds at rates many orders of magnitude above random sampling. Using IsoFLOP experiments on 15-tetrahedron triangulations, we observe neural scaling behavior, with optimal model size growing roughly as the square root of compute. Despite training only on spheres, the models also produce lens spaces, $S^2\times S^1$ and connected sums, and the fraction of non-sphere closed outputs stays roughly constant across model scales.

talks.speaker: Ms Natalie DiMichele
talks.title: Detecting Normal Surfaces with Benders Decomposition
talks.abstract: Detecting normal surfaces can provide answers to many topological questions. We will cover some normal surface theory, specifically the requirements for a vector to represent a normal surface. Then, we will discuss algorithmic approaches to finding normal surfaces. In particular, we will focus on a Benders Decomposition algorithm and look into more operations research tricks which have been tuned to the problem.

talks.speaker: Mr Alexander Elzenaar
talks.title: Teichmueller space and knots
talks.abstract: We present some recent work connecting the deformation theory of infinite covolume Kleinian groups to the structure (both combinatorial and geometric) of certain families of hyperbolic links, including fully augmented links, 2-bridge links, and links with unknotting tunnels.

talks.speaker: Dr Gianluca Faraco
talks.title: Real Branched projective structures on surfaces
talks.abstract: In this seminar, I introduce branched real projective structures on surfaces. We discuss the geometrisation process and show that every representation of the fundamental group of a compact surface into PSL(3,R) arises as the holonomy representation of a branched real projective structure, regardless of whether the surface is orientable. This is a joint work with Nicholas Rungi.

talks.speaker: Dr Alexander He
talks.title: Algorithmic recognition of bounded orientable Seifert fibred spaces using crushing
talks.abstract:
Seifert fibred spaces play an important role in the classification of 3-manifolds.
In particular, the JSJ decomposition gives a canonical collection of tori in any irreducible 3-manifold, such that each piece resulting from cutting along these tori is either atoroidal or Seifert fibred.
How efficiently can a computer recognise a triangulation of a Seifert fibred space?
For orientable 3-manifolds with non-empty boundary, the best known theoretical answer is due to Jackson (2024), who showed that (bounded orientable) Seifert fibred space recognition is in NP;
however, it is not feasible to implement or run Jackson's algorithm on an actual computer.
This talk will outline a new algorithm for this recognition problem, developed in joint work with Eric Sedgwick and Jonathan Spreer, which not only recovers Jackson's NP result, but also performs remarkably well in practice on a wide range of inputs.

talks.speaker: Dr Teresa Heiss-Synak
talks.authors: Bea Bleile, Adélie Garin, Teresa Heiss-Synak, Kelly Maggs, Vanessa Robins
talks.title: Topological Data Analysis for Images: Persistent Homology and the Choice of Pixel Connectivity
talks.abstract:
Suppose you want to count the connected components and holes of a binary (black-and-white) digital image, that is, compute its homology. Or suppose you have a greyscale image: you can threshold it to obtain a binary image and track how components and holes appear and disappear as the threshold varies. This is persistent homology.

Firstly, you have to decide which pixels count as adjacent, in particular whether diagonally adjacent pixels do. There are two standard choices: in 2D, 8-connectivity for the foreground with 4-connectivity for the background, or the other way round. Depending on the application, either may be the right one. Secondly, you have to choose software to compute (persistent) homology, and most persistent homology software supports only one of the two choices.

We show how to compute persistent homology with respect to either choice using software designed for the other. As a topologist might expect, the key is a duality: invert the image and reflect the homological degree. However, extra care is needed because the duality fails at the image boundary.

talks.speaker: Dr Edmund Xian Chen Heng
talks.title: Pick-up sticks (Mikado) and braids
talks.abstract:
Mikado (aka: Pick-up sticks, Jack straws etc.) is an old school board game that goes as follows. You begin by dropping a bunch of sticks on the ground. The rule is that you are only allowed to pick up one stick at a time, and in the process you are not allowed to move any other sticks. In other words, you have to pick up a stick that has no other sticks lying on top of it.

Braids are less rigid than sticks, but the same concept can be applied. Start with a braid $\beta$ with $n$-strands. If there exists a strand that has no strand lying on top of it, we can remove it to obtain a braid $\beta’$ with $n-1$ strands. If this process can be repeated until there are no strands left, the braid $\beta$ is called a Mikado braid.

In this talk, I will talk about how Mikado braids are related to paths in hyperplane arrangements. If time allows, I will give a fundamental groupoid description of this concept. This is based on an ongoing Honours project with my student Takaya Ueno.

talks.speaker: Mr William Hobkirk
talks.title: Z3-folded surfaces and the complexity of lens spaces
talks.abstract: In this talk, we introduce $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surfaces -- geometric representatives of classes in $H_2(M;\mathbb{Z}_3)$ for a $3$-manifold $M$. We define the $\mathbb{Z}_3$-Thurston “norm”, which measures the minimum complexity of these representatives. This function generalises the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-Thurston norm and provides information about triangulations of $M$. We determine the $\mathbb{Z}_3$-Thurston norm for the family of lens spaces $L(3n,1)$, uncovering some interesting properties of $\mathbb{Z}_3$-folded surfaces along the way. As a corollary, we show that any triangulation of $L(3n,1)$ must have at least $n$ tetrahedra. A refinement of this approach determines the exact minimum number of tetrahedra required to triangulate these spaces, in joint work with Jonathan Spreer.

talks.speaker: Dr Connie On Yu HUI
talks.title: When topologists learn algebraic number theory
talks.abstract: I would like to share a journey of how we started learning algebraic number theory when studying spinors and inter-cusp distances of arithmetic link complements. A beautiful result that relates the two fields is that the number of ends of a Bianchi orbifold $\mathbb{H}^3/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathcal{O}_d)$ is the same as the class number of the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_d$. If time permits, I will share a simple and clean argument of this theorem and its generalised version, and how these can help us understand spinors and inter-cusp distances of arithmetic link complements. This is based on an ongoing collaboration with Daniel Mathews, Joshua Howie, Nicola Harif, Dionne Ibarra, and Lecheng Su.

talks.speaker: Dr Dionne Ibarra
talks.authors: Dionne Ibarra, Daniel V. Mathews, Jessica S. Purcell, Jonathan Spreer
talks.title: Triangulations of the 3-sphere with knotted edge
talks.abstract: A classical result in combinatorial topology states that the presence of knotted edges in a triangulated 3-sphere may cause an obstruction to properties like shellability and constructibility. These properties tell us how computationally friendly a triangulation is. Historically, explicit examples of triangulations with complicated knotted edges have been difficult to construct and were limited to special families of knots. In this talk we will discuss how we used knot theory to overcome the difficulty of constructing triangulations that obstruct Shellability and Constructibility. In particular, by using the techniques of fully augmented links we show that for any knot in the 3-sphere, there is a 1-vertex triangulation of the 3-sphere with an edge forming the knot. (This is joint work with Daniel V. Mathews, Jessica S. Purcell, and Jonathan Spreer).

talks.speaker: Mr Tianyou Ma
talks.title: The integral cohomology of smooth abelian symplectic quotients
talks.abstract: Let a torus $T$ act on a compact symplectic manifold $M$, freely on the zero level set of the moment map, so that the symplectic quotient $M/\!/T$ is a manifold. Pomerleano and Teleman recently proved that the Kirwan map $H^*_T(M;\mathbb{Z})\to H^*(M/\!/T;\mathbb{Z})$ is surjective. I will describe its kernel, extending the rational description of Tolman and Weitsman, and discuss examples where the integral picture differs from the rational one.

talks.speaker: Mr Joel Richardson
talks.title: Converting braids into loops
talks.abstract: Homomorphic expansions, a kind of invariant from low-dimensional topology, sometimes encode interesting algebraic structures. In particular, expansions of braid groups are closely related to Drinfel'd associators, and those of the Goldman--Turaev Lie bialgebras of loops in punctured disks are closely related to solutions of the Kashiwara--Vergne equations. In this talk, we retell the story of how Drinfel'd associators induce Kashiwara--Vergne solutions by transforming braid groups into Goldman--Turaev Lie bialgebras using only homomorphic expansion compatible operations.

talks.speaker: Mr Siddharth Shrivastava
talks.title: Kirby diagrams for an infinite family of exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$'s
talks.abstract: Exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$'s are smooth manifolds that are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to the standard $\mathbb{R}^4$. Eli, Hom, and Lidman showed that the manifolds produced by attaching the simplest positive Casson handle $CH^+$ to a slice disc complement of the ribbon knot $T_{2,n}\#T_{2,-n}$ for $n\ge3$ and odd, and removing the boundary, form a countably infinite family of exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$'s. They provided a Kirby diagram for the case $n=3$. We extend this for $n\ge3$ and odd, and provide Kirby diagrams for two such families of exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$'s, which are then shown to be equivalent. We then generalise these diagrams to a family of exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$'s built using ribbon disc complements of the pretzel knots $P(n,-n,2k)$.

talks.speaker: Miss Finn Thompson
talks.authors: Finn Thompson, Agnese Barbensi, Daniele Celoria, Lavender Marshall
talks.title: The graph of grid moves as a knot invariant
talks.abstract: Motivated by the monotonic simplification of grid diagrams of unknots due to Dynnikov, we explore the sequences of moves between two grid diagrams of the same knot. We describe the graph associated to grid diagrams of each knot type, where vertices represent grid diagrams, and are connected by an edge if they are related by a grid move. We determine a colouring of the edges that allows us to recognise the moves performed along edges. By analysing particular cycles and walks in a finite section of the graph, we aim to reconstruct a minimal grid diagram of the knot.

talks.speaker: Mr Chengjing Zhang
talks.title: Topological quadratic forms on locally compact Hausdorff modules
talks.abstract:
I will discuss topological quadratic forms on locally compact Hausdorff modules over locally compact Hausdorff rings, as an analogue of quadratic forms over rings. In particular, I will describe the Witt group of topological quadratic forms
over finite fields, integers, and p-adic integers, and explain how they are related to quadratic forms over the real numbers and p-adic numbers.
